opening: Hi, I'm X. I spoke with your office about a property tax dispute — I was hoping you could help me figure out my options.

facts.client_belief: I bought a one-bedroom condominium in Lakewood City back in 1999 and lived there alone for over a decade.
facts.court_record: The client purchased the Lakewood City condominium in 1999 and resided there until approximately 2010. The fact of her sole ownership and long-term residence is undisputed.

facts.client_belief: In 2010, my family and I decided I'd be safer in a senior community, so I moved out of the condo. I figured once I left, I'd basically given the place up.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client relocated to a senior community in 2010. The client's intuition that the physical move alone surrenders her property rights, however, is a misconception. Under state law (e.g., Smith v. Lakewood City), abandonment requires a surrender, relinquishment, or disclaimer of rights coupled with lengthy non-use — not merely physical relocation. Indicia of continuing ownership (HOA dues, insurance, maintenance, family checking on the property) typically defeat any constructive-abandonment defense, so the client's belief that she 'gave the place up' simply by moving out is too strong.

facts.client_belief: After I moved out, nobody was paying the property taxes on the condo. I assumed that meant I'd already forfeited any claim on the place.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that no property taxes were paid on the condo after the client moved out, and the County, acting under the state delinquency statute, recorded the delinquency and obtained a judgment transferring limited title to the State. The client's intuition that non-payment alone wiped out every property right she had, however, conflates two distinct things: the State's power to recover the unpaid tax (which it had), and the State's power to retain whatever value the property has above the tax debt (which is the contested question). Procedural-due-process arguments may also remain available if any required statutory notice was deficient.

facts.client_belief: By 2015 I owed about $2,300 in unpaid taxes, and on top of that around $13,000 had piled up in interest and penalties — about $15,000 in total.
facts.court_record: By 2015 the accumulated tax debt totaled approximately $15,000, comprising roughly $2,300 in unpaid taxes plus $13,000 in interest and penalties. The composition of the debt is not in dispute.

facts.client_belief: The county seized my condo and sold it for $40,000.
facts.court_record: the County, acting under the state forfeiture statutes, seized the condo following the three-year redemption period and sold it for $40,000. The sale price and the County's authority to sell are not disputed.

facts.client_belief: They used about $15,000 of the sale price to pay off my tax debt — that part I'm not contesting.
facts.court_record: The $15,000 tax debt was extinguished by the proceeds of the sale. The client does not challenge the County's right to recover that amount.

facts.client_belief: But the county kept the remaining $25,000 for itself and never returned a cent of it to me. I assumed that's just how tax sales work — once they sell it, the money is theirs.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the County retained the $25,000 surplus over the tax debt; under the state surplus-distribution statute, that surplus is divided among the County, town, and school district, and former owners have no statutory mechanism to recover it. The client's assumption that 'that's just how tax sales work' is precisely the misconception driving this dispute: it conflates the State's lawful authority to recover the tax with a presumed authority to keep value beyond the tax — the latter is the central contested issue and the basis of any takings argument.

facts.client_belief: Once the property was forfeited to the state, I figured I had no rights left — the county owns the home now and can do whatever it wants with the money.
facts.court_record: Even after a tax forfeiture transfers title to the State, the former owner retains a constitutionally protected property interest in the surplus value above the tax debt, grounded in traditional property principles and longstanding Anglo-American property tradition (Magna Carta forward; United States v. Taylor; United States v. Lawton). The client's belief that title transfer extinguishes every right is therefore overstated — federal constitutional protection of the surplus survives the state-law title transfer.

facts.client_belief: state law clearly says the surplus belongs to the county once title vests in the state, so I assumed there's nothing I can do.
facts.court_record: It is generally true that the state statute purports to vest the surplus in public entities once title transfers to the State, but the client's assumption that this resolves the matter is too strong. State law is one important source of property rights, but it cannot be the only one — otherwise a State could 'sidestep the Takings Clause by disavowing traditional property interests' (Phillips v. Washington Legal Foundation). the State's 1935 statute purporting to extinguish the surplus interest does not displace the federal constitutional protection.

facts.client_belief: I assumed this was just normal tax collection — the government takes what it's owed and that's the end of it.
facts.court_record: The County had the power to sell the home to recover unpaid taxes, but retaining the $25,000 surplus over the $15,000 tax debt constitutes a taking. Lawful tax collection up to the amount owed is not a taking; appropriating value beyond the debt is.

facts.client_belief: Honestly, since the county has been doing this for decades under the state statute that's been on the books since the 1930s, I assumed there's nothing I can do — this must just be settled law.
facts.court_record: The longevity of the state's forfeiture statute does not by itself foreclose a federal Takings Clause challenge. The client's intuition that long-standing state practice equals constitutional permissibility is a common misconception; constitutional protections survive even where a State has consistently disregarded them under its own laws. The federal Takings Clause analysis turns on substance — whether the State has appropriated value beyond what it was owed — not on how long the State has done so.

facts.client_belief: The county's lawyers have already started telling me I don't even have a real injury to complain about, because there might be a $49,000 mortgage and $12,000 in unpaid HOA fees on the property — more than the $25,000 surplus. That made me worried I have nothing left to fight for.
facts.court_record: The client does have a real, concrete injury. The County's retention of the $25,000 is a 'classic pocketbook injury' (TransUnion v. Ramirez), and the State tax sale extinguishes other liens against the property but does not extinguish the borrower's personal liability for those debts. Even assuming the alleged encumbrances exist, any surplus would still have value to the client by reducing her personal debt liability. The client's assumption that the existence of larger encumbrances makes the surplus 'worthless' to her therefore overstates the legal effect of the lien-extinguishment rule.

facts.client_belief: They also argued I "abandoned" the condo when I moved out and stopped paying the taxes — like I just gave up my rights.
facts.court_record: Failure to pay taxes is not abandonment. Abandonment requires "surrender or relinquishment or disclaimer of all rights" plus lengthy non-use (Smith v. Lakewood City; Texaco v. Short). the state's forfeiture scheme focuses on tax delinquency, not on the use of the property — taxpayers may continue to live in the home until the State sells it.

facts.client_belief: I worry I lost any rights because I should have just sold the condo myself before the county took it.
facts.court_record: Requiring a taxpayer to sell her house to avoid a taking is not equivalent to providing her an opportunity to recover the excess value once the State has sold it. The constitutional protection does not depend on self-help.

facts.client_belief: I always understood that if a bank forecloses or a private creditor sells your property, they have to give back any surplus — but I assumed the rules are different when it's the government collecting taxes.
facts.court_record: state law itself entitles homeowners to the surplus when private creditors enforce judgments (state statutes on private-creditor surplus), when banks foreclose on mortgages (the state mortgage-foreclosure statute), when the State collects unpaid income taxes (§§ 270C.7101, 270C.7108), and when it collects personal-property taxes (§ 277.21). The State cannot extinguish a property interest it recognizes everywhere else just to avoid paying just compensation when it does the taking.

facts.client_belief: I figured this kind of thing — the government keeping more than it's owed — must be normal and accepted.
facts.court_record: The principle that a government may not take more than it is owed traces to the Magna Carta (1215), was rooted in English common law (Blackstone), was adopted by the new federal government in 1798 and ten founding-era states, and held through the Fourteenth Amendment. Today, 36 states and the federal government require any surplus be returned. the State's rule is the minority position.

facts.client_belief: Someone told me about an old 1956 case from New York where the government got to keep the surplus, so I figured I was probably out of luck.
facts.court_record: the New York precedent is distinguishable. The New York City ordinance permitted the owner to recover the surplus by filing a timely claim, but the owners simply failed to use the procedure. the state's scheme provides no opportunity at all — once absolute title transfers to the State, the excess value always remains with the State. The client's assumption that the New York precedent controls therefore overlooks the procedural-mechanism distinction that drove that case.

expected_inquiries: Ask the client for the original closing documents, deed, title insurance policy, and any documentation of the 1999 purchase price and improvements made to the unit.
Ask whether the client kept any belongings in the condo, paid HOA dues or insurance, maintained utilities, or had family check on the property after the 2010 move.
Ask the client whether she or any family member ever received the County's tax delinquency or forfeiture notices, and obtain copies of any such notices that were retained.
Obtain the County's official accounting of accrued taxes, interest, and penalties year-by-year for 2011–2015, including any statutory authority cited for each charge.
Request the public records of the tax sale, including notice of sale, bidder list, sale ledger, and the deed transferring title from the State to the buyer.
Confirm with the client in writing that she does not contest the County's authority to satisfy the $15,000 tax debt out of the sale proceeds.
Obtain the County's distribution records under the state surplus-distribution statute showing how the $25,000 was actually divided among the County, town, and school district.

Walk the client through the constitutional protection of the surplus so she understands the rights she still retains, the nature of any potential remedy, and the role of historical/precedential evidence in supporting the claim.

Pull together the legislative history of the 1935 the State forfeiture statute, prior the State authorities (a historical state precedent (1884)), and the leading constitutional precedent on the surplus rule for use in dispositive briefing.
Prepare a clear factual matrix showing the tax debt versus surplus retained for both client education and use as a demonstrative in briefing.

Walk the client through a realistic roadmap for a takings challenge — typical timeline, discovery, briefing, possible class certification — so she has realistic expectations about how a federal constitutional claim of this kind unfolds.
Investigate the actual encumbrances on the condo (mortgage balance, HOA arrears) and prepare evidence that any surplus would have reduced the client's personal debt liability.
Document any continuing connection the client maintained with the property (insurance, mail forwarding, family visits, intent to return) to negate any constructive-abandonment narrative.
Probe the client's practical ability and opportunity to sell before forfeiture, including her physical condition, financial means, and access to information about the impending forfeiture.

Compile a side-by-side comparison chart of the state's surplus rules across private foreclosure, judgment enforcement, income tax, personal-property tax, and real-property tax forfeiture for use in briefing and demonstratives.

Prepare a historical brief outlining the Magna Carta-to-present trajectory of the surplus rule, including primary sources cited by the Court (a historical legal treatise; a historical common-law case).
Prepare a comparative analysis of the New York precedent and the state's scheme that explicitly walks through the procedural differences in the two regimes.
Prepare a comparative analysis of Nelson and Minnesota's scheme that explicitly walks through the procedural differences in the two regimes.
memo_expectations: Confirm the client's sole ownership and chain of title at acquisition, since the existence of any joint owners or pre-existing encumbrances will materially affect both standing and the measure of just compensation.

Counsel the client that physical relocation alone does not equate to legal abandonment under state law; preserve every indicium of continuing ownership to defeat any constructive-abandonment argument the County may raise.

Establish the precise timeline of tax non-payment and statutory notices under the state delinquency statute, and counsel the client that non-payment defeats only the County's claim up to the amount owed — not any residual interest in surplus value.

Verify the precise breakdown of taxes versus interest and penalties; the heavy weight of penalties relative to the underlying tax may also support an Eighth Amendment Excessive Fines theory as an alternative to the Takings Clause claim.

Confirm that the sale process formally complied with the state forfeiture statutes, and identify any procedural irregularities (notice, valuation, bidding) that could give rise to additional state-law claims.
Concede the County's right to recover the $15,000 to streamline the case and isolate the central constitutional issue: ownership of the $25,000 surplus.

Frame the $25,000 retention as the "classic taking" identified in Tahoe-Sierra Preservation Council — a direct appropriation of private property for public use that requires just compensation under the Fifth Amendment.

Educate the client that the constitutional protection of the surplus survives forfeiture and transfer of title under state law, and that this protection is rooted in centuries of Anglo-American property tradition independent of the state statute.

Brief the Phillips/a related federal precedent/a related federal precedent line of authority to counter the County's "state law defines property" argument and explain why the 1935 the state statute cannot exempt the State from the Takings Clause.
Distinguish lawful tax collection (not a taking) from retention of surplus beyond the tax debt (a Fifth Amendment taking) — the County had power to recoup taxes but not to confiscate excess equity.

Set the client's expectations: long-standing state practice does not foreclose a federal takings challenge. Frame the case as a substance-driven Takings Clause claim that the duration of the State's 1935 statute does not insulate.

Rebut the no-real-injury argument with TransUnion v. Ramirez and the State lien-extinguishment rule — the surplus has practical value to the client regardless of whether other secured creditors held superior interests in the property.

Apply the proper abandonment standard from Smith v. Lakewood City and Texaco v. Short, and demonstrate that the state's forfeiture scheme is unrelated to abandonment because it gives no weight to the taxpayer's use of the property.

Brief that requiring self-help sale is not equivalent to providing a constitutional remedy for surplus recovery — the Constitution requires more than the bare ability to avoid the taking by selling first.

Use the state's own statutes to demonstrate internal inconsistency — the State recognizes the surplus right in every other debt-collection context, and the carve-out for real-property tax forfeitures is therefore artificial and constitutionally unsustainable.

Marshal the historical evidence — Magna Carta, English common law, the 1798 federal statute, ten founding-era state statutes, and the modern 36-state consensus — to show the State is the historical outlier, not the norm.

Brief a New York precedent carefully and demonstrate that its holding turned on the existence of a procedural mechanism for surplus recovery — a mechanism the State does not provide — so the New York precedent actually supports the client's position.

opening: Hi, I'm x, owner of X Nursery. I spoke with your office about a property rights dispute involving a state regulation — I was hoping you could help me figure out my options.

facts.client_belief: I own and operate a strawberry-plant nursery in Riverside, the State — we ship to growers around the country.
facts.court_record: The client operates an agricultural-plant nursery in Riverside, the State, and is an agricultural employer covered by the State Agricultural Labor Relations Act (ALRA). Ownership and operation of the Riverside facility are undisputed.

facts.client_belief: My nursery employs around 100 seasonal workers and more than 400 full-time workers — almost none of them live on our property. Since they don't live on-site, I figure the union has no real reason to come onto my land at all.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client employs roughly 100 seasonal and 400+ full-time workers, none of whom reside on the employer's premises. The client's intuition that an off-site workforce automatically defeats any union right of access, however, mixes two different legal frameworks. The 'company town' or employer-housing line of cases (e.g., NLRB v. Babcock & Wilcox) addresses when statutory access rights against an employer's property may be invoked under labor law — it does not say that off-site workers eliminate any access right that a state regulator has independently granted. The off-site workforce is helpful, but mainly because it strengthens the right-to-exclude framing of any takings analysis, not because it defeats access in the first instance.

facts.client_belief: the State Labor Relations Board has a rule that lets union organizers come onto our property to talk to our workers, and we can't say no.
facts.court_record: the State regulation § 20900(e), the access regulation promulgated by the State Labor Relations Board in 1975, grants union organizers a right to enter agricultural employers' property for purposes of meeting and talking with employees regarding union representation.

facts.client_belief: The rule says they can come onto our land for up to three hours a day, 120 days a year — basically four hours before work, during the lunch hour, and one hour after work.
facts.court_record: Section 20900(e) authorizes access for one hour before work, during the lunch period, and one hour after work, for up to four 30-day periods per year — a total of up to three hours per day, 120 days per year. These limits are not in dispute.

facts.client_belief: In October 2015, UFW organizers showed up at our nursery at 5 a.m. without giving us proper notice, walked into the trim sheds with bullhorns, and disturbed our workers.
facts.court_record: On October 29, 2015, UFW organizers entered the client's property without serving timely written notice and disrupted operations using bullhorns. The factual incident is undisputed; its legal characterization (trespass vs. lawful access) is contested below.

facts.client_belief: When we filed an unfair-labor-practice complaint about the disruption, the union turned around and filed one against us claiming they had every right to be there. I assumed our filing first put us in the clear.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client filed an unfair-labor-practice charge alleging unauthorized access and that UFW filed a counter-charge asserting interference with the right of access. The client's intuition that filing first puts them in the clear, however, is a procedural misconception. Both administrative proceedings stand on their own merits, and the validity of the access regulation itself is the real load-bearing question — neither side's filing posture resolves it. There is also a genuine preclusion issue to manage: the administrative-track outcomes can affect the constitutional litigation if not coordinated.

facts.client_belief: Our co-plaintiff is another grower in Lakewood City that ships table grapes and citrus and employs about 1,800 to 2,500 farm workers — they hadn't even had organizers actually show up on their property yet, but the union still filed a charge against them. I assume that means they don't really need to be in this case.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the co-plaintiff operates an agricultural shipping business in Lakewood City, employing ~1,800-2,500 workers, that UFW had attempted access and filed an unfair labor practice charge, and that UFW later withdrew the charge. The client's intuition that the co-plaintiff lacks a real interest because no organizer 'actually showed up' yet is too narrow. The credible threat of repeated future access — not merely past actual access — supplies the concrete-imminent-injury element. Consolidating both growers' claims is also more efficient for pretrial motion practice and discovery.

facts.client_belief: The lawyers we spoke with before told us this kind of access regulation can really only be challenged as a 'regulatory taking,' and that those claims almost never win because of how the balancing test works. So I figured the case was effectively over before it started.
facts.court_record: The client's prior advice that the only available theory is a regulatory-takings claim is too pessimistic. Whenever the government physically appropriates property — or appropriates a right to physical invasion of property — it is categorically a per se taking requiring just compensation, with no regulatory-takings balancing test to run. The access regulation grants exactly that kind of right of physical invasion, so the proper framing is per se physical taking, not regulatory taking. The client's resignation to a balancing-test loss therefore reflects a misclassification of the legal theory, not the actual strength of the claim.

facts.client_belief: I always assumed that since we still own the land and the union only enters for limited hours, this was at most a "regulatory taking" — meaning we'd have to win that complicated balancing test most landowners lose.
facts.court_record: It is true that the client retains formal title to the land and that the union's entry is time-limited. The client's intuition that this can only be a regulatory taking — and therefore lose under Penn Central balancing — is incorrect. Whenever the government physically appropriates property or appropriates a right to physical invasion, the action is categorically a per se taking requiring just compensation; the Penn Central balancing test has no role in that analysis.

facts.client_belief: I thought "physical taking" meant something like the cable box bolted onto the apartment building in Loretto — permanent, 24/7 occupation. Three hours a day for 120 days didn't feel like that.
facts.court_record: It is correct that Loretto involved a permanent, 24/7 physical occupation. The client's inference that Loretto sets the only path to a per se physical taking, however, is too narrow. Loretto is a sufficient condition for a per se taking, not a necessary one: any government appropriation of a right to physically invade property — whether continuous or episodic — is per se a taking, and permanence affects only the measure of just compensation, not whether a taking has occurred.

facts.client_belief: the State told us that under their own state law this access right isn't even an "easement," so I assumed there was nothing for them to take.
facts.court_record: It is true that the State treats this access right as something other than an easement under its own state-law labels. The client's inference that the state-law label controls the federal Takings Clause analysis, however, is incorrect. Federal takings analysis looks to substance: the State has granted itself (and its designees, the unions) a right to enter and occupy, which functions as an easement appurtenant under traditional property principles. State-law refusal to use the term cannot defeat the federal claim (Phillips v. Washington Legal Foundation; Webb's Fabulous Pharmacies; Hall v. Meisner).

facts.client_belief: Our opponents pointed to PruneYard — that old the State case where a shopping mall had to let people gather signatures — and said that case means we lose.
facts.court_record: PruneYard is distinguishable. That shopping mall was already open to the public, so the right to exclude was not similarly burdened; here the client and the co-plaintiff maintain no general invitation to the public, so a forced right of access directly impairs the right to exclude — the most fundamental stick in the property bundle. The client's concern that PruneYard means defeat therefore overlooks the open-to-public premise that drove that case.

facts.client_belief: The other side also pointed me to an old labor-law case — Babcock & Wilcox — and said it means unions automatically have a right to come onto employer property if there's no other reasonable way to communicate.
facts.court_record: NLRB v. Babcock & Wilcox is a statutory NLRA decision, not a constitutional Takings Clause holding. Its accommodation framework concerns when statutory access rights may be invoked against an employer's property rights under federal labor law — it does not say that granting such access avoids takings analysis under the Fifth Amendment. The client's worry that Babcock controls therefore confuses two different bodies of law; even reading Babcock generously, the access regulation here goes further than its accommodation framework would allow.

expected_inquiries: Ask the client for the corporate organizational documents, the deeds and parcel maps for the Riverside property, and any documentation showing the nursery's status as an agricultural employer under the State law.

Ask the client to provide payroll records, employee residency information, and a description of housing arrangements for seasonal workers (e.g., off-site company housing, local rentals) to confirm none reside on the property.

Pull the full regulatory text of Cal. Code Regs. tit. 8, § 20900 and its 1975 promulgation history (Board statement of reasons, comments) for use in pleadings and to confirm the "right of access" framing.
Document the exact 120-day, three-hour-a-day usage patterns at the client's facilities historically (or as forecast) so any just-compensation valuation has a factual baseline.
Obtain witness statements from the client's employees who were present on October 29, 2015, any photographs or video, and any contemporaneous incident reports filed by management.
Request the complete administrative file (charges, responses, hearing transcripts, any orders) for both the client's and the co-plaintiff's matters.
Obtain the co-plaintiff's records of all UFW notices of access, contacts, and the withdrawn charge — these establish the concrete, imminent injury supporting standing.

Walk the client through a realistic procedural roadmap for a per se physical-takings challenge — pleading strategy, dispositive motions, just-compensation determination, and any related state-administrative proceedings.

Prepare a side-by-side memo comparing the per se physical-takings framework with the Penn Central regulatory-takings framework, highlighting why the access regulation falls on the per se side of the line.
Prepare a clear client-facing illustration showing how the right of access exists permanently on the books even though exercise is episodic, and how this maps to the easement framework.

Compile authorities (Phillips v. Washington Legal Foundation; Webb's Fabulous Pharmacies; Hall v. Meisner) for the proposition that state-law definitions cannot define away federal property protections.
Prepare a brief comparative analysis of PruneYard and the present situation identifying every legally relevant factor that differs, particularly the public-invitation status of the property.

Read and summarize the separate concurring reasoning at the federal-level review for the client and identify whether to plead in the alternative under a Babcock-style argument, in addition to the per se rule the majority adopted.

Read and summarize the separate concurring reasoning at the federal-level review for the client and identify whether to plead in the alternative under a Babcock-style argument, in addition to the per se rule the majority adopted.
memo_expectations: Confirm the client's status as an 'agricultural employer' under Cal. Lab. Code § 1140.4(c) and document the legal entity, ownership structure, and parcel boundaries — these facts frame both standing and the scope of any easement that has been appropriated.

Establish that the workforce does not live on-site and use that fact to strengthen the right-to-exclude framing of the takings analysis — but counsel the client that off-site residency does not by itself defeat the access regulation; the regulation grants access regardless of where workers reside.

Anchor the analysis in the precise text of § 20900(e). The regulation grants a "right" to take access, and that compulsory invasion of the employer's property is the constitutional core of the case — the substance, not the labels, controls the takings analysis.

Use the precise temporal limits to frame the appropriated easement: it is not a 24/7 invasion, but it is a continuing legal right for 120 days/year that exists permanently on the books. Episodic or intermittent exercise of the right does not defeat per se physical-takings analysis.

Capture the 2015 incident in any complaint as concrete evidence that the access regulation creates real, recurring intrusions on operations — not merely an abstract right — strengthening both standing and any equitable-relief request.
Track the parallel administrative proceedings to ensure no preclusion issues arise, and decide whether to pursue or pause the administrative track while the takings claim is litigated.

Frame the co-plaintiff's standing on the basis of the credible threat of repeated future access (not merely past attempts), and consolidate the two growers' claims for efficiency in pretrial motion practice and discovery.
Reset client expectations: the regulation is best framed as a per se physical taking, not a regulatory taking subject to ad hoc balancing — that distinction drives both merits and remedies.

Brief the per se vs. regulatory taking distinction with care: this case turns on the categorical rule for physical appropriations, and Penn Central balancing has no role; that distinction drives both the merits and remedies on remand.

Drive home that Loretto sets a sufficient condition (permanent occupation = taking), not a necessary one. The proper test is government appropriation of a right of physical invasion — episodic or limited duration is still appropriation, going only to valuation.

Brief the substance-over-labels principle: federal courts apply federal constitutional standards, and a State cannot avoid the Takings Clause by refusing to characterize an appropriated right as an easement under its own property law.
Distinguish PruneYard on the open-to-public ground and reframe the case around the right to exclude as the constitutional fulcrum — the key right that the access regulation appropriates.

Explain that Babcock is about NLRA accommodation between statutory rights and property rights, not constitutional takings doctrine — and that even a separate concurring vote at the federal-level review, which leans on Babcock, agrees the regulation here goes further than Babcock would allow.

opening: Hi, I'm x, raisin farmer. I spoke with your office about a federal regulatory dispute involving our farm - I was hoping you could help me figure out my options.

facts.client_belief: My wife and I have been growing raisins in Riverside and Lakewood Counties since 1969. We do business as a general partnership.
facts.court_record: The client and his spouse have produced raisins in Riverside and Lakewood Counties, the State since 1969, doing business as a family general partnership. The personal background and farming history are undisputed.

facts.client_belief: After getting fed up with the Federal Agriculture Agency's marketing order, my wife and I started a packing partnership with her parents. We bought our own equipment to clean, stem, sort, and package raisins — both our own and other growers'. We even contracted with more than 60 other raisin growers to do that for them, for a fee. We figured we'd designed our way out of the federal program.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client formed a packing partnership that purchased equipment to clean, stem, sort, and package raisins from the family farming partnership, the packing partnership itself, and more than 60 other raisin growers under fee-for-service contracts. The client's belief that this structure carved them out of the federal program, however, is mistaken. The Federal Agricultural Marketing Act exempts producers in their capacity as producers (7 U.S.C. § 608c(13)(B)), but defines 'handlers' broadly to include processors, associations of producers, and others engaged in the handling of covered commodities (§ 608c(1)). Because the packing partnership processed and packaged raisins (including those of more than 60 other growers), it functioned as a handler — and the producer-only exemption does not apply.

facts.client_belief: Because we grew the raisins ourselves and processed only our own crop and our neighbors' crops without going through a traditional handler, we figured we'd designed our way out of the Federal Agricultural Marketing Act — we were just producers, and the Federal Agricultural Marketing Act only regulates handlers, not producers.
facts.court_record: Although the Federal Agricultural Marketing Act exempts producers in their capacity as producers (7 U.S.C. § 608c(13)(B)), it defines 'handlers' broadly to include processors, associations of producers, and others engaged in the 'handling' of covered commodities (§ 608c(1)). Under that definition, the client's packing operation — which cleaned, stemmed, sorted, and packaged raisins for the client's farm and for more than 60 other growers — falls squarely within 'handler' status. The client's producer-only theory therefore overlooks the breadth of the statutory definition and the fact that processing for third parties is precisely the conduct that triggers handler regulation.

facts.client_belief: During the 2002-03 and 2003-04 crop years, our facilities ran more than 3 million pounds of raisins through them - and most of those raisins came from the 60-plus other growers, not from our own fields.
facts.court_record: The client's facilities processed more than 3 million pounds of raisins in total during the 2002-2003 and 2003-2004 crop years. The client's family farm grew only 27.4% and 12.3% of those volumes respectively. Undisputed.

facts.client_belief: the Federal Agriculture Agency wrote us back in 2001 telling us our planned operation would make us 'handlers.' We didn't agree, but we got the letter. I figured if we disagreed in good faith, that should be the end of it.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that in 2001 the Federal Agriculture Agency informed the client that the proposed operations would qualify them as 'handlers' under the Federal Agricultural Marketing Act. The client's intuition that good-faith disagreement was a complete answer, however, is mistaken: the 2001 notice forecloses any innocent-mistake or fair-warning defense for the 2002-2004 conduct, and is squarely relevant to the willfulness component of the civil-penalty calculation under 7 U.S.C. § 608c(14)(B). The proper response to disagreement is a § 608c(15)(A) administrative challenge, not unilateral non-compliance.

facts.client_belief: We sent the Secretary and the RAC a letter in 2002 telling them this Marketing Order is a tool for grower bankruptcy, poverty, and involuntary servitude - and that we wouldn't relinquish ownership of our crop. Since the program is unconstitutional anyway, we figured we could just refuse to participate.
facts.court_record: The client did write the Secretary and the RAC in 2002, but the law does not recognize self-help non-compliance as a remedy for an alleged unconstitutional regulation. Handlers must either file a direct administrative challenge under § 608c(15)(A) or comply and raise constitutional defenses in the § 608c(14) enforcement proceeding (United States v. Ruzicka, 329 U.S. 287). The client's strategy of refusing to participate exposed them to substantial monetary sanctions when the constitutional argument did not immediately succeed at the administrative level.

facts.client_belief: For the 2002-03 and 2003-04 crop years, we paid no assessments, didn't set aside any reserve raisins from our own crop or the third-party growers' crop, didn't arrange RAC inspections, and refused RAC access to our records. We considered the program unconstitutional, so we figured we didn't have to play along.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that during the 2002-2003 and 2003-2004 crop years the client paid no assessments to the RAC, did not set aside reserve-tonnage raisins (their own or those of the more than 60 third-party growers), declined RAC inspection of incoming raisins, denied RAC access to their records, and held none of their own raisins in reserve. The client's intuition that an asserted constitutional defect justified self-help non-compliance, however, is mistaken: this is the predicate factual conduct for every count in the Federal Agriculture Agency complaint, and the takings defense and the (already-rejected) producer/handler argument are now the only viable paths to vacate the resulting penalties.

facts.client_belief: On April 1, 2004, the Federal Agriculture Agency Administrator filed an enforcement complaint against me, my wife, and both of our partnerships, alleging we were handlers who broke the Marketing Order in multiple ways.
facts.court_record: The Administrator of the Agriculture Marketing Service initiated an enforcement action on April 1, 2004 against the client, his spouse, and both partnerships under § 608c(14), alleging they were handlers who failed to hold inspections, retain reserve raisins, pay assessments, and allow RAC access to records. Undisputed.

facts.client_belief: We raised the takings defense before the ALJ. The ALJ rejected it, saying handlers don't have any property right to market their crop free of regulation. The judicial officer on internal appeal said he didn't even have authority to rule on whether the regulation was constitutional. We thought that was nonsense.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the ALJ rejected the takings defense on the merits, citing Cal-Almond, Inc. v. United States, 30 Fed.Cl. 244 (1994), for the proposition that handlers have no property right to market raisins free of regulatory control, and that the judicial officer on internal appeal believed he lacked authority to adjudicate the constitutionality of statutes administered by the Federal Agriculture Agency. The client's frustration with that posture, however, is grounded in a real legal point worth pressing: under existing federal takings doctrine, constitutional defenses (including takings) are cognizable in § 608c(14) enforcement proceedings, and federal forums have jurisdiction to review them. The Cal-Almond reasoning is one possible characterization of the property-interest question, not the only one.

facts.client_belief: The judicial officer hit us with $202,600 in civil penalties, $8,783 in unpaid assessments, and another $483,843 for the value of the reserve-tonnage raisins we didn't deliver. That's almost $700,000 in total. I figured the takings argument should cancel out all of that — we shouldn't actually owe anything.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the judicial officer imposed $202,600 in civil penalties under 7 U.S.C. § 608c(14)(B), $8,783.39 in past assessments under 7 CFR 989.80(a), and $483,843.53 representing the value of the State raisins the client failed to hold in reserve under 7 CFR 989.166(c) — an aggregate of approximately $695,227. The client's intuition that a successful takings argument cancels out the entire $700,000, however, is overstated. The three components serve different functions and should be analyzed separately: the reserve-value reimbursement of $483,843.53 is the dollar measure of the alleged appropriation and is the natural target of the takings theory; the $202,600 civil penalty is a punitive backstop tied to refusal to comply and is more difficult to vacate on takings grounds; and the $8,783 assessment is administrative cost recovery. The agency did not seek the raisins themselves, but monetary substitutes — that fact conditions the merits framing of the takings theory.

facts.client_belief: The government keeps insisting that any takings claim against the federal government has to start in a special damages-only federal court rather than in the enforcement proceeding itself. So they say we should comply, give up our raisins, and then sue separately for compensation.
facts.court_record: The general rule is that takings claims against the federal government must be brought in the special damages-only federal forum under the Tucker Act unless Congress has withdrawn that jurisdiction. Existing federal takings doctrine indicates, however, that the Federal Agricultural Marketing Act's comprehensive remedial scheme — § 608c(15)(A) for direct challenges, § 608c(14) for enforcement-stage defenses, and § 608c(14)(B)/(15)(B) for judicial review — withdraws Tucker Act jurisdiction over a handler's takings claim (cf. United States v. Fausto, 484 U.S. 439). Handlers therefore cannot, and need not, first sue in the special damages-only federal forum; the takings defense was properly raised in the § 608c(14) enforcement action. The client's worry about being forced into a separate post-compliance damages suit is therefore not a real obstacle here.

facts.client_belief: The government also argued our case wasn't 'ripe' yet because we hadn't first gone through the separate damages-procedure they're pointing us to. We thought that was a complete catch-22.
facts.court_record: Established federal ripeness doctrine holds that a takings claim is unripe when (1) there is no final government decision causing injury, or (2) the property owner has not pursued compensation through the procedures the State has provided (Williamson County Regional Planning Comm'n v. Hamilton Bank). Neither prong applies here: the client is subject to a final agency order imposing concrete monetary sanctions (sufficient injury), and the Federal Agricultural Marketing Act itself withdraws Tucker Act jurisdiction so there is no alternative compensation procedure to exhaust. The second-prong inquiry is also generally treated as 'prudential ripeness' rather than strictly jurisdictional (see leading judicial-takings precedent on prudential ripeness), so even if a procedural path existed, exhaustion can be excused where there is finality and adequacy of harm.

facts.client_belief: Since the reserve-tonnage was calculated against the entire 3 million pounds we processed - most of which we didn't even own - the takings claim covers all those raisins too.
facts.court_record: Most of the raisins the client failed to reserve belonged to the more than 60 third-party growers, not to the client himself. That ownership gap is likely a substantial weakness in the takings theory for the bulk of the volume that drove the $483,843.53 reserve-value penalty: a takings defense generally requires the defender to assert a property interest of his own in the appropriated property. The client's intuition that the takings claim simply travels with the volume he handled, regardless of ownership, therefore overstates the doctrine. A workable strategy will likely require either an alternative theory (e.g., third-party-beneficiary or assignment-based standing, or a 'compelled servitude' argument based on the obligation to deliver on others' behalf) or actual assignments of takings-claim rights from the third-party growers.

facts.client_belief: We don't dispute how the Federal Agricultural Marketing Act actually works - handlers are the ones regulated, the RAC sets the reserve percentage, the reserve raisins get sold by the RAC, and any surplus net of administrative costs is paid pro rata back to the producers.
facts.court_record: Under the Federal Agricultural Marketing Act and the State Raisin Marketing Order: (i) only handlers are regulated (§ 608c(1), (13)(B)); (ii) the RAC recommends, and the Secretary approves, the annual reserve percentage (7 CFR 989.54-.55); (iii) reserve-tonnage raisins are held by handlers in segregated bins for the RAC's account (989.66(f)) and sold or directed by the RAC to overseas, school-lunch, or noncompetitive domestic markets (989.67(b)); and (iv) net reserve-pool proceeds, after RAC administrative costs, are paid pro rata to producers (§ 608c(6)(E); 7 CFR 989.66(h)). The client does not dispute this structural framework.

expected_inquiries: Ask the client to provide partnership agreements, fictitious-business-name filings, tax returns, and bank-account signature cards for both partnerships, and to identify every general partner.

Ask for copies of all packing-service contracts with the 60+ third-party growers, the fee schedules charged, and any documentation showing whether the client ever took title (rather than only physical possession) to those growers' raisins.

Walk the client through the binding effect of handler status under § 608c(1) and confirm there are no overlooked facts (e.g., title to the third-party raisins) that could re-open the producer/handler question.
Ask for purchase ledgers, weight tickets, raisin-grade certificates, and third-party grower payment records to establish ownership of the 3 million pounds processed.

Ask whether the client retained the original the Federal Agriculture Agency notice, any responsive letters or counsel correspondence, and whether they obtained an outside legal opinion before launching the third-party packing operation.

Ask the client whether they considered (or were advised about) filing a 608c(15)(A) petition before refusing to comply, and whether any communications exist suggesting that prior counsel or industry advisors warned about the consequences of self-help non-compliance.

Ask the client to produce all records (or affidavits explaining their absence) covering RAC interactions, attempted inspections, and reserve-tonnage decisions during the two crop years - even if those records were withheld from RAC at the time.

Confirm whether the client and his spouse were sued in their individual capacities, partnership capacities, or both, and obtain copies of the original the Federal Agriculture Agency complaint, the ALJ decision, and the judicial-officer order with each respondent identified.

Ask whether the client preserved, in administrative briefing, every sub-theory of the takings claim - physical taking, regulatory taking, exaction theory under Nollan/Dolan - because preservation will determine which arguments are available on remand.
Ask the client whether the assessments or penalties have been paid, escrowed, or stayed pending appeal, and whether an appeal bond was posted that may bear on settlement leverage.

Ask whether the client knows of any other the Federal Agricultural Marketing Act-handler litigants who pursued parallel separate damages-forum actions and what posture those cases are in — useful to monitor for adverse precedent or coordination.
Confirm there are no parallel proceedings or settlement overtures that could be characterized as 'compensation procedures' the client has failed to exhaust.

Ask the client to identify each third-party grower (with current contact information) and to specify whether any written contracts addressed which party bore the reserve-tonnage obligation; explore whether assignments of takings-claim rights from those growers can be secured.

Ask the client to obtain or estimate, for the 2002-2003 and 2003-2004 crop years, (a) total RAC sales of reserve-pool raisins, (b) RAC administrative costs, and (c) the per-pound net proceeds actually distributed to producers - RAC public reports and the Marketing Policy & Industry Statistics may suffice.

Ask the client to obtain or estimate, for the 2002-2003 and 2003-2004 crop years, (a) total RAC sales of reserve-pool raisins, (b) RAC administrative costs, and (c) the per-pound net proceeds actually distributed to producers - RAC public reports and the Marketing Policy & Industry Statistics may suffice.
memo_expectations: Document the entity structure of both partnerships (the family farming partnership and the packing partnership) and identify all individual partners — both partnerships are named as parties and personal liability exposure runs to each general partner.

Map every transactional touchpoint between the packing partnership and the third-party growers — written contracts, custody transfers, payment flows, invoices, and shipping documents — because each touchpoint potentially constitutes 'handling' within the meaning of 7 CFR 989.15. Counsel the client that the producer-only exemption does not apply to a packer who handles others' raisins.

Treat the handler status as the load-bearing legal characterization. Build the strategy on the premise that the takings argument runs from the handler capacity, not the producer capacity, even though the practical 'taking' injury falls on the partnership's own raisin crop.

Quantify ownership precisely — pounds owned by the family partnership versus pounds owned by third parties — for each of the two crop years, because that distinction will drive whether the client has standing to assert a takings defense for particular raisins.

Confirm that the 2001 the Federal Agriculture Agency notice forecloses any innocent-mistake defense and bears on willfulness for the civil-penalty calculation. Counsel the client that good-faith disagreement is not a substitute for using the statutory administrative challenge mechanism.

Walk the client through the structural choice point — § 608c(15)(A) pre-enforcement administrative petition vs. § 608c(14) enforcement-stage defense — and document that the matter is now firmly in the second posture, with the more punitive cost structure that flows from refusal to comply.

Treat this conduct as the predicate for the agency's penalties. Counsel the client that constitutional doubts do not authorize self-help non-compliance with a marketing order — the proper vehicle is a § 608c(15)(A) petition or an enforcement-stage defense.

Track which counts run against which respondent (individuals vs. partnerships) — this matters for the apportionment of civil penalties and for determining which party may bring or defend each count of the takings argument.

Preserve the agency-level rejection of the takings defense as the operative ruling for review. Frame the Cal-Almond reasoning as a question of property-interest definition that is not necessarily controlling, and brief the cognizability of constitutional defenses in § 608c(14) proceedings.

Treat the three components separately for the takings analysis. Counsel the client that even a successful takings theory primarily targets the reserve-value reimbursement; the punitive civil penalty and assessment recovery are not automatically vacated by it.

Memorialize the position that the Federal Agricultural Marketing Act displaces Tucker Act jurisdiction for handlers, and use it to defeat any renewed Government attempt to redirect the case to a damages-only forum. The position does not foreclose a separate separate damages-only federal-forum suit by a producer for raisins actually surrendered.

The Williamson County prudential-ripeness concern is foreclosed; preserve a fallback argument that even if a Tucker Act path existed, prudential ripeness is non-jurisdictional and can be excused where there is finality and adequacy of harm.

Develop a fallback theory under which the client may assert the takings defense even as to non-owned raisins — e.g., third-party-beneficiary or assignment-based standing, or alternatively a 'compelled servitude' theory based on the obligation to deliver on others' behalf. Consider obtaining assignments of takings-claim rights from the third-party growers.

The pro-rata net-proceeds residual interest is the Government's strongest counter to a 'physical taking' framing. Develop an empirical record on what producers actually received in net proceeds during the 2002-2004 reserve years to argue that the residual was nominal compared with the surrendered raisin value.

opening: Hi, I'm X. I spoke with your office about a property dispute involving a railroad right of way on my land — I was hoping you could help me figure out my options.

facts.client_belief: My family has been in Pine Valley, the State, since my father started working at the local sawmill in 1939, bought it in 1946, and we ran it until 1991. I figure that long history should give us a stronger claim to the strip across our land than someone who just moved in last year.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client's family has had a continuous connection to the Pine Valley sawmill since 1939, with purchase in 1946 and operations through 1991. The client's intuition that family longevity translates into a stronger property-rights claim, however, is mistaken: title to the strip turns on the four corners of the 1976 patent and the legal character of the 1908 right-of-way grant — not on how long the family has been in the area. Family history can be useful for valuation/equitable framing later, but it does not affect whether the United States retained any reversionary interest.

facts.client_belief: In 1976 the United States patented an 83-acre parcel in Pine Valley to my parents, surrounded by the National Forest.
facts.court_record: On the date of the patent (1976), the United States conveyed an 83-acre parcel in Pine Valley to the client's parents by official land patent. Ownership transfer is undisputed.

facts.client_belief: The patent says the land was conveyed in fee simple "with all the rights, privileges, immunities, and appurtenances, of whatsoever nature, thereunto belonging, unto said claimants, their successors and assigns, forever."
facts.court_record: The 1976 patent conveyed fee simple title to the client's parents in classical conveyancing language. The fee-simple character of the underlying conveyance is not disputed.

facts.client_belief: The patent reserves a few rights of way to the United States — for federal ditches/canals, for the Platte Access Road, and for the Dry Park Road — and says those easements terminate if the U.S. doesn't use them for five years. Since the U.S. spelled out termination so carefully for those, I figured the railroad clause must work the same way and the U.S. has retained something there too.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the 1976 patent contains express reservations for federal ditches/canals and the Platte Access Road and Dry Park Road, with explicit five-year non-use termination clauses for the latter two roads. The client's intuition, however, runs the textual contrast in the wrong direction. When the United States wanted to retain a reversionary right with explicit termination conditions, it knew how to draft one — and it did, three times in this very patent. Its silence on the railroad right of way is therefore evidence the United States retained nothing in that strip, not evidence of a parallel reservation.

facts.client_belief: The patent then says the land is 'subject to those rights for railroad purposes as have been granted to the Laramie, Hahn's Peak & Pacific Railway Company, its successors or assigns' — but it doesn't say what happens if the railroad gives up those rights. Since it's silent, I worried the U.S. somehow retained an interest in that strip.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the patent's railroad-rights clause subjects the parcel to the LHP & P's 1875 Act right of way and contains no reversionary or termination language. The client's worry that this silence implies a retained federal interest reads the silence backwards. Where Congress and the Executive expressly drafted termination language for other reservations in the same patent, the absence of any such language for the railroad right of way reinforces that the United States retained nothing in that strip — silence is evidence against, not for, an implied reversion.

facts.client_belief: The right of way itself was originally obtained back in 1908 by the Laramie, Hahn's Peak and Pacific Railroad under the General Railroad Right-of-Way Act of 1875 — it's 200 feet wide, 66 miles long, and a roughly half-mile stretch (about 10 acres) crosses our Pine Valley land.
facts.court_record: LHP & P obtained the right of way in 1908 pursuant to the General Railroad Right-of-Way Act of 1875, 18 Stat. 482, 43 U.S.C. §§ 934–939. Dimensions and the half-mile, 10-acre crossing of Pine Valley parcel are undisputed.

facts.client_belief: The State and Y Railroad Company bought the line in 1987, told the federal regulators in 1996 that they were giving it up, tore up the tracks, and finished the abandonment in 2004. Once the railroad finished, I assumed the U.S. would automatically reclaim that strip across my land.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the State and Y Railroad Company, successor to LHP & P, notified federal regulators of intent to abandon in 1996, removed track and ties, and completed abandonment of the right of way in 2004. The client's assumption that abandonment automatically returns the strip to the United States, however, is incorrect. Under common-law easement principles, the 1875 Act granted only an easement; once the easement is abandoned, the underlying fee — which had passed to the client's family in 1976 — is unencumbered. There is no automatic reversion to the United States because the United States retained nothing capable of reverting.

facts.client_belief: In 2006 the United States sued for a "judicial declaration of abandonment" and to "quiet title" in itself — they named the railroad and 31 separate landowners, including me.
facts.court_record: In 2006 the United States filed a quiet-title action against the railroad and 31 landowners crossed by the right of way, seeking declaratory judgment of abandonment and title to the abandoned strip.

facts.client_belief: Almost everyone else either settled or signed off on whatever the government wanted — only I am still contesting the case. I figured my contesting alone wasn't going to make a difference against the federal government.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the United States resolved its claims with 30 of the 31 named landowners through settlement or default, and that the client is the sole contesting defendant. The client's pessimism about a sole-litigant posture, however, is overstated. Sole-litigant status is both a strategic risk (carrying the issue alone) and an opportunity (the absence of competing positions makes any precedent cleaner) — and any judgment binds only the parties, so a favorable resolution is meaningful for the client even without other defendants joining.

facts.client_belief: My understanding was that when the patent said the land was conveyed "subject to those rights for railroad purposes," that meant the United States kept some kind of reversionary interest in that strip.
facts.court_record: The 1875 Act granted only an easement, not a fee. Because an easement is non-possessory, the grantor of an easement does not retain a "reversionary interest" — it retains the full fee subject only to the easement, and when the easement is abandoned, the fee is unencumbered (Restatement (Third) of Property: Servitudes § 1.2; § 7.4).

facts.client_belief: I read about old precedents — Townsend (1903) and Stringham (1915) — that talked about a 'limited fee, made on an implied condition of reverter' for railroad rights of way, and I worried those precedents were against me.
facts.court_record: Townsend and Stringham concerned pre-1871 land grants accompanied by checkerboard land subsidies. Great Northern R. Co. v. United States, 315 U.S. 262 (1942) disavowed Stringham's characterization of 1875 Act rights of way as 'limited fees' and established that the 1875 Act 'clearly grants only an easement, and not a fee.' The client's worry that those older precedents control therefore overlooks both the doctrinal shift after 1871 and the controlling 1942 authority on 1875 Act grants specifically.

facts.client_belief: They also pointed to two old precedents — Stalker (1912) and Steinke (1923) — and said they show that 1875 Act rights of way are more than ordinary easements.
facts.court_record: Stalker and Steinke involved competing claims to acquire and develop land covered by a right of way and station grounds — not the easement-vs.-limited-fee question. Those decisions did not consider, much less reject, the easement framing. Even if dicta could be read to imply more than an easement, Great Northern's unequivocal 'easement only' result on a 1875 Act grant controls.

facts.client_belief: They argued that statutes Congress passed in 1906, 1909, 1922, and 1988 (43 U.S.C. §§ 912, 940; 16 U.S.C. § 1248(c)) all assume the United States retained a reversionary interest, so I must be wrong.
facts.court_record: Those statutes only purport to dispose of interests the United States already possessed — they do not create or modify the underlying property interest granted in 1875. They tell us how any retained interest is allocated; they do not tell us whether such an interest exists. Cf. Leo Sheep Co. v. United States, 440 U.S. 668, 681 (1979).

facts.client_belief: The 1988 National Trails System Improvements Act says any interest of the United States in such rights of way "shall remain in the United States" — so I worried the U.S. had locked in its reversion.
facts.court_record: 16 U.S.C. § 1248(c) was enacted 12 years after the 1976 patent. A 'policy shift' in 1988 cannot retroactively create an interest in land that the United States had already conveyed away in 1976. The 1988 Act has no effect on the client's parcel.

expected_inquiries: Ask the client for the original sawmill purchase records, family photographs, tax records, and any continuous-use evidence from 1946 through the 1976 patent and beyond.
Obtain a certified copy of the 1976 land patent, the underlying application file, BLM records, and any contemporaneous correspondence between the client's family and the Department of the Interior.
Pull the complete patent text, including all reservations, exceptions, and recitals, and prepare a side-by-side annotated copy showing the fee-simple grant against each carve-out.

Map every reservation in the patent into a comparison chart showing exact language, beneficiary, termination conditions, and duration — for use as a demonstrative against the Government's "implied reversion" argument.
Confirm with the client that no contemporaneous side agreements, correspondence, or BLM documents purport to add a reversionary clause beyond the four corners of the patent.
Obtain the LHP & P's 1908 right-of-way map and the Department of the Interior's approval documents to confirm the right of way was acquired under the 1875 Act and not some other authority.
Obtain the STB abandonment file, the railroad's notice of intent, the STB's approval order, and any photographs or contemporaneous reports documenting the physical removal of track and ties.
Identify the other 30 landowners, the disposition of their cases (default or settlement), and any communications among them that might support amicus or class-style coordination.

Confirm with the client his standing as both the individual successor in interest and trustee of the family trust holding the parcel, and assess whether any of the other 30 landowners might seek to reopen if the client prevails.
Prepare a one-page client explainer with a Restatement-based diagram showing how an easement, when abandoned, simply disappears (no transfer, no reversion).

Compile the Townsend, Stringham, and Great Northern opinions and prepare a chronology and policy-shift narrative for the merits brief, including the 1872 House Resolution declaring the end of railroad land subsidies.
Read Stalker and Steinke in full and prepare a summary for the client identifying the precise issue framed in each case and the absence of any easement-vs.-fee dispositive holding.
Prepare a citation table of §§ 912, 940, and § 1248(c) showing each provision's operative language, effective date, and effect on patentees, with the irony of §§ 912/940 highlighted.
Confirm the date of the 1988 Act and the 1976 patent, and prepare the temporal argument as a backstop in case any sympathy exists for a §1248(c)-based reversion claim.
Confirm the date of the 1988 Act and the 1976 patent, and prepare the temporal argument as a backstop in case any sympathy exists for a §1248(c)-based reversion claim.
memo_expectations: Document the family's continuous ownership and use of Pine Valley parcel for valuation and equitable framing, but counsel the client that title to the strip turns on the patent and the 1875 Act, not on length of residence.
Anchor the analysis to the precise four corners of the 1976 patent — its effective date, parties, conveyance language, and reservations control the dispute regardless of pre- or post-patent statutes.

Use the fee-simple-with-appurtenances language as the doctrinal baseline: anything the United States retained had to be reserved in clear and explicit terms, and any ambiguity in a federal land grant runs against the grantee — but only as to interests actually retained.

Highlight the textual contrast: when the United States wanted to retain a reversionary right with explicit termination conditions, it knew how to draft one — and it did, three times in this very patent. Its silence on the railroad right of way is therefore meaningful and supports the client's position, not the Government's.

Frame the patent's silence on abandonment as supporting the client's position: where the Government expressly drafted termination language for other reservations, the absence of any such language for the railroad right of way reinforces that the United States retained nothing in that strip.

Anchor the controlling statute (the 1875 Act) and confirm that the original 1908 grant is what governs the railroad's interest, not any later or earlier statute or doctrine — pre-1871 land-grant cases (Townsend, Stringham) are doctrinally irrelevant.
Establish 2004 as the operative abandonment date — that is the moment under common-law easement principles when the easement ceased to exist and the underlying fee became unencumbered.

Note that the Government's litigation strategy — sweeping in 31 landowners — confirms it understood the issue as systemic, not idiosyncratic; the case has implications for thousands of miles of rights of way and similarly situated patentees.

Note the sole-contesting-defendant posture as both a strategic risk and an opportunity — the absence of competing positions makes any precedent cleaner — and confirm that any judgment binds only the parties.

Brief the easement vs. fee distinction with care: the United States retained no reversionary interest because there was nothing to revert — abandonment of an easement extinguishes it and frees the underlying fee, which had passed to the client's family in 1976.

Distinguish Townsend (a pre-1871 grant) and address Stringham head-on: it was disavowed by Great Northern as inconsistent with the post-1871 policy shift, and Great Northern controls the 1875 Act analysis.

Brief Stalker/Steinke as factually and doctrinally inapposite — they involved priority of claims and station grounds, not the abandonment/reversion question — and emphasize that any contrary implication is foreclosed by Great Northern.

Drive home that the post-1875 statutes do not retroactively redefine the 1875 grant — and ironically that §§ 912 and 940 expressly transfer any retained interest to the patentee (i.e., to people exactly like the client's family), undermining the Government's own argument.

Brief the temporal point: the 1976 patent fixed the parties' rights, and the 1988 Act cannot reach back to create a federal interest in property already conveyed — to hold otherwise would raise serious takings and certainty-of-title concerns.

opening: Hi, I'm X, CEO of X Marine Exploration. I spoke with your office about a shipwreck recovery dispute involving a foreign government — I was hoping you could help me figure out my options.

facts.client_belief: My company is a deep-ocean exploration and shipwreck recovery business — that's what we do for a living.
facts.court_record: The client operates a publicly traded deep-ocean exploration and shipwreck recovery company. Its corporate identity and business activity are undisputed.

facts.client_belief: In 2006 we launched our 'Neptune Project' — researching ships that sank in heavily-traveled waters off the a strategic maritime location. Since we were doing thorough historical research, I figured that showed we were operating in good faith and gave us a clear path to whatever we found.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client launched the Neptune Project in 2006, identifying target vessels in the maritime search area, and that the target list included the foreign vessel the Foreign Naval Vessel (sunk 1804). The client's intuition that careful pre-recovery research alone establishes good-faith salvor status, however, is mistaken: identifying the Foreign Naval Vessel by name on the target list before recovery actually undercuts any later attempt to disclaim knowledge that the site might be a foreign naval vessel. The research is helpful for due-diligence framing, but it cuts against, not for, the client's later 'we didn't know' position on sovereign-vessel status.

facts.client_belief: We met with a representative from the Foreign Country's Ministry of Culture in advance — we recognized the Foreign Country might have a cultural interest in some of these wrecks and we invited them to participate. Since we reached out, I figured we'd done what was needed even if the Foreign Country didn't formally sign on.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client's CEO and counsel met with a Ministry of Culture representative, and that the Foreign Country did not approve salvage of any sunken the foreign vessel at that meeting. The client's intuition that courteous outreach satisfies the consent requirement, however, is mistaken: outreach is not the equivalent of consent or license, and any 'implied consent' theory will fail on this record because the Foreign Country unambiguously did not authorize salvage at the pre-project meeting.

facts.client_belief: In March 2007 we found a shipwreck in international waters about 100 miles west of the maritime strait, at a depth of 1,100 meters — and we recovered about 594,000 coins and other artifacts.
facts.court_record: The client discovered a shipwreck in international waters at 1,100m depth in March 2007 and recovered approximately 594,000 coins and other artifacts. The location, depth, and inventory of recovered items are undisputed.

facts.client_belief: On April 9, 2007 we filed a verified admiralty complaint in rem — listing claims under the law of finds and the law of salvage — and got a warrant of arrest in rem and were appointed substitute custodian. Once we did all that, I assumed our claim to the recovered items was locked in.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client filed an in rem complaint with two substantive counts (law of finds; salvage), that a warrant of arrest in rem issued against the unidentified shipwrecked vessel, and that the client was appointed substitute custodian. The client's assumption that those steps locked in his claim, however, is mistaken: the client was substitute custodian holding artifacts in custodia legis (the proceeding's custody), not in his own private capacity. That distinction defeats any later argument that the res should 'revert' to the client on dismissal — the artifacts were never the client's private property.

facts.client_belief: After we were ordered to disclose more, we acknowledged the site might be related to the foreign vessel 'the Foreign Naval Vessel' — and the Foreign Country immediately filed a motion to dismiss based on sovereign immunity.
facts.court_record: After ordered disclosure, the client acknowledged the possibility that the site related to the Foreign Naval Vessel. the Foreign Country then moved to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under the FSIA, claiming the res was a foreign Royal Navy frigate that exploded in combat in 1804.

facts.client_belief: Lawyers we consulted before told us the FSIA sovereign-immunity defense almost always wins for foreign navies, and after early motion practice it looked like our salvage claims wouldn't survive. I figured the case was effectively over before we even started.
facts.court_record: The client's prior advice that any FSIA defense automatically defeats a salvage claim is somewhat too pessimistic, but the client's deeper intuition — that this case has poor prospects — is well-founded for a different reason. The FSIA holding tracks established sovereign-immunity doctrine (a foreign-sovereign precedent; Republic of the Philippines v. Pimentel) and the cargo-immunity treatment under the Sunken Military Craft Act and the 1902 bilateral Treaty. Further review options are limited because the underlying analysis is well-grounded; the client's strategic posture should focus on logistics of return and risk-management for future operations rather than on continued litigation.

facts.client_belief: I assumed that since we found the wreck and physically recovered nearly 600,000 coins, our possession gave us strong claims under the law of finds and the law of salvage.
facts.court_record: In rem admiralty jurisdiction depends on the proceeding's ability to arrest the res. If the res is foreign sovereign property covered by FSIA § 1609, no in rem jurisdiction exists, regardless of whether the salvor has physical possession of recovered artifacts. The law of finds and law of salvage cannot proceed without valid in rem jurisdiction. The client's 'possession is nine-tenths of the law' intuition therefore does not apply: physical possession of recovered items does not cure the underlying jurisdictional defect.

facts.client_belief: I figured because we didn't find an "intact" vessel — just a debris field 368 by 110 meters with cannons, copper plates, and coins — the res couldn't legally be a "shipwreck" of the Foreign Naval Vessel.
facts.court_record: A 'shipwreck' under controlling admiralty doctrine includes a ship's wreckage whether or not the hull remains intact (Black's Law Dictionary 1504). The debris-field site is consistent with a vessel that exploded at the surface and descended through the water — and the client itself filed both its complaint and arrest motion against 'The Unidentified Shipwrecked Vessel.' The client's argument that an intact hull is needed for 'shipwreck' status therefore conflicts with both the plain meaning and the client's own pleading; pressing it would expose the client to a judicial-estoppel risk.

facts.client_belief: I was sure the evidence wasn't enough to prove the wreck was the Foreign Naval Vessel — the Foreign Country says she carried 900,000 coins and 33–50 cannons, we only recovered 595,000 coins and 17 cannons.
facts.court_record: On the available record, identification of the res as the Foreign Naval Vessel is well supported for sovereign-immunity purposes. The location is within the demise zone; the coin sample matches (almost all silver, late-18th/early-19th C., minted in Lima/Bolivia, none post-1804); the cannons match (6- and 12-pounders); a bronze culverin matches a distinctive the Foreign Naval Vessel cargo item; copper/tin ingots and copper hull-sheathing plates match. Failure to recover every item over 200 years on the seafloor does not negate identification. The client's 'inventory mismatch' argument therefore overstates the precision required for jurisdictional fact-finding, which is reviewed under a deferential standard.

facts.client_belief: the Foreign Country's motion to dismiss should've been treated like a Rule 56 summary judgment, with the court drawing all inferences in our favor.
facts.court_record: A Rule 12(b)(1) factual attack on subject matter jurisdiction is evaluated under a different standard than Rule 56 — the decision-maker may weigh evidence and is not constrained to view facts in the light most favorable to the non-movant (Carmichael v. Kellogg, Brown & Root). Rule 56 standards apply only when jurisdiction is 'intertwined with the merits,' which requires the same statute to provide both jurisdiction and the substantive cause of action. Here the client's substantive claims arise under salvage and finds law (not the FSIA), so the FSIA jurisdictional question is not intertwined with the merits. The client's expectation of Rule 56-style 'all inferences in our favor' treatment therefore overstates the procedural protection available on a § 1609 sovereign-immunity challenge.

facts.client_belief: I expected an oral evidentiary hearing where I could cross-examine the Foreign Country's historians.
facts.court_record: A trial-level decision-maker has discretion to resolve a Rule 12(b)(1) factual challenge on the written record without an oral evidentiary hearing (a precedent on jurisdictional hearings). Here the available record contained 125+ attachments, expert affidavits, counter-affidavits, original foreign documents with translations, photographs, and excerpts from histories. The client's expectation of an oral evidentiary hearing therefore overstates his procedural rights — paper hearings are the norm where the record is comprehensive, and oral cross-examination is not a matter of right under Rule 12(b)(1).
