opening: Hi, I'm X. I spoke with your office about a property rights dispute involving a government beach restoration project — I was hoping you could help me figure out my options.

facts.client_belief: I own beachfront property in the State. Part of what makes it valuable is that I have special legal rights as a waterfront owner — including the right to receive new sand that naturally washes up on my beach over time.
facts.court_record: Under state law, littoral (beachfront) property owners have certain special rights regarding the water and foreshore, including the right of access to the water, the right to use the water for certain purposes, the right to an unobstructed view, and the right to receive accretions (gradual additions of sand/sediment) and relictions. the State-law authority has long recognized these as property rights akin to easements.

facts.client_belief: The mean high-water line is the boundary between my private property and the state's public land. That line naturally shifts over time, and when it shifts seaward, my property grows — so I figured any process that interferes with that growth must be a taking.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that, under state law, the mean high-water line (the average reach of high tide over the preceding 19 years) is ordinarily the boundary between private littoral property and state-owned land, and that when the mean high-water line moves seaward through gradual accretion, the littoral owner automatically takes title to the newly dry land. The client's intuition that any state interference with the boundary's natural movement is automatically a taking, however, is overstated. The right to receive accretions is itself contingent on the cause of the boundary movement (accretion vs. avulsion), and state law has long treated avulsion-type changes differently — a sudden or state-engineered fill can lawfully fix the boundary without disturbing the underlying right.

facts.client_belief: There's a difference between gradual sand buildup and a sudden dramatic change to the shoreline. When sand builds up gradually, that becomes my property. A sudden change — like from a hurricane — is treated differently. So a state-engineered fill must clearly count as my gain, since it isn't a hurricane.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that state law, consistent with common law, distinguishes between accretion (gradual and imperceptible addition of land) and avulsion (sudden or perceptible change to the shoreline), and that littoral owners automatically gain title to accretions but not to avulsions. The client's intuition that a state-engineered beach-fill project must therefore count as accretion-type 'gain' for the upland owner, however, runs the doctrine in the wrong direction. the State precedent (Martin v. Busch; Bryant v. Peppe) treats sudden or state-engineered changes as avulsion-type events for boundary purposes, so the boundary does not move with the project even though the new sand is added quickly.

facts.client_belief: Several hurricanes eroded about 6.9 miles of beach along the project area. The local municipality then got permits to dump dredged sand onto the beach, adding about 75 feet of dry sand seaward of where my property line used to be. The government basically created a new strip of beach in front of my property.
facts.court_record: In 2003, The local municipality applied for permits to restore 6.9 miles of hurricane-eroded beach by depositing dredged sand. The project added approximately 75 feet of dry sand seaward of the mean high-water line (which became the erosion-control line). The scope and mechanics of the project are undisputed.

facts.client_belief: Because the government put that new sand there, the state set a fixed 'erosion control line' right at the old mean high-water line. That line is now the permanent boundary of my property — it doesn't move anymore. So even if the sea naturally deposits more sand and the water retreats further, I get no benefit from that.
facts.court_record: Under the State's Beach and Shore Preservation Act, once a beach restoration project is undertaken, the Board sets a fixed erosion control line to replace the fluctuating mean high-water line as the boundary between littoral and state property. Once recorded, common law ceases to add to upland property by accretion. Thereafter, even if natural accretion moves the mean high-water line seaward, the littoral owner's property remains bounded by the permanent erosion-control line.

facts.client_belief: I believe the state just took two of my property rights away without paying me a dime: (1) my right to receive future accretions — any new sand will now belong to the state, not me; and (2) my right to have my land physically touch the water, which is now separated from my property by this new state-owned beach strip.
facts.court_record: On the available record, the project's order has eliminated, in some readings, two previously held littoral attributes: (1) the prospective right to receive accretions (because the boundary is now fixed at the erosion-control line), and (2) any independent right of physical contact between the upland and the water. the State-law authority, however, treats the right to accretions as not yet 'taken' because the project is treated as an avulsion-type event under Martin v. Busch and Bryant v. Peppe, and treats the contact-with-water concept as protected only through the still-preserved right of access. The client's view that two distinct rights have been taken outright therefore overstates the doctrinal status of those interests under state law as it currently stands.

facts.client_belief: The state created this new beach strip on purpose — it wasn't a natural event. So the whole 'avulsion' rule shouldn't apply here. Avulsion is about sudden natural events like storms, not government-engineered fill projects. The government can't just manufacture an avulsion to take away my property rights.
facts.court_record: The client argues that state-caused avulsions should be treated differently from natural avulsions with respect to the right to accretion. Prior state law, however, treats state-engineered changes the same way for boundary purposes (Martin v. Busch; Bryant v. Peppe analogized state drainage to avulsion). The client's intuition that 'state-manufactured' avulsion is doctrinally distinguishable therefore runs against existing the State-law authority, which would have to be revisited or distinguished for that argument to succeed.

facts.client_belief: My right to future accretions is a vested property right, not some contingent future interest. The state's framing of it as a 'future contingent interest' is just a legal fiction designed to justify taking it without compensation.
facts.court_record: the State-law authority on the subject describes the right to receive accretions as a future contingent interest rather than a vested property right, and treats it as not 'implicated' by a beach-restoration project performed under the Beach and Shore Preservation Act. The client's view that this characterization is a 'legal fiction' overlooks that future contingent classification is consistent with how the right has historically been treated under the State property law. Whether that classification is itself a 'judicial taking' is a separate question on which the controlling federal authority is splintered.

facts.client_belief: The State Beach and Shore Preservation Act preserved 'all common-law riparian rights' — those are the exact words in the statute. So even if the Act is constitutional in general, the Department's order violated the Act itself by eliminating two of my common-law littoral rights.
facts.court_record: Earlier the State-appellate analysis treated the Act's preservation of 'all common-law riparian rights' as meaning that eliminating the right to accretions and the right of contact with water would be impermissible under the Act and would require additional administrative process. Subsequent the State-law authority, however, found no unconstitutional taking and accepted the project under the Act. The client's intuition that the statutory text gives an independent route to victory therefore ran into the State's reading of how the Act interacts with avulsion-type events.

facts.client_belief: The state's new beach creates a permanent public strip between my property and the water. Every other beachfront property owner in the State can at least touch the water. I'm essentially no longer a waterfront owner even though I paid for waterfront property.
facts.court_record: Existing the State-law authority holds that there is no independent littoral right to have the property's boundary always be the mean high-water line or to have the property maintain physical contact with the water, separate from the right of access. The right of contact with the water exists to preserve the upland owner's core littoral right of access, which the Act does not infringe — the client retains the right of access to the water. The client's view that the new strip of public beach makes him 'no longer a waterfront owner' therefore overstates the legal effect: he retains access (and view, and use), even though the boundary is now fixed.

facts.client_belief: I still have my other littoral rights — the right to access the water, the right to an unobstructed view, the right to use the water. So even if some rights are gone, the rest haven't been taken — I should still be okay.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the State's Beach and Shore Preservation Act expressly preserves all common-law riparian rights other than the right to accretions for the footprint covered by the project, that § 161.201 states property owners 'continue to be entitled to all common-law riparian rights' other than the right to receive accretions, and that the client retains the rights of access, view, and water use. The client's intuition that the retention of these other rights means 'no real taking,' however, is overstated. Even partial extinction of property attributes (the right to accretions; arguably contact-with-water) can support a takings claim — preservation of unrelated rights does not foreclose the claim, although it does cabin the scope of any compensation.

facts.client_belief: We formed a nonprofit corporation to fight this project on behalf of all the affected beachfront homeowners. The corporation itself has standing to sue.
facts.court_record: The client is a nonprofit corporation formed by owners of beachfront property bordering the project.

expected_inquiries: Ask the client to identify precisely which littoral rights they believe have been affected — accretion, contact with water, access, view, or use — to triage which are still viable claims and which have been definitively foreclosed by this ruling.

Ask whether the erosion-control line was set at exactly the pre-existing mean high-water line (as assumed in this case) or landward of it, because any landward placement would constitute a taking even under the State-law analysis adopted at the state level.

Ask whether the client has experienced any concrete economic harm — reduced property value, inability to sell, changed tax assessments — so the lawyer can assess whether a damages or inverse-condemnation claim remains viable at the state level.

Ask whether any natural accretion has occurred since the erosion-control line was recorded, and if so, whether the state has claimed that newly accreted land, to determine whether a concrete deprivation of the accretion right has materialized.

Ask whether the beach has eroded back landward of the erosion-control line over a substantial portion of the shoreline since the project, which would trigger the cancellation mechanism in § 161.211(2)-(3) and potentially restore the fluctuating mean high-water line.

Clarify whether the client intends to challenge the project itself (as a regulatory or physical taking) or solely the existing the State-law ruling that no taking occurred — these are distinct theories with different procedural postures.

Ask whether the client's property is still held, whether they have sold or plan to sell, and whether any title insurance company has raised issues about the erosion-control line, as these facts affect both standing and remedy.

Ask whether the client's property is still held, whether they have sold or plan to sell, and whether any title insurance company has raised issues about the erosion-control line, as these facts affect both standing and remedy.
memo_expectations: Analyze whether the doctrine of avulsion, as applied in Martin v. Busch and Bryant v. Peppe, applies to state-engineered beach fill projects and whether any State precedent supports an exception when the State itself causes the avulsion.

Evaluate whether the client had an 'established' property right to future accretions that was superior to the State's right to fill its own submerged land, as that threshold showing is required under both the judicial-takings analysis and the broader Takings Clause analysis.

Analyze whether there is an independent littoral right to maintain physical contact between private property and the water, distinct from the right of access, and whether the erosion-control line eliminated that right.

Assess the scope and applicability of the State's Beach and Shore Preservation Act, including whether § 161.201's preservation of 'all common-law riparian rights' (except accretions) adequately protects the client' remaining littoral rights.

Examine whether the judicial-takings doctrine (the plurality opinion in this area) provides a viable avenue for future claims and what standard of 'established property right' must be met to trigger it.

Analyze the standing requirements for prospective and retrospective relief, including whether the client (a nonprofit association of beachfront owners) has associational standing and whether the ripeness/compensation-exhaustion requirements of Williamson County affect the litigation strategy.

Assess the protective mechanism in § 161.211 — the erosion-control line becomes null and void if the beach erodes back landward of that line over a substantial portion — and whether it adequately compensates for the loss of the accretion right.

opening: Hi, I'm X. I spoke with your office about a property dispute involving the government — I was hoping you could help me figure out my options.

facts.client_belief: I own land north of State Highway 10 between Riverside City and Lakeside City. The State built a barrier along the highway median. That barrier was installed as part of a flood-evacuation project.
facts.court_record: The client and more than 120 other landowners own property north of State Highway 10 between Riverside City and Lakeside City, the State. The State installed a roughly 3-foot-tall barrier along the highway median as part of a flood-evacuation infrastructure project. These facts are not disputed.

facts.client_belief: The barrier works like a dam — it keeps the south side of the highway dry during heavy rain. But it does that by pushing all the floodwater onto my land to the north. That's exactly what happened during Hurricane A in 2017 and Tropical Storm B in 2019, so this has to count as a taking automatically.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the median barrier performed as designed during Hurricane A (August 2017) and Tropical Storm B (2019), keeping the south lane open by holding back stormwater, which in turn submerged the client's land north of the highway. The client's intuition that the dam-like causal mechanism alone establishes a taking, however, is overstated. Causation is one element of the inverse-condemnation analysis, but the State can still contest whether the harm was 'reasonably foreseeable,' whether it constitutes a substantial physical invasion (and not merely incidental damage), and whether the State took the property 'for public use' within the meaning of the Takings Clause.

facts.client_belief: The flooding destroyed crops, killed livestock, damaged businesses, and ruined family heirlooms. Some owners were displaced from their homes entirely. With damage that severe, we should obviously be compensated.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the operative complaint alleges the flooding displaced the client and other owners from their homes, damaged businesses, ruined crops, killed livestock, and destroyed family heirlooms. The client's intuition that severity of damage automatically translates into compensation, however, overlooks two distinct doctrinal problems. First, severity addresses the measure of damages, not the threshold takings question of whether a 'taking' occurred. Second, certain categories of loss (e.g., personal-property contents like family heirlooms) may not be compensable under takings doctrine even when the underlying real-property taking is established — those losses typically run through tort theories that face their own sovereign-immunity hurdles.

facts.client_belief: Because southeast the State gets heavy rain regularly, this isn't a one-time problem. That barrier is still there, and it will flood my land again in future storms.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that heavy rainfall is not uncommon in southeast the State and that the median barrier will continue to cause flooding on the client's land during future storms. This ongoing-harm allegation is accepted as true at the pleading stage.

facts.client_belief: the State took my property to store stormwater — that's a taking, plain and simple. I should be compensated under the Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause, and I figured I could just sue directly under the federal Constitution to enforce that right.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the Takings Clause of the Fifth Amendment guarantees that private property shall not be taken for public use without just compensation, and that an inverse-condemnation claim may arise when government action floods private land. The client's intuition that the federal Constitution itself supplies a direct cause of action against a State, however, is contested doctrine. Existing federal authority leaves open whether the Takings Clause is self-executing against the States; in practice, the State's parallel inverse-condemnation cause of action is usually the operative vehicle, and federal jurisdiction may turn on whether that state-law remedy is adequate.

facts.client_belief: I filed my case in state court, and the State removed it to federal court. All the similar suits were consolidated into one federal proceeding with a combined complaint.
facts.court_record: The client filed in state court, the State removed the case to federal court, and the cases were consolidated into a single proceeding with one operative complaint raising inverse-condemnation claims under both the State Constitution and the Fifth Amendment Takings Clause. These procedural facts are undisputed.

facts.client_belief: An earlier appellate ruling in our case threw out the federal Takings Clause claim, holding that there's no direct federal cause of action against a state under the Takings Clause. I figured that meant my federal claim was effectively dead.
facts.court_record: It is correct as a matter of intermediate appellate practice in this area that the Takings Clause as applied to the States through the Fourteenth Amendment has been read not to provide a direct right of action for takings claims against a State. The client's intuition that this dooms the federal claim entirely, however, is too pessimistic: the question whether the Takings Clause supplies its own cause of action remains contested, and where the State provides an adequate inverse-condemnation procedure, the substantive Takings Clause right can still be vindicated through that state-law vehicle. The intermediate appellate result therefore narrows the procedural path, but does not foreclose recovery.

facts.client_belief: A subsequent appellate review specifically agreed to decide whether a property owner can sue directly under the Takings Clause. I expected a ruling on that question.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that subsequent appellate review on the cause-of-action question ultimately declined to answer it. Because the State law provides a cause of action through which Takings Clause rights can be vindicated, the predicate for reaching the constitutional question was absent. The client's expectation of a definitive constitutional ruling, however, overstates what the appellate record actually delivered: the case was vacated and remanded on the narrower ground that an adequate state-law vehicle exists, and the deeper constitutional question remains formally open for a future case.

facts.client_belief: I may need to amend my complaint to proceed under state-law cause of action rather than directly under the Fifth Amendment.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the State acknowledged proceeding under the state-law inverse-condemnation cause of action would require an amendment to the complaint, and that the State confirmed it would not oppose such an amendment. The client is to be permitted to pursue Takings Clause claims through state-law cause of action.

expected_inquiries: Ask the client for documentation of all flooding events, including dates, photographs, and estimated property damage, to build a timeline of harm tied to specific storms.

Request copies of any prior communications with the State or its agencies — including any condemnation offers, administrative proceedings, or formal notices — that may affect the pleading or litigation posture.

Clarify whether the client's complaint has been formally amended (or whether a motion for leave to amend has been filed) to assert state-law inverse-condemnation cause of action, and confirm the State has not reversed its non-opposition assurance.
Ask whether any of the other 120+ petitioners have already settled or reached individual agreements with the State, as this could affect class dynamics and damages valuation.

Inquire whether the client has obtained a professional appraisal of property value before and after the barrier installation, and whether any crop, livestock, or business-loss records have been preserved.

Ask whether the client has consulted the State-licensed property or condemnation attorney who can advise on the state-law cause of action, since the appellate ruling channels the claims through state law.
Ask whether the client preserved arguments below preserving the direct-federal-cause-of-action theory for any continued review, and identify which arguments are still live versus foreclosed.
Confirm whether the State has formalized its non-opposition to the amendment to assert the state-law cause of action and whether any limitations or exhaustion deadline affects the pleading strategy.

Confirm the State's non-opposition assurance is on the record, identify any conditions the State attached to it, and verify the proposed amended pleading conforms to the State inverse-condemnation requirements.
Confirm Texas's non-opposition assurance is on the record, identify any conditions Texas attached to it, and verify the proposed amended pleading conforms to Texas inverse-condemnation requirements.
memo_expectations: Analyze whether state-law inverse-condemnation cause of action is adequate to vindicate the petitioners' rights under the federal Takings Clause, including whether the State courts may award the full just compensation required by the Fifth Amendment.

Counsel the client that the dam-like causal mechanism is necessary but not sufficient — the inverse-condemnation theory still requires foreseeability, substantiality, and a public-use purpose, each of which the State can contest on a fuller record.

Evaluate whether the proposed amendment to the operative complaint to invoke state-law cause of action is procedurally permissible and strategically advisable, including any statute-of-limitations concerns and the cabined scope of the just-compensation remedy versus tort-style consequential damages.

Examine the strength of the underlying inverse-condemnation claim on the merits — specifically whether repeated flooding caused by a permanent government structure constitutes a compensable taking under both the State and federal law.

Address the ongoing-harm dimension and the cause-of-action question together: even with strong substantive merits, the federal-vehicle question is a real litigation risk if the State's inverse-condemnation procedure is later found inadequate. Counsel the client that the right to compensation is real, but the procedural vehicle for asserting it is the live dispute.
Identify all potential defendants (state agencies, highway authorities) and assess sovereign-immunity issues under the State law that may affect the scope of available relief.

Reset the client's expectations: the intermediate appellate ruling forecloses a direct federal cause of action on this record, but the substantive Takings Clause right can still be vindicated through the State's inverse-condemnation procedure. Frame the engagement around the state-law vehicle.

Walk the client through the state-law-vehicle pivot: the case proceeds through the State inverse-condemnation cause of action, not the federal Takings Clause directly, and the substantive merits remain to be litigated.
Move quickly to file the amended complaint asserting state-law inverse-condemnation cause of action, before any non-opposition assurance is reconsidered or any limitations deadline runs.

opening: Hi, I'm X. I spoke with your office about a land-use permitting dispute with a state water management district — I was hoping you could help me figure out my options.

facts.client_belief: I bought a 14.9-acre tract south of County Road 50, east of the City, all the way back in 1972. It's right next to one of the City's major tolled expressways.
facts.court_record: In 1972 the client purchased an undeveloped 14.9-acre tract on the south side of County Road 50, less than 1,000 feet from the expressway interchange in Lakeside County, the State. Ownership and acreage are not disputed.

facts.client_belief: Most of my land is classified as wetlands by the State, but the northern part actually drains pretty well — the only standing water is in tire ruts on a dirt road used to access the power lines.
facts.court_record: Most of the property is classified as wetlands under the State law. The northern 3.7 acres drains well, with the most significant standing water occurring in ruts in an unpaved access road; the southern section has a small creek, forested uplands, and wetlands sometimes a foot deep. These factual conditions are undisputed.

facts.client_belief: Because the land is mostly wetlands, the State law says I need two permits — an MSSW permit and a WRM permit — before I can build anything on it. I figured that since the regulators have all this authority, anything they ask of me is just part of the permitting trade-off and not really a 'taking.'
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that under the State's 1972 Water Resources Act and the 1984 the State Wetlands Protection Act, an applicant wishing to build on wetlands must obtain both a Management and Storage of Surface Water (MSSW) permit (state statute § 373.413(1)) and a Wetlands Resource Management (WRM) permit (Fla. Stat. § 373.414(1)). The client's intuition that broad permitting authority insulates any condition the District attaches, however, is mistaken. The District has statutory authority to impose 'reasonable conditions,' but that authority is bounded by the federal Takings Clause as construed in Nollan, Dolan, and now the unconstitutional-conditions framework — not every condition is permissible just because some condition would be.

facts.client_belief: In 1994 I applied for both permits to develop just 3.7 acres on the north end — raise the elevation, build on it, grade it down to the power-line corridor, and put in a dry-bed pond for stormwater. Since I'm only developing a small fraction of the property, I assumed any mitigation requirement would be modest.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client applied to the District for MSSW and WRM permits to develop the 3.7-acre northern section by raising the elevation, grading to the power-line elevation, and installing a dry-bed stormwater retention pond. The client's intuition that a small footprint guarantees a modest mitigation demand, however, overlooks how the District actually structures mitigation: the demand is anchored to the offsetting environmental impact, but the District retains broad discretion in how it values that impact and what 'mitigation' it accepts. The 3.7-acre framing matters for nexus and rough proportionality, but does not by itself ceiling the scope of what the District can demand.

facts.client_belief: To make up for any wetland impact, I offered to give the District a permanent conservation easement on the roughly 11-acre southern part of my property — basically locking up almost three-quarters of my land. I figured an offer that generous would obviously be enough.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client offered to deed to the District a conservation easement on approximately 11 acres of the southern section to mitigate the environmental impact of development on the 3.7-acre northern section. The client's intuition that the size of the volunteered offer is itself dispositive, however, is mistaken. Mitigation adequacy under the District's policies turns on the qualitative match between offered offset and project impact (e.g., wetland type, hydrologic function, location), not raw acreage. A nominally 'generous' offer can still fall short on the District's metrics, which is exactly what triggered the District's two-alternative counterproposal.

facts.client_belief: The District said an 11-acre conservation easement wasn't enough. They told me I had to either (a) shrink my development from 3.7 acres down to 1 acre and put a 13.9-acre easement on the rest, or (b) keep the 3.7-acre project but pay contractors to fix culverts or fill ditches on District-owned wetlands miles away. Both options are obviously illegal demands and I figured presenting two options doesn't fix that.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the District found the 11-acre easement inadequate and offered the client two alternatives: (1) reduce development to 1 acre and grant a 13.9-acre conservation easement; or (2) build on the full 3.7 acres and pay to enhance approximately 50 acres of District-owned wetlands several miles away. The District also indicated it would consider equivalent alternatives. The client's intuition that 'both options are obviously illegal' is too strong: each alternative must be analyzed independently under Nollan/Dolan, and presenting an option set does not by itself prove that the District has fixed an unconstitutional condition. The client's later doctrinal win established that offering an option does not automatically immunize the offsite-mitigation alternative — but it does not automatically condemn it either.

facts.client_belief: I refused both options because I thought they were way too much for the actual environmental impact of building on 3.7 acres. So the District denied my permits, and I sued under Fla. Stat. § 373.617(2). I figured that statute clearly gives me damages whenever an agency does something unconstitutional in a permitting context.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client refused both alternatives, that the District denied the permit applications, and that the client sued under Fla. Stat. § 373.617(2), which authorizes monetary damages for agency action that is an 'unreasonable exercise of the state's police power constituting a taking without just compensation.' The client's intuition that the statute reaches any unconstitutional permit condition, however, may overstate its scope: the holding that no taking occurs when a permit is denied and no condition is actually imposed creates a serious open question whether § 373.617(2) supports a damages remedy at all in a no-taking, unconstitutional-conditions scenario.

facts.client_belief: After a 2-day bench trial, the trial court found that the offsite mitigation demand had no nexus and no rough proportionality to my development's environmental impact, so the District's actions were unlawful under Nollan and Dolan.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that, after a 2-day bench trial, the trial-level finder of fact found that the property's northern section had already been 'seriously degraded' by surrounding construction, and that further mitigation through payment for offsite improvements lacked both a nexus and rough proportionality to the environmental impact of the proposed development. The trial-level finder therefore held the District's actions unlawful under Nollan and Dolan, and the intermediate appellate court affirmed.

facts.client_belief: Higher-level state authority reversed and basically said Nollan and Dolan don't apply when the government denies my permit, and don't apply when the demand is for money instead of land. I think both of those rulings were wrong.
facts.court_record: Higher-level state-law authority (77 So.3d 1220) distinguished Nollan and Dolan on two grounds: (1) the District denied rather than approved the permit; and (2) the District demanded money rather than a real-property interest. The client is correct that both distinctions are doctrinally weak under federal unconstitutional-conditions doctrine — Nollan/Dolan apply to denied-permit conditions and to monetary exactions alike — but securing that doctrinal corrective is not the same as winning the merits, which depend on whether a 'demand' was made and whether nexus and proportionality are satisfied.

facts.client_belief: The District's lawyer keeps saying the offsite-mitigation demand never amounted to a real 'demand' — they say it was just a suggestion in a back-and-forth negotiation. That's nonsense; they told me my permit was denied because I refused.
facts.court_record: Available authority is split on whether the District's communications crossed the line from non-exclusive negotiation suggestions into a Nollan/Dolan-grade 'demand.' One reading characterizes the District as offering non-exclusive suggestions for bringing the application into compliance, including offsite mitigation 'in broad strokes.' Another reading treats the District's behavior as sufficiently concrete to constitute a demand. The federal review expressly left this question 'open' for the state-court remand. Whether a demand of sufficient concreteness was made is therefore unresolved, and the client's confidence that 'they told me my permit was denied because I refused' will need to be supported by a record showing the offsite condition was concrete rather than negotiable.

facts.client_belief: I figured the District couldn't get away with calling its money demand a 'tax' to dodge Nollan and Dolan — that would just be a workaround.
facts.court_record: Taxes and user fees are not takings (Brown v. Legal Foundation of Wash., 538 U.S. 216, 243 n.2). The Court declined to draw a precise line between permitting fees and impermissible exactions but observed that the State law sharply circumscribes the District's taxing power (Fla. Stat. §§ 373.503, 373.109), and the District itself has consistently maintained that the money demanded was a substitute for a conservation easement, not a tax. State courts routinely distinguish taxes from exactions when policing local taxing authority, and that body of state law will inform the federal question on remand.

facts.client_belief: Now that I have a favorable federal-level ruling on the legal questions, the merits of my Nollan/Dolan claim should be a slam dunk on remand — the trial-level finder already found no nexus and no rough proportionality.
facts.court_record: The federal-level review 'expresse[d] no view on the merits' of the client's claim that the District's actions failed to comply with Nollan/Dolan. The case was remanded for further proceedings, including the open questions of whether a demand of sufficient concreteness was made and whether nexus and rough proportionality are satisfied. Trial-level findings were favorable but the higher-level state ruling did not affirm them, and remand reopens those issues. The client's expectation that the favorable legal-framework ruling translates automatically into merits victory therefore overstates what the federal-level decision actually decided.

facts.client_belief: Since the federal-level ruling agreed Nollan and Dolan apply, I should be entitled to monetary damages under Fla. Stat. § 373.617(2) — the District's action was unconstitutional, so it must be a 'taking' for purposes of the statute.
facts.court_record: The doctrinal holding that 'where the permit is denied and the condition is never imposed, nothing has been taken' applies here. The Fifth Amendment mandates just compensation only for takings, not for unconstitutional-conditions claims that never ripened into a taking. Whether Fla. Stat. § 373.617(2) — which provides damages for action 'constituting a taking without just compensation' — covers an unconstitutional-conditions claim where no actual taking occurred is a question of state law that has not been decided at the federal level, and the available state-law signals (including the available authority advanced by the District) read the statute to provide damages only for consummated takings.

facts.client_belief: The District also says I sued in the wrong court — that I should have gone to the State appellate court under the Administrative Procedure Act, not filed for damages in the trial court. I think they're just trying to delay.
facts.court_record: The District argued that under Key Haven Associated Enterprises, Inc. v. Board of Trustees of Internal Improvement Trust Fund, 427 So. 2d 153 (Fla. 1982), the client should have first sought review of the permit denial in the appropriate the State appellate forum under the State APA (Fla. Stat. §§ 120.68(1)–(2)). At the federal level, this state-procedural question was not second-guessed and remains potentially open. The client's intuition that the District is just trying to delay therefore underestimates the doctrinal seriousness of the exhaustion argument — it could be dispositive even if the merits favor the client.

facts.client_belief: Worst case, even if I can't get money damages, I should at least be entitled to an injunction making the District issue my permit without the unconstitutional conditions.
facts.court_record: Available remedies under federal law were not directly decided because the client brought the claim under state law: federal authority did not 'decide whether federal law authorizes plaintiffs to recover damages for unconstitutional conditions claims predicated on the Takings Clause' on this record. Whether injunctive relief, declaratory relief, or damages is available will depend on the State statutory and common law and on the scope of any state-court remand.

expected_inquiries: Ask the client (or the estate's representative) for the 1972 deed, current title commitment, surveys, parcel maps, tax bills, and any inheritance or estate documents.

Ask the client for any wetland delineations, hydrology reports, prior environmental site assessments, photographs, and the wildlife survey referenced at trial; identify the experts who testified at the 2-day bench trial.

Ask the client to produce the original MSSW and WRM permit applications, all District correspondence, the District's policy and rule materials, and the Henderson Act criteria the District actually applied to this proposal.
Ask the client for the engineering plans, stormwater calculations, environmental impact submissions, and any expert reports that accompanied the original 1994 applications.

Ask the client for the draft conservation-easement language and any appraisals or valuations (then and now) of the 11-acre easement; obtain expert assistance to value the offered easement against the actual environmental impact of the 3.7-acre project.

Obtain the District's written communications setting out both alternatives, internal District staff reports, the cost estimates the District relied on for the offsite work, and any documentation of the District's 'never require a particular project' policy.

Ask the client for the operative state-court complaint, all amendments, the District's answer, and the State case law construing the scope of § 373.617(2) — including whether it has ever been read to cover an unconstitutional-conditions claim.

Obtain the full trial transcript, exhibits, expert reports, the trial-level findings of fact and conclusions of law, the intermediate appellate opinion (5 So.3d 8), and the higher-level state opinion (77 So.3d 1220) to build a complete record.

Subpoena District staff communications, internal memoranda, draft permits, and hearing transcripts; depose the District officials who handled the application about whether they viewed the alternatives as conditions or merely as suggestions; obtain documents from the final hearing where the District asked the client to 'go back with the staff over the next month and renegotiate.'

Pull the District's prior pleadings and oral-argument transcripts confirming the money demand was framed as a substitute for an easement; obtain the State statutes and authority on the District's narrow taxing and fee-setting authority.

Develop a remand strategy memo identifying every issue the District can re-litigate, the standard of review on each, and the evidentiary record needed; coordinate with the State-licensed counsel on procedural posture before the higher-level state forum.

Research every State decision construing § 373.617(2) and the underlying Bert Harris Act framework; identify any State case that has awarded damages for an unconstitutional condition that was never accepted; draft alternative pleadings seeking permit issuance and declaratory relief in addition to damages.

Obtain the State case law on the Key Haven exhaustion doctrine and on the interaction between the Bert Harris/§ 373.617 cause of action and the State APA; coordinate with the State appellate counsel; consider conditional protective filings before any limitations or exhaustion deadline.

Research whether a § 1983 Takings Clause / unconstitutional-conditions claim remains viable in federal court after the recent overruling of Williamson County's state-litigation requirement, and identify any limitations or claim-preclusion issues; draft amended pleadings adding equitable and declaratory counts if not already pleaded.

Research whether a § 1983 Takings Clause / unconstitutional-conditions claim remains viable in federal court after the recent overruling of Williamson County's state-litigation requirement, and identify any limitations or claim-preclusion issues; draft amended pleadings adding equitable and declaratory counts if not already pleaded.
memo_expectations: Confirm the client's record title, the 1972 purchase date, and the precise legal description of the parcel — these facts establish standing, the relevant 'parcel as a whole' for any Penn Central or per se takings analysis, and the temporal baseline for investment-backed expectations.

Lock down the wetlands-classification facts and the actual hydrology of the parcel — useful for the nexus/proportionality analysis on remand, since the District's mitigation demand must offset effects of development on wetlands of a particular character and quality, not wetlands in the abstract.

Frame the regulatory baseline carefully: the District has statutory authority to impose 'reasonable conditions' on permits, but that authority is bounded by the federal Takings Clause as construed in Nollan, Dolan, and the unconstitutional-conditions doctrine.

Treat the 1994 development plan as the operative 'proposed land use' for nexus and rough-proportionality analysis. Any constitutional review must compare the District's exactions to the impacts of this specific development, not a hypothetical larger or different project.

Document the offered 11-acre conservation easement as the client's baseline mitigation proposal. This offer is the comparator against which the District's counter-demands must be measured for nexus and rough proportionality.

Catalogue both alternatives in detail. Both must be analyzed under Nollan/Dolan; the offer of a less-ambitious 1-acre alternative does not obviate the need to scrutinize the offsite-mitigation alternative for the 3.7-acre project the client actually proposed.

Pin down the precise statutory cause of action invoked. Fla. Stat. § 373.617(2) authorizes damages only for action 'constituting a taking without just compensation.' The doctrinal holding that no taking occurred here (because no condition was imposed) creates a serious open question whether the statute supports a damages remedy.

Treat the trial-level findings on nexus and rough proportionality as a meaningful but contingent asset: those findings are intact and were affirmed by the intermediate appellate court, but the higher-level state ruling reversed on legal grounds and the merits of the constitutional question were not addressed by the federal review — they remain open.

Treat 'whether a demand was made' as the most vulnerable open question on remand. Build a factual record that the District's communications crossed from negotiation into a concrete condition: written staff reports tying the permit denial to refusal of specific offsite work, hearing transcripts, and the District's contemporaneous understanding that approval was conditioned on acceding to one of the two listed alternatives.

Pre-empt any pivot by the District to recharacterize the offsite-mitigation demand as a 'tax' or 'user fee.' the State-law constraints on the District's taxing power and the District's own litigation positions make that recharacterization implausible — but anticipate it and brief the tax/exaction distinction (Brown, Phillips, Webb's, Brushaber).

Reset client expectations: SCOTUS resolved the legal framework but did not decide the merits. On remand the District may litigate (i) whether it made a Nollan/Dolan-grade demand, (ii) whether the demand had nexus, (iii) whether it was roughly proportional, (iv) whether the demand was a tax outside the doctrine, and (v) whether the State law authorizes damages for an unconstitutional condition that was never accepted.

Brief the state-law remedy question carefully. The federal Takings Clause does not itself supply a damages remedy in this no-taking scenario. The viability of damages turns on the State-statutory question that the higher-level state forum has not yet answered, and that prevailing state-law signals predict will be answered against the client. Prepare alternative remedies (injunction directing issuance of the permit on lawful conditions; declaratory relief; attorneys' fees if available) in case damages are unavailable.

Identify and research the exhaustion and forum-selection arguments preserved by the District. The state-procedural questions remain open for the State courts to address in the first instance; they could be dispositive even if the merits favor the client.

Plan remedies in tiers: (1) primary — declaratory and injunctive relief ordering issuance of the permit on lawful conditions; (2) secondary — damages under § 373.617 if covered; (3) backup — separate § 1983 federal claim if state remedy is unavailable, subject to the State court rulings and any abstention or preclusion issues.

opening: Hi, I'm X. I spoke with your office about a land-use dispute involving a fee the county charged me as a condition of getting a building permit — I was hoping you could help me figure out my options.

facts.client_belief: I own a parcel in the County near a state highway that the county's General Plan classifies as Low Density Residential. My wife and I applied for a permit to build a small prefabricated house there so we could raise our grandson.
facts.court_record: The client owned a parcel near a state highway classified as 'Low Density Residential' under the County's General Plan. He and his wife applied for a residential building permit for a prefabricated home to raise their grandson. These background facts are undisputed.

facts.client_belief: The county told me I had to pay a $23,420 traffic impact fee just to get my building permit. That's a huge amount for a modest home — I figured a fee that disproportionate to a single small house has to be unconstitutional on its face.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that, as a condition of the building permit, the County required the client to pay a traffic impact fee of $23,420 dictated by the General Plan's rate schedule, that the client paid under protest and obtained the permit, and that a refund request was not granted. The client's intuition that the dollar amount alone shows facial unconstitutionality, however, overstates the doctrine: Nollan/Dolan analysis is comparative, not categorical — the fee must be measured against the development's traffic impact, not against the client's subjective sense of what a 'modest home' should cost. The dollar amount matters only in conjunction with the underlying impact and the County's nexus/proportionality showing.

facts.client_belief: The $23,420 figure wasn't tailored to my specific project at all. It was just pulled from a fixed rate schedule based on the type of development and its location in the county — the county never calculated how much traffic my particular house would actually cause. So the fee can't possibly satisfy any individualization requirement.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the traffic impact fee was determined by a rate schedule considering the type of development (e.g., residential, commercial) and its location within the County rather than by costs specifically attributable to the client's particular project, and that the lower appellate court expressly acknowledged this. The client's intuition that absence of project-specific calculation automatically defeats the fee, however, runs ahead of unsettled doctrine: how individualized a class-based fee schedule must be under Nollan/Dolan is itself a contested question — the controlling federal-level decision did not resolve whether the schedule must be calibrated parcel-by-parcel or whether the same general standard can be met through a class-based scheme.

facts.client_belief: I believe the county's fee schedule was enacted by the Board of Supervisors as part of its General Plan — that makes it a legislative act, not something an individual administrator decided to impose on me personally.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the County's Board of Supervisors is a legislative body under California law, and that the adoption of the General Plan — including the traffic impact fee schedule — is a legislative act (see Cal. Govt. Code Ann. § 65300 et seq.). The legal dispute turns on what standard applies to such legislative conditions.

facts.client_belief: Because the fee was set by legislation and applied to a broad class of property owners, not just me, I thought any court would have to treat it differently from an ad hoc fee an administrator slapped on a single project.
facts.court_record: It is true that the lower appellate authority on this case held the Nollan/Dolan test applies only to permit conditions imposed 'on an individual and discretionary basis,' and that fees imposed on a broad class of property owners through legislative action need not satisfy that test. The controlling federal-level ruling has rejected that distinction: the Takings Clause does not categorically distinguish between legislative and administrative permit conditions. The client's intuition therefore captured the prior California rule but the prior California rule has been overridden — both kinds of conditions are now subject to the same scrutiny.

facts.client_belief: The county's fee scheme is basically extortion — it had nothing to do with the actual traffic impact of my small house, and the government was just leveraging its permitting power to shake money out of developers.
facts.court_record: Under Nollan and Dolan, permit conditions that lack an 'essential nexus' to a legitimate land-use interest or that are not 'roughly proportional' to the development's impact can amount to an unconstitutional exaction. Whether the County's rate schedule satisfies those requirements remains to be decided by the California courts on remand.

facts.client_belief: The federal-level ruling now establishes that Nollan and Dolan do apply, which means the county had to meet a constitutional standard it never even tried to meet. I feel vindicated — surely I win on remand.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the controlling federal-level ruling held legislative permit conditions are not categorically exempt from Nollan/Dolan scrutiny. It explicitly declined to address whether the fee satisfies the essential-nexus and rough-proportionality tests, whether the parties' other arguments are preserved, and whether a class-based fee schedule must be individualized to the same degree as a parcel-specific condition. All of these issues must be resolved on continued review. The client's confidence that the framework win translates into automatic merits victory therefore overstates what the federal-level ruling decided.

facts.client_belief: The court mentioned something about 'unconstitutional conditions' — I think that's the legal framework connecting the Takings Clause to permit conditions, but I'm not sure how it works.
facts.court_record: The Nollan/Dolan test is rooted in the unconstitutional conditions doctrine, which prohibits the government from withholding a benefit (here, a building permit) in order to coerce a person into giving up a constitutional right (here, the right to just compensation for a taking).This doctrine applies to both legislative and administrative conditions, and that the Takings Clause receives no less protection than other constitutional rights such as free speech or free exercise of religion.

facts.client_belief: The higher-level California review denied my case, so even the highest California authority essentially sided with the county before the federal-level review stepped in.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the higher-level California review denied review of the lower appellate decision, leaving in place the rule that the Nollan/Dolan test does not apply to legislatively imposed fees, and that the controlling federal-level ruling has rejected that rule. On continued review, the California courts must now apply constitutional scrutiny to the County's traffic impact fee without the benefit of the prior categorical exemption.

expected_inquiries: Ask the client for all documentation related to the permit application, fee payment, and protest, including receipts, correspondence with the County, and any written denial of the refund request.
Ask whether the client has any evidence of what traffic impact, if any, his specific prefabricated home was projected to cause, such as a traffic study, engineer's report, or County assessment.
Ask the client to obtain a copy of the General Plan's rate schedule and supporting documentation showing how the fee amounts were calculated for each development category and location zone.
Clarify the status of the permit and construction: whether the home has been built, whether the client still owns the property, and whether any other conditions were imposed as part of the permit.
Ask whether the client received any explanation from the County about how the $23,420 figure related to his specific project's traffic impact, or whether the County merely cited the schedule.

Ask whether the client is aware of other the County property owners who paid similar traffic impact fees under protest, as coordinated litigation or amicus support could strengthen the proportionality arguments on remand.
Ask whether the client or his attorney made any strategic concessions during the California proceedings that could limit the scope of arguments available on remand.
Confirm the procedural posture on continued review and identify the timeline for any briefing or motion practice in the California forums.

memo_expectations: Confirm record title, current ownership, and the precise legal description of the parcel — these facts establish standing and the relevant 'parcel as a whole' for any takings analysis.

Analyze whether the fee satisfies 'rough proportionality' under Dolan's second prong, including whether a rate-schedule approach can constitute an adequate individualized determination or whether parcel-specific analysis is required.

Address the threshold question raised in the federal-level concurrences: whether a class-based fee schedule must be individualized to the same degree as a parcel-specific condition, or whether a generally calibrated schedule can meet Nollan/Dolan if the underlying methodology has nexus and proportionality.

Assess the significance of the Kavanaugh concurrence (class-based fee schedules may be permissible) versus the Gorsuch concurrence (same standard applies regardless of scope) in predicting how the California courts will rule on remand.
Evaluate preservation issues: identify which arguments the client preserved below and which were not reached by the California courts, given the Court of Appeal's categorical-exemption ruling.

On continued review, the County may litigate (i) whether the rate schedule has nexus and is roughly proportional to the client's project's traffic impact, (ii) whether the demand was a tax outside the doctrine, and (iii) whether the client preserved every necessary argument.

opening: Hi, I'm X. I spoke with your office about a property dispute with state and county zoning regulators — I was hoping you could help me figure out my options.

facts.client_belief: My siblings and I own two adjacent lots — Lot E and Lot F — along the Blue River in our area of the State. They're side by side on the riverfront.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client (and his three siblings) own two contiguous lots, designated Lot E and Lot F, located along the Blue River in Lakeside County, the State. The contiguity, location, and ownership are undisputed.

facts.client_belief: My parents bought Lot F in 1960 and built a small recreational cabin on it, then bought neighboring Lot E in 1963. So even though we acquired the lots later, the original family acquisition pattern shows they were always separately developable.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client's parents purchased Lot F in 1960, built a small recreational cabin on Lot F, and purchased adjacent Lot E in 1963. The client's intuition that this original separate-acquisition pattern locks in permanent separable status, however, is mistaken: the regulatory baseline is set by the merger rule and the grandfather clause as they applied at the relevant cutoff (January 1, 1976), not by the original acquisition pattern. The 1960/1963 acquisitions are useful baseline facts but do not by themselves freeze the lots' status against later regulatory consequences of unification.

facts.client_belief: In 1961 my parents transferred Lot F to the family plumbing company while keeping Lot E in their own names — so the two lots had different owners on paper for decades. I figured that long history of separate ownership had to count for something permanent.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that Lot F was conveyed in 1961 to the family plumbing company while Lot E remained in the parents' personal names, and that the lots were therefore in separate (titled) ownership satisfying the grandfather-clause condition as of January 1, 1976. The client's intuition that long historical separate ownership creates a permanent vested grandfather right, however, overstates the doctrine: the grandfather clause preserves substandard lots in separate ownership as of the cutoff date, but does not freeze that protected status if and when the lots later come under common ownership. The historical separate-titling fact qualified the lots in 1976 but did not insulate them from later merger consequences.

facts.client_belief: Lot F was conveyed to my siblings and me in 1994; Lot E was conveyed to us a year later, in 1995.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that Lot F was transferred to the client (and his siblings) in 1994, and Lot E was transferred to them in 1995, and that the 1995 transfer brought both lots into common ownership for the first time. Transfer dates are undisputed.

facts.client_belief: Each lot is about 1.25 acres, but a steep bluff cuts through the middle of each — so neither has a full acre of buildable land, and even combined we only have about 0.98 acres of buildable area. With that little buildable land, I figured the regulators were going too far in restricting our use.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that each lot is approximately 1.25 acres, that a steep bluff bisects each lot leaving level land suitable for development above the bluff and along the riverfront below, that each lot has less than one acre of buildable land, and that even combined, total buildable area is approximately 0.98 acres. The client's intuition that the buildable-acreage shortfall itself shows the regulation goes 'too far,' however, conflates the substandard-lot determination (which triggers the merger provision) with the takings analysis (which examines the parcel as a whole). The bluff topography is what makes the lots substandard under the 1-acre rule — it explains why the merger provision applies — and is therefore evidence supporting the regulatory regime, not evidence of constitutional excess.

facts.client_belief: For our area, the state and county rules require at least one acre of buildable land for a lot to be used as a separate building site.
facts.court_record: the State Administrative Code §§ NR 118.04(4), 118.03(27), 118.06(1)(a)(2)(a), 118.06(1)(b), and the parallel Lakeside County Ordinance § 17.36I.4.a (2005), prevent the use of lots as separate building sites unless they have at least one acre of land suitable for development. Regulation undisputed.

facts.client_belief: We always understood that an old 'non-conforming' lot could still be sold and built on. So I figured Lot E was protected under that grandfather regime no matter what we did with the title later.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that Wis. Admin. Code § NR 118.08(4)(a)(1) grandfathers substandard lots that were 'in separate ownership from abutting lands' on January 1, 1976, and that the clause permits use of qualifying lots as separate building sites. The client's intuition that grandfather status follows the lot regardless of subsequent ownership changes, however, is mistaken: the grandfather-clause text is conditional on the separate-ownership fact, and that condition can fail if a later transfer brings the substandard adjacent lots into common ownership. The grandfather right was real in 1976; the question is whether the client's family's later voluntary unification of title defeated it.

facts.client_belief: I tried to move our cabin and sell Lot E to fund the project, but the Board of Adjustment denied our variance request, and the lawyers told me earlier appeals had agreed with the Board. I figured that meant we were locked out of treating Lot E separately.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client sought variances from the Lakeside County Board of Adjustment, including authorization for separate sale or use of Lots E and F, and that the Board denied the requests. Earlier intermediate appellate authority agreed in relevant part, treating the local ordinance as 'effectively merg[ing]' the lots so the client 'could only sell or build on the single larger lot' (the client v. Lakeside County Board of Adjustment, 332 Wis.2d 172). The client's intuition that this forecloses any further challenge, however, is too pessimistic: the variance pathway and the earlier appellate result fix the merger result for state-administrative purposes but do not by themselves resolve the federal Takings Clause question, which is reviewed under federal doctrine — that constitutional channel remains the live question.

facts.client_belief: The Blue River where my property sits has been federally protected for decades — long before we acquired the lots.
facts.court_record: The Blue River was designated under the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act in 1968/1972 (Blue River Act of 1972, 16 U.S.C. § 1274(a)(9)). the State DNR was authorized under Wis. Stat. § 30.27(l) (1973) to issue rules limiting development. The federal/state protective scheme predates the client's acquisitions by more than two decades. Undisputed.

facts.client_belief: Our claim is about Lot E specifically — the rules made Lot E unsellable and undevelopable on its own, so the takings analysis should focus on Lot E by itself.
facts.court_record: The proper unit of property — the "denominator" — must be determined by an objective, multifactor inquiry into reasonable expectations: (1) treatment under state and local law; (2) physical characteristics of the property; and (3) prospective value of the regulated land, including its effect on adjacent holdings. Under that test, Lots E and F are evaluated together as one parcel.

facts.client_belief: Lot lines are recorded on the plat — they're the obvious legal boundary of the property, so they should automatically define what counts as "the parcel" for a takings claim.
facts.court_record: Lot lines are creatures of state law and can be overridden by the State in the reasonable exercise of its police power. Lot lines also have varying degrees of formality across jurisdictions and can be subject to informal adjustment, creating gamesmanship risk. The merger provision is precisely such a legitimate state-law override.

facts.client_belief: If you treat Lot E by itself, it has been totally wiped out economically — our appraiser said it's only worth $40,000 as an undevelopable lot, when it would otherwise be a buildable river-frontage lot worth far more. That's a complete deprivation under Lucas.
facts.court_record: With the lots evaluated as a single parcel, combined value is $698,300; the unregulated comparison value is $771,000 — a decrease of less than 10%. Under Lucas, "complete deprivation of all economically beneficial use" is required for the categorical rule.

facts.client_belief: I assumed because we cannot build a separate house on Lot E and cannot sell it on its own, the regulation has destroyed all economically beneficial use.
facts.court_record: The client (and the client's siblings) "have not been deprived of all economically beneficial use of their property" because they retain multiple residential uses: preserving the existing cabin, relocating it, eliminating it and building a new residence on Lot E or Lot F or across both, and using Lot E for recreation, privacy, and improvement-siting. Under Palazzolo, a regulation permitting a substantial residence does not leave property "economically idle."

facts.client_belief: When we acquired Lot E in 1995, we expected we could later sell or develop it as a separate parcel — that was our investment plan.
facts.court_record: The merger and grandfather rules predated the client's acquisition of both lots. Under Palazzolo, a reasonable pre-existing regulation can shape investment-backed expectations. the client (and the client's siblings) were "charged with knowledge of the existing zoning laws"; expecting separate treatment "became unreasonable when they chose to acquire Lot E in 1995, after their having acquired Lot F in 1994."

facts.client_belief: We didn't do anything to "merge" the lots — we just inherited them through family transfers. The merger should not be treated as our doing.
facts.court_record: The client's lots were "subject to this regulatory burden ... only because of voluntary conduct in bringing the lots under common ownership after the regulations were enacted." The 1994/1995 inter-family transfers placing both lots in the client's joint names were voluntary acts that triggered the merger; the regulation does not apply against will, but in response to chosen ownership structure.

expected_inquiries: Obtain deeds for both lots, the county plat, surveys showing the shared boundary line, and any title insurance commitments referencing the merger or grandfather provisions.
Pull the original 1960 and 1963 deeds, building permits for the cabin, and any historical photographs or assessor records confirming separate ownership and the cabin's presence.

Obtain a topographic survey, a buildable-area calculation by a licensed engineer or surveyor, and photographs or LIDAR data showing the bluff and the river-frontage configuration.

Pull the Board of Adjustment record, the variance application, the denial decision, and the prior intermediate appellate authority interpreting the merger provision (332 Wis.2d 172).

Obtain the chronology of when the client (and the client's siblings) learned of NR 118 and the merger provision, any pre-acquisition due diligence files, and any contemporaneous correspondence about plans for the separate use of Lot E.

Investigate alternative ownership structures (e.g., separate trusts, retention of one lot in the family company, life estates) that might have preserved the grandfather status — useful for client education and for any future similar transactions.
