Establish the original-acquisition baseline (1960/1963) — pre-dating the 1976 grandfather-clause cutoff is what kept the lots separately developable while in the parents' separate ownership.

Document the historical separate ownership through January 1, 1976 — this is what made the lots qualify for the grandfather clause and triggers the legal question whether unification later defeats that grandfathered status.
Pin down the precise 1994 (Lot F) and 1995 (Lot E) transfer dates: the 1995 transfer is what triggered the merger because it produced common ownership of substandard adjacent lots.

Pin down the buildable-acreage shortfall as a physical fact: this is why both lots are 'substandard' under the 1-acre rule, and why the merger provision was triggered. It is not by itself evidence that the regulation goes 'too far' under takings doctrine.
Quote the regulatory text precisely (NR 118 series and county ordinance § 17.36I.4.a) — these are the authority for the substandard-lot determination.

Frame the grandfather clause precisely: it preserves substandard lots in separate ownership as of 1/1/1976, but does not freeze that protected status if and when the lots later come under common ownership.

Frame the procedural posture: the variance pathway and the earlier appellate result both rejected separate state-law treatment, fixing the merger result before any federal constitutional takings claim is litigated.

Establish the long history of federal/state river protection (Wild and Scenic Rivers Act, NR 118) that predated the client's acquisition — directly relevant to investment-backed expectations under Penn Central.

Reset client expectations on the parcel question: post-the client, the "denominator" is determined by an objective multifactor test, not by the owner's unilateral choice to focus on the regulated portion. A lot-only framing of the takings claim is foreclosed.

Brief the rejection of any lot-line presumption: the client (and the client's siblings)' theory would force courts to credit the aspect of state law they like (lot lines) and ignore what they don't (merger provision). the client forecloses this asymmetric reliance on state law.

Prepare an appraisal critique on the parcel-as-a-whole basis: a $40,000 valuation of Lot E as a separately saleable but undevelopable lot has no purchase under the client because Lot E cannot be sold without Lot F under the regulation.
Catalog the retained uses (residential, recreational, expansion across the lot line, improvement-siting) — these expressly defeat the Lucas categorical claim under Palazzolo.

Reset the investment-backed-expectations argument under Penn Central: pre-existing, well-publicized regulations cannot serve as the basis for reasonable expectations of separate use, especially where the merger was triggered by the client (and the client's siblings)' own voluntary unification of ownership.

Reset the "involuntary merger" theory: voluntary transfers (even within a family) that produce common ownership of substandard contiguous lots trigger the merger provision and inform the reasonable-expectations analysis under the client factor one.

opening: Hi, I'm X, property owner. I spoke with your office about a dispute with a federal environmental agency over my residential property — I was hoping you could help me figure out my options.

facts.client_belief: My wife and I bought a small lot near Silver Lake in Lakeside County, the State, in 2004 — we wanted to build a modest home on it.
facts.court_record: The client and his spouse purchased a small residential lot near Silver Lake, in Lakeside County, the State, in 2004. The acquisition, location, and residential purpose are undisputed.

facts.client_belief: In preparation for building the home, we began backfilling the lot with dirt and rocks. We figured this was just ordinary site prep on our own property.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that, in or around 2004, the client began backfilling the lot with dirt and rocks to prepare for building a modest home. The client's intuition that this is just ordinary site prep with no federal interest, however, overlooks how the Clean Water Act actually defined 'discharge of dredged or fill material' under § 1344 at the relevant time. Backfilling a parcel that the agency classified as containing 'waters of the United States' triggered federal jurisdiction even on a small residential lot — the activity itself, not the lot's residential character, is what the agency targeted.

facts.client_belief: A few months after we started, the Federal Environmental Agency sent us a compliance order saying our backfilling violated the Clean Water Act because our property contains protected wetlands.
facts.court_record: the Federal Environmental Agency issued a compliance order asserting that the client's backfilling violated the CWA because the lot contained wetlands classified as 'waters of the United States.' The order demanded that the client immediately undertake activities to restore the site under a Restoration Work Plan provided by the Federal Environmental Agency. Issuance of the order is undisputed.

facts.client_belief: The order threatened us with penalties of more than $40,000 per day if we didn't comply. I figured that on a residential property dispute that has to be empty bluster.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the compliance order threatened civil penalties of over $40,000 per day for noncompliance. Under 33 U.S.C. § 1319(c), property owners who negligently discharge 'pollutants' face severe criminal penalties including imprisonment; § 1319(d) imposes over $60,000/day in civil fines per violation. The client's intuition that the dollar threat is empty bluster on a residential lot is mistaken: the statutory penalty schedule applies regardless of lot type, the agency does not need to litigate to begin accruing exposure, and the 5-year limitations period under 28 U.S.C. § 2462 keeps cumulative exposure live for years.

facts.client_belief: the Federal Environmental Agency says the wetlands on our lot are 'adjacent to' an unnamed tributary on the other side of a 30-foot road. That tributary feeds a non-navigable creek, which feeds Silver Lake. With a road right between us and the tributary, I figured the agency couldn't possibly have authority over our lot.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the Federal Environmental Agency classified the wetlands on the client's lot as 'waters of the United States' because they were near a 30-foot-wide road, on the other side of which lies an 'unnamed tributary' that feeds a non-navigable creek that feeds Silver Lake. The client's intuition that the road interruption automatically defeats jurisdiction, however, overstates how the doctrine worked at the relevant time. Under the agency's prior interpretation, 'adjacent' wetlands could be lumped with downstream waters even across a road if the aggregate had a 'significant nexus' to navigable waters. The road interruption is dispositive only under the more recent continuous-surface-connection test — it was not dispositive under the standard the agency applied.

facts.client_belief: the Federal Environmental Agency 'lumped' our lot together with a large nearby wetland complex called the Kalispell Bay Fen to argue we have a 'significant nexus' to Silver Lake. I figured that kind of aggregation has to be obviously unlawful — they shouldn't be allowed to pile properties together to manufacture jurisdiction.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the Federal Environmental Agency used aggregation reasoning, treating the client's lot as 'similarly situated' to the Kalispell Bay Fen and concluding that taken together they 'significantly affect' Silver Lake's ecology under the prior 'significant nexus' test. The client's intuition that this aggregation theory was obviously unlawful, however, overstates the legal landscape at the time of the agency action: the prior 'significant nexus' / 'similarly situated' test was the agency's official rule and had been treated as permissible by lower-court authority. The client's instinct turned out to be vindicated by the more recent doctrinal shift, but it was not 'obvious' at the time the agency acted.

facts.client_belief: We sued the Federal Environmental Agency back in 2008 alleging they had no jurisdiction, but the trial-level review initially dismissed it saying the compliance order wasn't a 'final agency action.'
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client filed an APA suit alleging the Federal Environmental Agency lacked CWA jurisdiction and that the trial-level review initially dismissed it as not reviewable. the Federal Environmental Agency compliance orders are now established to be final agency action reviewable under the APA, opening the procedural pathway the client originally sought.

facts.client_belief: After seven more years on remand, the trial-level review granted summary judgment to the Federal Environmental Agency, and the next-level appellate review affirmed in 2021. I figured at that point the case was effectively dead.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that, after remand, the trial-level review entered summary judgment for the Federal Environmental Agency in 2019 and that the next-level appellate review affirmed in 2021, holding the CWA covers adjacent wetlands with a 'significant nexus' to traditional navigable waters and that the client's wetlands satisfied that standard. The client's reading of those rulings as case-ending, however, overlooks the doctrinal instability of the underlying test: the 'significant nexus' standard the lower courts applied was itself the contested issue and was open to further review on a higher legal-doctrinal question, which is precisely what subsequently occurred.

facts.client_belief: Silver Lake is intrastate — it doesn't cross state lines.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that Silver Lake is a wholly intrastate body of water that has been designated as 'traditionally navigable.' The designation rests primarily on interstate tourism and the lake's attenuated connection to navigable waters. The intrastate character of the lake and the navigability designation are undisputed; the legal sufficiency of that designation is contested under an expanded Daniel Ball test.

facts.client_belief: I could just build without doing anything — it's my own property and there's no river or lake on it.
facts.court_record: Under the prior agency interpretation, the client's lot was treated as 'waters of the United States' via the significant-nexus aggregation theory. The agency's own admission was that, under that test, 'almost all waters and wetlands' are potentially susceptible to regulation, and the Corps found jurisdiction in approximately 75% of jurisdictional determinations. The client could not lawfully build until the legal regime was clarified — the client's intuition that 'no visible water = no federal jurisdiction' therefore overlooked the practical reach of the agency's pre-shift regime.

facts.client_belief: the Federal Environmental Agency told us our wetlands had a "significant nexus" to Silver Lake, so we were covered. I never understood how that test was supposed to work.
facts.court_record: CWA jurisdiction over adjacent wetlands now requires (1) the adjacent body of water to be a relatively permanent body of water connected to traditional interstate navigable waters, and (2) the wetland to have a continuous surface connection with that water "making it difficult to determine where the 'water' ends and the 'wetland' begins." The aggregation/ecology-based test is no longer good law.

facts.client_belief: the Federal Environmental Agency says that even after we win, it can rewrite its rule and come back at us. So nothing really changes.
facts.court_record: the Federal Environmental Agency's 2023 rule must yield to the controlling federal-level holding. Any future rule attempting to revive aggregation/significant-nexus or to expand 'adjacent' beyond 'adjoining-equivalent continuous surface connection' would conflict with the controlling holding and the background principles requiring clear congressional authorization. the Federal Environmental Agency can refine the test but cannot return to the rejected reasoning. The client's intuition that the win is meaningless because the Federal Environmental Agency can simply rewrite the rule therefore overstates the agency's flexibility — the controlling holding is durable doctrinal ground.

expected_inquiries: Obtain the deed, parcel map, title report, original residential building plans, county zoning compliance, and any pre-purchase due diligence on environmental constraints.
Obtain construction logs, trucking invoices, photographs, and any contemporaneous correspondence with contractors documenting the fill work and its timing.

memo_expectations: Document the precise lot location, parcel description, and the residential intent at the time of acquisition — these anchor the takings/property-rights framing and the timing of any agency notice.
Pin down the precise nature, volume, and timing of the fill activity — relevant to whether the activity qualifies as a 'discharge of dredged or fill material' within § 1344 and to penalty exposure.
Frame the compliance-order posture: the order itself is the operative agency action that triggered the litigation pathway, and is now reviewable under the APA in this kind of dispute.

Quantify the exposure: $40,000+/day CWA civil penalties plus criminal liability under § 1319(c) for negligent violations, with a 5-year statute of limitations under 28 U.S.C. § 2462 — a 'potent weapon' with 'crushing consequences.'

Document the specific physical chain: lot wetlands → 30-foot road → unnamed tributary → non-navigable creek → Silver Lake. The road interruption is the dispositive physical fact under the more recent continuous-surface-connection test, but it was not dispositive under the prior 'significant nexus' / aggregation test the agency applied.

Capture how the Federal Environmental Agency constructed jurisdiction through Kalispell Bay Fen aggregation rather than direct connection of the client's lot — the aggregation-based significant-nexus theory has now been rejected, but it was the operative agency theory at the time of the action.

Frame the procedural backdrop: APA review of the Federal Environmental Agency compliance orders is now established, enabling private landowners to challenge jurisdictional overreach without first incurring crushing penalties or going through the permit process.
Establish the procedural posture leading to higher review: 17-year litigation, two adverse lower-court rulings under the prior 'significant nexus' test that has subsequently been rejected.

Note Silver Lake's intrastate character and the Federal Environmental Agency's tourism-based navigability theory — flagged as suspect in Thomas's concurrence under the expanded Daniel Ball test, though the majority assumed traditional-navigability arguendo.

Reset the practical reality at the time of consultation: even on a residential lot far from any visible water, federal jurisdiction under the pre-2023 the Federal Environmental Agency interpretation was nearly automatic — and proceeding without resolution carried catastrophic penalty exposure.

Brief the post-shift two-step test (relatively permanent body + continuous surface connection) and confirm that the prior 'significant nexus' / 'similarly situated' aggregation theory is foreclosed; the agency may not return to that test by rulemaking.

Counsel that the controlling holding is durable doctrinal ground: while the Federal Environmental Agency can clarify edge cases (year-round vs seasonal connection, ditches/swales, low tides, dry spells), it cannot resurrect the significant-nexus or 'neighboring' tests after this ruling.

opening: Hi, I'm X, representing the State. I came to your office about a state property and natural-resources dispute — I was hoping you could help me figure out where things stand and what we can do next.

facts.client_belief: The energy operator on the other side runs ten hydroelectric facilities built on the beds of three rivers that run through our state — the River A, River B, and River C. Some of those dams have been in place for over a century.
facts.court_record: The opposing energy operator owns and operates ten hydroelectric facilities on riverbeds underlying segments of the upper reach of River A, Madison, and River Cs. The facilities have existed at their locations for many decades, some for over a century. The Missouri-Madison and the Falls site projects are licensed by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. These facts are undisputed by either party.

facts.client_belief: For decades the State knew about these dams — our agencies even participated in the federal licensing — but we never tried to charge Y Energy Corp or its predecessors any rent for the use of the riverbeds, and Y Energy Corp paid rent to the federal government instead.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that, until the 2003 lawsuit by parents of schoolchildren, the State did not seek compensation for use of the riverbeds despite full awareness of the projects (state agencies participated in the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission licensing), and that Y Energy Corp and the federal government understand Y Energy Corp paid rents to the United States. The available legal authority treats the State's long failure to assert title as 'some evidence' supporting the conclusion that the disputed segments were nonnavigable for purposes of the equal-footing doctrine, while reserving the question whether laches or estoppel could ever bar a sovereign's claim. The client's intuition that the State's century of silence is doctrinally irrelevant therefore overstates the position: it functions as substantive nonnavigability evidence even if it is not a formal bar.

facts.client_belief: After parents of schoolchildren filed a federal suit in 2003 saying the riverbeds were state school-trust land, our state joined that case and for the first time started seeking rent from Y Energy Corp.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that, in 2003, parents of schoolchildren brought a federal suit claiming Y Energy Corp's facilities were on state-owned school-trust riverbeds; that the State joined the suit and, for the first time, sought rents from Y Energy Corp; that the federal case was dismissed for lack of diversity jurisdiction; and that Y Energy Corp then filed a state-level declaratory action and the State counterclaimed for title under the equal-footing doctrine. Procedural facts are undisputed.

facts.client_belief: We won at the trial level: the trial-level decision-maker granted us summary judgment on navigability and title and ordered Y Energy Corp to pay us about $41 million in rent for 2000–2007. Higher-level review affirmed in a divided opinion, but the federal-level review reversed.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the trial-level decision granted the State summary judgment on navigability for purposes of riverbed title and ordered Y Energy Corp to pay $40,956,180 in rent for riverbed use between 2000 and 2007; that the higher-level state review affirmed in a divided decision; and that the federal-level review reversed and remanded. The procedural and quantum facts are not contested; only the legal underpinnings are.

facts.client_belief: We thought the right way to look at this was the river as a whole — if a river is generally navigable for trade and travel, then we own the bed all the way through, even if there are some difficult stretches in the middle.
facts.court_record: This was an 'infirm legal understanding' of the equal-footing navigability rule. To determine riverbed title, the navigability inquiry must be conducted on a segment-by-segment basis (United States v. Utah, 283 U.S. 64; Brewer-Elliott Oil & Gas Co., 260 U.S. 77; Oklahoma v. Texas, 258 U.S. 574). The higher-level state-review approach erred in discounting that 'well-settled approach' and in adopting a generally 'liberal' construction without segmenting the analysis. The client's preferred 'river as a whole' framing is therefore foreclosed under the corrected legal standard.

facts.client_belief: The waterfalls and rapids on these rivers — including the Falls reach on River A — were just short interruptions. Lewis and Clark and later travelers got around them by carrying their boats overland (portage), so commerce continued and the rivers should still count as navigable through those stretches.
facts.court_record: Portages generally defeat navigability for title purposes because they require transportation over land rather than over water; even a single day's portage demonstrates the need to bypass a nonnavigable segment. The higher-level state review was wrong to treat portageable stretches as 'short interruptions' that did not defeat navigability. The Montello, 20 Wall. 430, was misapplied: it dealt with federal commerce-power navigability (a continued interstate channel for regulatory purposes), not with equal-footing title. The client's intuition that 'short portages' preserve title navigability therefore conflates two different bodies of doctrine.

facts.client_belief: Looking at our rivers as long, useful waterways for trade, all of the disputed beds belong to us. It would be administratively impossible to chop a river up into navigable and nonnavigable pieces.
facts.court_record: The State's 'river as a long, useful waterway' position is rejected on the corrected legal standard. Segmentation is well settled (Utah, Brewer-Elliott, Oklahoma); is supported by practical considerations (physical conditions like gradient, rapids, and tributaries vary along a river and supply natural start/end points); and is consistent with how private riparian rights are apportioned at common law. The State's own apportionment of the riverbeds to value the rents (used to calculate the $41 million figure) demonstrates that segmentation is administrable — the State 'cannot suggest that segmentation is inadministrable when [it] managed to apportion the underlying riverbeds for purposes of determining their value and Y Energy Corp's corresponding rents.'

facts.client_belief: Present-day evidence — including modern recreational fishing and boating on River B — proves that the river was navigable at statehood, so the bed under Y Energy Corp's two Madison dams is ours.
facts.court_record: Present-day, primarily recreational use is not a freestanding proxy for statehood-era navigability. Navigability for title is assessed at the time of statehood (1889) and concerns commercial 'trade and travel,' not recreation. Present-day evidence may inform the susceptibility analysis only if (1) the watercraft are meaningfully similar to those in customary commercial use at statehood and (2) the river's poststatehood physical condition is not materially different from its 1889 condition. Neither finding has been made on the present record; Y Energy Corp's fluvial-geomorphology expert affidavit suggests the dams have made River B less torrential in high flows and less shallow in low flows, meaning the river may well be easier to navigate now than at statehood. The client's reliance on present-day boating to prove statehood-era navigability is therefore doctrinally weak.

facts.client_belief: If the State doesn't hold title to these riverbeds, the public's right to use the rivers above them — for navigation, fishing, and recreation — will be undermined.
facts.court_record: This argument 'underscores [the client's] misapprehension of the equal-footing and public trust doctrines.' The public-trust doctrine concerns public access to waters and is a matter of state law (subject to federal regulatory power), whereas the equal-footing doctrine is the federal constitutional foundation for the navigability rule of riverbed title. The two doctrines are doctrinally distinct, and denying the State title to specific riverbeds does not displace the State's residual power to determine the scope of the public trust over waters within its borders. The client's intuition that bed-title loss undermines public access therefore conflates two doctrinally separate regimes.

facts.client_belief: The Falls reach of River A — where five of Y Energy Corp's upper-reach dams on River A sit, including dams on the three tallest waterfalls — is part of a navigable river and the bed is ours.
facts.court_record: On the available record, the 17-mile the Falls reach 'at least from the head of the first waterfall to the foot of the last' is not navigable for purposes of riverbed title under the equal-footing doctrine. The State itself conceded that 'the falls themselves were not passable by boat at statehood,' and the trial-level findings indicate the falls had never been navigated. Title to the bed under that reach therefore did not pass to the State at statehood. The client's hope of preserving title to that segment is therefore foreclosed under the corrected legal standard.

facts.client_belief: The two Y Energy Corp dams in canyons on the Ferry stretch of the upper reach of River A are also on beds we own, because that stretch was navigable in 1889.
facts.court_record: There is 'a significant likelihood' that some of the other disputed river stretches also fail the federal navigability-for-title test. The Ferry stretch is described in the record as having steep gradient and being 'much obstructed by rocks and dangerous rapids' (1895 Secretary of War report). Whether title passed to the State for that stretch must be determined on continued review under a properly segmented analysis, and the State's position is no longer presumed correct. The client's optimism on the Ferry stretch overstates the strength of the record under the corrected framework.

facts.client_belief: The Falls site on River C was also on a navigable river, so we own that riverbed too.
facts.court_record: The operator introduced contemporaneous evidence — including an an 1891 federal engineering report and a 1910 federal-level decree (a historical federal decree) — describing the River C between the City and Lake Pend Oreille (which includes the Falls site location) as 'a mountain torrential stream, full of rocks, rapids, and falls, ... utterly unnavigable, and incapable of being made navigable except at an enormous cost,' with the Falls site itself a 'complete obstruction to navigation.' The earlier higher-level state characterization of that evidence as 'conclusory' was incorrect. On continued review, this segment is at high risk of being held nonnavigable, and the client's continued claim to title overstates the record.

facts.client_belief: The River B — including the canyon stretches where Y Energy Corp's two Madison dams are located — was navigable at statehood, and we own those beds.
facts.court_record: The River B segment determinations were tainted by the higher-level state review's reliance on present-day recreational use, which has been held misapplied as a matter of law. Without proper findings about (i) the similarity of modern watercraft to commercial watercraft used at statehood and (ii) the river's physical condition relative to 1889, present-day recreational use 'did not bear on navigability for purposes of title.' The navigability of the River B canyon segments must be reassessed on continued review. The client's confidence in those segments based on modern boating evidence is therefore vulnerable.

facts.client_belief: The $41 million rent award for 2000–2007 is justified compensation for Y Energy Corp's use of our beds.
facts.court_record: The summary-judgment grant on which the rent award rested was reversed. Because the underlying title determination was vacated, the monetary award cannot stand on the present record. Whether — and to what extent — the State can recover any rent depends on what segments are ultimately held to have been navigable at statehood under the corrected legal standard.

facts.client_belief: Even if some segments turn out to be 'nonnavigable' in 1889, surely the State should still get title to the beds — they're inside our borders.
facts.court_record: The United States 'retains any title vested in it before statehood to any land beneath waters not then navigable' (Utah, 283 U.S. at 75). For segments that were nonnavigable in 1889, title remained in the federal government and was not transferred to the State under the equal-footing doctrine. Y Energy Corp's understanding — and the federal government's amicus position — that Y Energy Corp has been paying rent to the United States for use of those beds is consistent with this allocation. the State cannot reach segments nonnavigable at statehood by invoking a generalized in-state-borders argument.

facts.client_belief: The fact that we waited a long time to ask for rent shouldn't matter — the State is sovereign, and laches and estoppel can't run against us.
facts.court_record: While the State's premise may ultimately be correct in a strict doctrinal sense, the Court treated Y Energy Corp's long-standing reliance on the State's silence as 'some evidence supporting the conclusion that the river segments over those beds were nonnavigable.' The State's delay, although not formally a bar, has independent evidentiary force against its title claim on remand.

expected_inquiries: Ask the State to obtain (from Y Energy Corp or via the federal record) the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission license documents (Missouri-Madison and the Falls site projects), the as-built drawings showing the precise footprint of each dam on each riverbed, and any title surveys conducted at the time of original construction.

Ask the client whether any pre-2003 internal records (memos, opinions of the Attorney General, Land Board minutes, Department of Natural Resources files) reflect a State understanding that the disputed riverbeds were not state-owned, and whether any such records would be discoverable on remand.

Ask the client whether the school-trust beneficiaries (the original 2003 plaintiffs) intend to be re-engaged on continued review, whether they are aligned with or adverse to the State's position, and whether their participation creates conflicts of interest for the State's office.

Ask the client to produce the trial court's segment-by-segment valuation methodology underlying the $41 million figure, since the State's own apportionment of the beds for valuation purposes will be useful evidence that segmentation is administrable.

Ask the client which segments the State considers most defensible under a properly segmented analysis (i.e., reaches lacking continuous rapids or falls and supported by historical commercial-use evidence), and which segments the State is willing to concede without further litigation.

Ask the client whether any historical record shows commercial cargo or passengers being carried by water — without portage — through any of the disputed reaches at or near 1889, and identify the specific water-only voyages that the State will rely on at trial.

Ask the client for the maps, GIS data, and survey methodology used by the trial court (or by the State's experts) to apportion the riverbeds for the $41 million rent calculation, and confirm whether those segment boundaries can be re-used for the navigability-in-fact inquiry.

Ask the client to retain (if not already retained) a qualified fluvial geomorphologist to rebut Y Energy Corp's expert on whether River B's post-dam condition is materially different from its 1889 condition; ask whether the State has any historical naval-architecture evidence about commercial watercraft customarily used in 1889.

Ask the client whether it intends to assert state public-trust authority over the surface waters as an independent ground for regulating Y Energy Corp's use, separate from any bed-title claim, and whether parallel state-law regulatory tools (water-rights administration, instream-flow rules, fishing-access statutes) are being preserved.

Ask the client whether it accepts the Falls determination as final and, if so, what restitution arrangements (if any) need to be made to Y Energy Corp for any rent already collected attributable to that reach, and what arrangements need to be coordinated with the United States, which now appears to hold title to the Falls bed.

Ask the client whether the State has, or can obtain, contemporaneous shipping records, riverboat-company logs, fur-trading records, or newspaper accounts documenting commercial water traffic on the Ferry stretch in or near 1889.

Ask the client whether the State has, or can obtain, evidence post-dating the 1891 the federal engineering report or the 1910 a historical federal decree decree that would rebut their characterizations of the River C at the Falls site as 'utterly unnavigable.'

Ask the client whether the State has historical evidence of commercial trade or travel on River B canyon segments at or before 1889 (and not on the wider, slower-flowing stretches) and whether it can document the pre-Hebgen, pre-River Town natural condition of the river.

Ask the client what portion of the $41 million is attributable to each specific segment under the trial court's apportionment, so that the State can model its recovery range for each plausible remand outcome.

Ask the client whether there are any active negotiations, communications, or potential litigation with the United States (Department of Interior, BLM, or DOJ) regarding title to or rent for nonnavigable segments, and whether the State has been put on notice of any federal back-rent claim.

Ask the client whether any pre-2003 internal records (memos, opinions of the Attorney General, Land Board minutes, Department of Natural Resources files, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission license-process correspondence) reflect the reasons for the State's non-assertion of title, and whether those records can be marshaled to neutralize the evidentiary use of the State's silence.

Ask the client whether any pre-2003 internal records (memos, opinions of the Attorney General, Land Board minutes, Department of Natural Resources files, FERC license-process correspondence) reflect the reasons for the State's non-assertion of title, and whether those records can be marshaled to neutralize the evidentiary use of the State's silence.
memo_expectations: Catalogue each of Y Energy Corp's ten facilities by river, by dam, and by latitude/longitude so that the segment-by-segment navigability inquiry on continued review can be tied to specific physical locations and to specific the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission license boundaries.

Anticipate that Y Energy Corp will deploy the State's century of silence and the federal-rent history not as a formal laches/estoppel defense but as substantive evidence of nonnavigability under Y Energy Corp itself; develop a counter-narrative explaining the State's silence on grounds other than concession of nonnavigability.

Map the procedural history clearly, because the school-trust beneficiaries' continuing interest may shape both the State's litigation incentives on remand and any settlement architecture; the school-trust theory remains a constitutional/statutory hook independent of the equal-footing analysis.

Brief the consequences of the SCOTUS reversal for the rent award: the summary-judgment grant has been vacated, and on remand the state-level forums must reapply the corrected legal standard before any rent can be re-awarded; reset client expectations about recovery on a per-segment basis.

Walk the client and the trial court on remand through the segment-by-segment framework: identify the precise start and end points of each disputed segment using physical-condition markers (gradient changes, waterfalls, rapids, tributary confluences) and tie each segment to the dam or facility it underlies.

Distinguish equal-footing portage doctrine from federal-power portage doctrine in the merits memo: under Y Energy Corp, portage almost always defeats title navigability, and the State's 'short interruptions' theory cannot be salvaged by reference to The Montello.

Use the State's own apportioned-rent valuation methodology as a judicial admission that segmentation is administrable; build the remand brief around segment definitions that match the boundaries already used to value Y Energy Corp's rents.

On continued review, develop the expert and historical record needed to satisfy the federal-level two-prong present-day-evidence test (similar watercraft + unchanged physical condition), or pivot to historical-only evidence; lightweight modern rafts and kayaks are unlikely to qualify as 'meaningfully similar' to 1889 commercial watercraft.

Reframe the public-interest narrative: even where bed title is held to be federal, the State retains independent authority under state public-trust law and federal Commerce Clause regulation of the surface waters; the bed-title loss does not threaten public access, fishing, or recreational rights.

Treat the Falls reach as effectively foreclosed under the corrected federal-level standard; advise the client to abandon any title claim to that 17-mile segment and concentrate resources on the still-open segments, while preserving any non-title regulatory and public-trust theories.

Build the strongest possible record of historical commercial use of the Ferry stretch — keelboat, mackinaw, or steamboat traffic between the Capital City and Cascade Town or Fort Trading Post at or near 1889 — to overcome the rapid-and-rocks evidence highlighted by the Court.

Rigorously assess whether any title claim to the River C bed at the Falls site remains tenable in light of the 1891 the federal engineering report and the 1910 a historical federal decree decree; if not, advise concession of that segment to conserve resources for stronger segments.

On remand, replace the present-day-use evidence with statehood-era evidence specific to the River B canyon segments, and rebut Y Energy Corp's fluvial-geomorphology evidence that Lake A and River Town Lake (post-statehood reservoirs) materially changed the river's physical condition.

Manage client expectations on damages: the $41 million is no longer a floor; on remand the State will at most recover rent attributable to segments held navigable at 1889, and may face refund or offset claims as to segments determined to be federal.

Counsel the client on the federalism reality: nonnavigable segments at statehood belong to the United States, not the State; coordinate with the federal government regarding any segment held nonnavigable, since the United States may seek back-rent or future rent for those beds.

Develop a counter-narrative for why the State did not assert title for over a century — e.g., absence of perceived economic interest, federal licensing context, ambiguity of pre-Y Energy Corp case law — that does not concede nonnavigability; build a record explaining the silence so that Y Energy Corp cannot use it as substantive evidence.

opening: Hi, I'm X. I spoke with your office about a civil forfeiture matter involving my car — I was hoping you could help me understand my rights and options.

facts.client_belief: I loaned my car to my son while he was away at college. A police officer in Riverside City, the State pulled him over and found marijuana and a handgun in the car. They arrested him and then seized my car — even though the car belongs to me, not my son.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client loaned her sedan to her college-aged son; that on February 17, 2019, police in Riverside City, the State stopped the car while her son was driving, found marijuana and a loaded handgun, and arrested her son for possessing marijuana; and that officers seized the client's car incident to that arrest under Ala. Code § 20–2–93(b)(1). The fact of the seizure itself is undisputed.

facts.client_belief: They took my car even though I did nothing wrong. I am an innocent owner — I had no idea my son would have drugs or a gun in the car. I just wanted him to have transportation at school.
facts.court_record: the State's civil forfeiture statute at the time provided an affirmative 'innocent owner' defense allowing an owner to recover forfeited property by showing she lacked knowledge of the car's connection to the drug crime. The client's innocent-owner status was the basis for her eventually recovering the car, but the statute placed the burden of proving innocence on the owner. The federal-level review noted this burden-shifting feature.

facts.client_belief: the State filed a forfeiture case pretty quickly — within ten days — so they must have done something right. But they still kept my car for about twenty months total before I got it back.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the State filed a forfeiture complaint against the client's car on February 27, 2019, just 10 days after seizure — satisfying the statutory 'promptly' requirement. However, the client waited six months before answering the complaint and another year before raising the innocent-owner defense on a motion for summary judgment. Summary judgment was granted on October 30, 2020, ordering the car's return — approximately 20 months after seizure. The client's intuition that the State's quick filing means it 'did something right' overstates the protective effect: prompt filing addresses one statutory requirement, but does not address the deeper due-process question of whether retention of the car for the multi-month/multi-year forfeiture process is itself constitutionally adequate.

facts.client_belief: Under the State law I could have gotten my car back while the forfeiture case was pending if I posted a bond equal to double the car's value. But that's not something most people can realistically afford.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the State law permitted a seized car's owner to recover it during the forfeiture proceeding by posting bond at double the car's appraised value. The federal-level review acknowledged this bond option as an existing procedural safeguard. Whether bond-at-double-value adequately substitutes for a retention hearing in all cases was not decided, and one body of authority on the issue argues it is often unaffordable and therefore illusory for low-income owners. The client's framing — that bond-at-double-value is unrealistic for most owners — is therefore correct as a practical matter, even if it has not been resolved as a constitutional matter.

facts.client_belief: I sued in federal court arguing that the Constitution requires a preliminary hearing — before the final forfeiture trial — where a judge could decide whether there's really a basis to hold my car while the case plays out.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client and a similarly situated owner filed § 1983 class-action complaints in federal-level review seeking money damages, claiming officials violated due process by retaining their cars without a preliminary (retention) hearing, and that they argued such a hearing was required under the Mathews v. Eldridge balancing test. The controlling federal-level holding is that existing precedent ($8,850; Von Neumann) already resolves the issue: due process requires only a timely forfeiture hearing, not a separate preliminary hearing. The client's intuition that the Mathews balancing test should drive the analysis is therefore foreclosed by the structural choice for the timely-hearing rule.

facts.client_belief: The federal-level reasoning pointed to history going back to the Founding era — early customs and revenue laws didn't have preliminary hearings — to justify ruling against us. But those old laws are nothing like modern civil forfeiture, which sweeps in innocent owners.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that, since the Founding era, federal and state statutes have authorized seizure of personal property pending a forfeiture hearing without a preliminary hearing, and that no pre-late-20th-century statute requiring a preliminary hearing in civil forfeiture cases has been identified. The controlling federal-level reasoning treated this historical absence as 'weighty evidence' that due process does not require such hearings. The client's intuition that historical practice is doctrinally irrelevant because Founding-era forfeitures differed structurally from modern civil forfeiture (which sweeps in innocent owners) overstates the doctrinal weight courts give to those distinctions in the timely-hearing analysis — although the structural-difference argument remains live in legislative-reform settings.

facts.client_belief: My case should also have been about the fact that police departments have a financial incentive to seize cars and drag out the process because the forfeiture proceeds go directly into their budgets.
facts.court_record: Available authority extensively documents law enforcement's financial incentives in civil forfeiture: in 32 states forfeiture proceeds flow directly to agency budgets, over 60% of policing agencies report dependence on forfeiture revenue, and forfeiture activity reportedly increases when local budgets tighten. The controlling federal-level holding did not address these incentive-structure arguments in its constitutional analysis, but separate reasoning in the same decision noted the concerns as unresolved questions for future cases. The client's intuition that the financial-incentive structure should drive the constitutional analysis therefore identifies a real doctrinal seam, even though it has not yet been operationalized into a controlling rule.

facts.client_belief: Loss of my car for twenty months had a devastating practical impact on my life — I couldn't commute, handle basic errands, or access healthcare easily.
facts.court_record: Available authority documents that over 85% of Americans drive to work, and that car loss is linked to job loss (e.g., 42% of people in New Jersey lost their jobs after driver's license suspension). One body of authority characterizes these practical harms as constitutionally relevant. The controlling federal-level holding did not separately analyze the severity of the deprivation beyond holding that a timely forfeiture hearing adequately protects against it. The client's framing — that 20 months of car loss is constitutionally weighty — is therefore live as a factual narrative but not yet operationalized into a separate constitutional remedy.

expected_inquiries: Ask the client for the complete state-court forfeiture case docket — every filing, hearing date, and order — to assess both $8,850 timeliness and any government-attributable procedural delay.

Ask the client to describe in detail every practical hardship caused by the 20-month loss of her car (lost income, transportation costs, missed medical care) and request documentary support for each category.

Ask why the client waited six months to answer the forfeiture complaint and another year to raise the innocent-owner defense, and assess whether the delay was attributable to inability to afford counsel or confusion about the process.
Ask whether the client ever contacted law enforcement or the court to request an earlier hearing or expedited proceeding during the 20-month period.

Ask whether the client would be willing to share her experience in legislative or advocacy forums, given that the controlling federal-level reasoning explicitly endorsed state legislative innovation as the preferred remedy.
Ask whether the client explored or was offered any settlement or redemption-fee arrangement during the forfeiture proceeding, as evidence of coercive pressure inconsistent with due process.

Ask the client for any documents related to the State's allocation of forfeiture proceeds (statutory framework, departmental budget filings, forfeiture revenue reports) for use in any continued advocacy.

Ask the client to provide records of the practical harm caused by the 20-month loss of her car (employment records, transportation expense records, medical-appointment records) for use in any further proceedings or advocacy.

Ask the client to provide records of the practical harm caused by the 20-month loss of her car (employment records, transportation expense records, medical-appointment records) for use in any further proceedings or advocacy.
memo_expectations: Analyze whether the four-factor timeliness test ($8,850; Barker v. Wingo) was satisfied in the client's specific forfeiture proceeding, taking into account both the government's 10-day filing and the client's 6-month delay in answering — and advise whether a timely-hearing challenge remains viable.
Assess whether the 'innocent owner' burden-shifting structure of the State's forfeiture statute independently raises a due process challenge not resolved by the majority's holding in this matter.
Evaluate the practical and constitutional adequacy of the State's bond-at-double-value mechanism as an alternative to a preliminary hearing, particularly for low-income property owners.

Advise on the impact of the State's 2021 amended forfeiture statute (Ala. Code § 15–5–63) on future clients in that jurisdiction and whether post-the client legislative reform advocacy is the most viable path.

Identify any surviving § 1983 due-process theories — such as inadequate notice, non-neutral adjudicator, or unreasonable government-caused delay — that were not foreclosed by the controlling federal-level holding.

Identify any surviving § 1983 due-process theories — such as inadequate notice, non-neutral adjudicator, or unreasonable government-caused delay — that were not foreclosed by the controlling federal-level holding.

Track the financial-incentive line of argument as a potential future doctrinal opening — note that it remains an unresolved question, not yet a dispositive constitutional rule, and consider whether to preserve it through legislative-reform pathways rather than further litigation.

Document the practical impact of the multi-month deprivation (lost income, transportation costs, missed medical care, missed family obligations) — relevant to any future constitutional argument that severity of the deprivation should drive the timeliness analysis under Barker.

opening: Hi, I'm X. I was hoping to speak with someone about a legal dispute — the state took my vehicle after my criminal case, and I'm not sure if that's allowed.

facts.client_belief: I pleaded guilty and took my punishment — one year of home detention, five years of probation, and fees. I don't see why my car should be taken on top of all that.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client pleaded guilty to dealing in a controlled substance and conspiracy to commit theft, and was sentenced to one year of home detention, five years of probation (including a court-supervised addiction-treatment program), and fees and costs totaling $1,203.

facts.client_belief: I bought my an SUV with life insurance money I received when my father died — it was my own money, nothing to do with drugs.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client purchased the an SUV for approximately $42,000 using proceeds from an insurance policy paid out upon his father's death. The source of funds is relevant to the proportionality analysis but did not, on its own, immunize the vehicle from forfeiture proceedings; the question is whether the vehicle was used to transport heroin, not how it was purchased.

facts.client_belief: The police used the fact that I had driven the car while doing something illegal as an excuse to seize it forever. That's like a punishment on top of a punishment, and that has to be unconstitutional.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the trial-level finder of fact found the client's vehicle had been used to facilitate violation of a criminal statute, and that the State engaged a private law firm to pursue civil forfeiture of the an SUV on the ground it was used to transport heroin. The client's intuition that 'punishment-on-top' is automatically unconstitutional, however, overstates the doctrine. Civil in rem forfeiture proceedings are doctrinally distinct from criminal sentencing and are not categorically barred as 'double-counting'; established federal authority (Austin v. United States, 1993) treats civil forfeitures as falling within the Excessive Fines Clause when they are at least partially punitive — but the question is whether the forfeiture is 'grossly disproportionate' to the offense, not whether layering forfeiture on top of a criminal sentence is itself a constitutional violation.

facts.client_belief: The car was worth $42,000. The biggest fine I could have gotten for the drug charge was $10,000. Taking the car feels way more extreme than anything else in my sentence.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the trial-level finding and the intermediate appellate authority both found the forfeiture would be grossly disproportionate to the gravity of the client's offense because the vehicle's value ($42,000) was more than four times the maximum statutory monetary fine ($10,000) for the drug conviction, and that those levels of review denied the forfeiture on Eighth Amendment grounds. Higher-level state authority did not reach the proportionality merits; it reversed solely on the ground that the Excessive Fines Clause does not bind the States.

facts.client_belief: Higher-level state authority said the Eighth Amendment's ban on excessive fines simply doesn't apply to what the State did here. That can't be right — the Constitution should protect me from my own state.
facts.court_record: Higher-level state authority held that the Excessive Fines Clause constrains only federal action and is inapplicable to state impositions. That position was reversed at the federal level: the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause incorporates the Excessive Fines Clause and renders it fully applicable to the States. There is therefore no daylight between the federal and state conduct the Clause prohibits. The client's intuition that the Constitution should protect against state action was therefore vindicated by the federal-level holding, but it was not the prevailing rule under the higher-level state authority that initially controlled.

facts.client_belief: I figured a constitutional protection like the Excessive Fines Clause would apply to states automatically — it's been around since Magna Carta.
facts.court_record: It is true that, when ratified in 1791, the Bill of Rights applied only to the Federal Government, and that selective incorporation through the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause is the mechanism by which Bill of Rights protections become binding on the States. A right is incorporated only if it is 'fundamental to our scheme of ordered liberty' or 'deeply rooted in this Nation's history and tradition.' The Excessive Fines Clause has been held to meet that test unanimously at the federal level. The client's intuition that the protection 'should apply to states automatically' captures the right outcome but skips the incorporation step that the doctrine requires.

facts.client_belief: The protection against excessive fines goes back to Magna Carta — that's more than 800 years.
facts.court_record: The Excessive Fines Clause traces its lineage to Magna Carta (1215), was reinforced in the English Bill of Rights (1689), appeared in the Virginia Declaration of Rights, and was adopted verbatim in the Eighth Amendment. By 1787, eight state constitutions forbade excessive fines; by 1868 (ratification of the Fourteenth Amendment), 35 of 37 state constitutions expressly prohibited excessive fines. The historical and logical case for incorporation was described as 'overwhelming.'

facts.client_belief: the State argued that even if the Excessive Fines Clause applies to states in general, it still shouldn't apply to civil asset forfeiture specifically. I thought that argument might give the court an out.
facts.court_record: Higher-level state authority on the State's behalf argued that the Clause's specific application to civil in rem forfeitures was neither fundamental nor deeply rooted, and that Austin v. United States (1993) — which extended the Clause to such forfeitures — was wrongly decided. Both arguments have been rejected on the corrected federal-level standard: the incorporation inquiry asks whether the right itself is fundamental, not whether every particular application of that right is fundamental. The Austin-overruling argument was also not properly before the federal-level review because the State had not raised it at the higher state level. The client's intuition that this technical-application argument might give the State 'an out' therefore overstates how the doctrine actually allocates incorporation analysis.

facts.client_belief: I thought the state's main move would be to challenge whether the forfeiture was actually excessive under the proportionality test — not to argue the Clause didn't apply to them at all.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that, at the higher-level state stage, the State argued only that the forfeiture would not be excessive, and that the higher-level state forum resolved the case entirely on the incorporation question and never addressed proportionality. The matter has now been vacated and remanded without a federal-level decision on whether the client's forfeiture was in fact excessive — that proportionality question remains open on continued review. The client's expectation that the State's main move would be on proportionality therefore captures the real merits-stage battle, even if the higher-level state forum had not actually engaged with that argument.

facts.client_belief: Once the federal-level review says the Clause applies to the states, I win and I get my car back, right?
facts.court_record: The proportionality question — whether forfeiture of the $42,000 an SUV is 'grossly disproportionate' to the client's offense — was not decided at the federal level and must be addressed on continued review. The lower trial-level and intermediate appellate authority had previously ruled in the client's favor on that question, but those rulings were not final, and the State may litigate the merits on continued review. The client's intuition that the framework win automatically delivers the car back therefore overstates the operative scope of the federal-level holding, which decided incorporation only.

facts.client_belief: The state hired a private law firm to go after my car. That seems like a conflict of interest — they profit from the forfeiture.
facts.court_record: Available federal-level reasoning notes that the State engaged a private law firm to bring the civil forfeiture suit. The reasoning cited the broader concern that fines can be used 'not in service of penal purposes, but as a source of revenue,' and that governments 'increasingly depend heavily on fines and fees as a source of general revenue.' The federal-level reasoning did not, however, hold that the use of private counsel in forfeiture proceedings is independently unconstitutional; that issue was not before it. The client's intuition that the private-counsel arrangement is constitutionally objectionable therefore identifies a real concern, but the concern has not been operationalized into a controlling rule.

expected_inquiries: Ask the client to provide complete documentation of the criminal proceedings, including the plea agreement, judgment of conviction, and sentencing order, to frame the proportionality comparison between the forfeiture and the criminal penalty.

Ask the client for the original purchase records for the an SUV ($42,000) and any documentation of the insurance proceeds from his father's estate, to establish that the vehicle was not purchased with drug proceeds.
Request any records or correspondence from the State's forfeiture proceedings, including the civil complaint filed by the private law firm and any valuations of the vehicle.

Ask whether the client was offered any opportunity to contest the forfeiture before the vehicle was seized or whether summary seizure occurred, to assess any procedural due process issues running parallel to the Excessive Fines claim.

Inquire whether the client has received any communication from the private law firm retained by the State, and whether any settlement offer was made, to evaluate potential avenues for resolving the forfeiture without further litigation.

Ask about the client's current circumstances — addiction treatment progress, employment, probation compliance — to frame any equitable arguments on proportionality and to assess the vehicle's practical importance to the client's rehabilitation.

Identify whether the State's forfeiture statute has any provisions allowing return of property pending a constitutional challenge, and advise the client on whether a motion for interim relief is viable on remand.
Identify whether the State has preserved any narrow-application or Austin-overruling theory in any current or potential continued review, and what record support exists for or against it.

Compile expert valuations of the an SUV (then and now), the maximum-fine schedule for the underlying offenses, and any comparable forfeiture cases to support the gross-disproportionality showing on continued review.

Walk the client through the realistic continued-review timeline, the evidentiary record needed for proportionality, and the possibility of further motion practice and continued review on the proportionality question.

Obtain documents related to the State's engagement of the private law firm, including the engagement letter, any contingency-fee or compensation arrangement, and any communications reflecting fee-driven incentives.

Obtain documents related to the State's engagement of the private law firm, including the engagement letter, any contingency-fee or compensation arrangement, and any communications reflecting fee-driven incentives.
memo_expectations: Analyze whether the Eighth Amendment's Excessive Fines Clause, as incorporated against the States through the Fourteenth Amendment, bars the civil in rem forfeiture of the client's an SUV.

Apply the gross-disproportionality test from United States v. Bajakajian (1998) to the specific facts: vehicle value ($42,000) versus maximum statutory fine ($10,000), the nature of the offenses, any harm to victims, and the client's sentence as a whole.
Assess whether the civil forfeiture here is 'at least partially punitive' within the meaning of Austin v. United States (1993) so as to bring it within the Excessive Fines Clause.

Evaluate the significance of the State's engagement of a private law firm on a contingency or fee basis to pursue forfeiture, and whether that creates any additional constitutional or statutory challenges.
Survey the State's own excessive-fines jurisprudence and any state constitutional provisions that may provide an independent, potentially broader, ground for challenging the forfeiture.

Address the procedural posture going forward: higher-level state authority must now apply the incorporated Excessive Fines Clause; assess what standard of review applies and what additional fact-finding, if any, may be needed.

Consider whether any arguments exist for overruling or limiting Austin if the State continues to resist on remand, and the likelihood that the current Court would revisit Austin given the split concurrences on the incorporation methodology.

Brief the structural answer to any 'narrow application' argument: incorporation analyzes the right itself, not the particular application; once the right is incorporated, all settled applications travel with it.

Plan the proportionality merits as the load-bearing battleground on continued review: marshall the gross-disproportionality factors (vehicle value vs. maximum statutory fine, nature of offense, harm, sentence as a whole) and prepare for fresh evidentiary findings.

Reset the client's expectations: the federal-level holding decided incorporation only. On continued review, the State may relitigate (i) whether the forfeiture is grossly disproportionate, (ii) the comparator (statutory fine vs. sentence as a whole), (iii) the nature and harm of the offense, and (iv) any procedural questions left open below.

Track the private-counsel concern as a potential future doctrinal opening; it has not yet ripened into a controlling rule, so consider preserving it through legislative reform or as a parallel due-process / structural-conflict argument.

opening: Hi, I'm X. I spoke with your office about a bankruptcy dispute — my car was impounded and I was hoping you could help me understand my rights after filing.

facts.client_belief: I had unpaid fines for traffic violations and the City impounded my car because of those unpaid fines.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client's vehicle was impounded by the City for failure to pay fines for motor vehicle infractions.

facts.client_belief: I filed for Chapter 13 bankruptcy, I asked the City to give me my car back.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client filed a Chapter 13 bankruptcy petition and requested return of his vehicle. Filing a bankruptcy petition does trigger an automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. § 362(a), but the precise scope of that stay — and whether it compels a creditor to affirmatively return property — is the central legal dispute.

facts.client_belief: The City flat-out refused to return my car after I filed for bankruptcy. I thought that once I filed, every creditor had to stop what they were doing — including holding my property.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the City refused to return the impounded vehicle. The intermediate appellate ruling in this matter held that the refusal violated § 362(a)(3)'s automatic stay; the controlling federal-level holding has now reversed that result. The client's intuition that 'every creditor must stop, including holding my property' is partly correct (the stay does freeze most affirmative actions) but overstates the stay's reach against passive retention of pre-petition possessions — that is precisely the question § 362(a)(3) does not answer in the client's favor.

facts.client_belief: I thought the automatic stay meant the City legally couldn't keep my car without violating the law. The court below agreed with me.
facts.court_record: § 362(a)(3) prohibits only affirmative acts that disturb the status quo as of the bankruptcy filing; passive retention of property the City already possessed is not such an act. The provision's text — 'any act to exercise control' — connotes affirmative conduct, not mere continued possession.

facts.client_belief: I need my car to get to work. Without it, I can't keep earning income, and without income I can't make my Chapter 13 plan payments. The City is basically sabotaging my entire bankruptcy — that practical reality has to give me a stronger legal claim.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that, for many Chapter 13 debtors — who must have 'regular income' to qualify — a vehicle is essential to employment and plan completion. The client's intuition that this practical hardship has to translate into a stronger legal claim, however, is mistaken: the equitable concern is recognized as a policy matter but does not alter the statutory interpretation of § 362(a)(3). The hardship strengthens an emergency-turnover petition under § 542(a) but does not expand the stay's reach over passive retention.

facts.client_belief: Lawyers told me earlier that some courts had said keeping a debtor's car after bankruptcy violates the automatic stay, so I had a solid legal position.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that, on the question presented here, intermediate appellate authority was split — some appellate courts had held that retention of a debtor's property after a bankruptcy filing violated § 362(a)(3), while others had reached the opposite result. The controlling federal-level holding has now resolved that split against the client's position by reading § 362(a)(3) to require affirmative conduct, not mere continued possession.

facts.client_belief: The City impounded my car before I filed for bankruptcy, so they got it legally. But once I filed, keeping it should have been a different story — they should have had to give it back immediately.
facts.court_record: Where a creditor lawfully seized property prebankruptcy, mere continued possession after the petition filing is not an 'act to exercise control' within the meaning of § 362(a)(3). The prebankruptcy legality of the seizure is relevant: the stay preserves the status quo as of filing, rather than mandating an immediate reversal of that status quo.

facts.client_belief: The City was demanding I pay $1,250 upfront or wait until the court confirmed my bankruptcy plan before getting my car back. That's clearly them trying to collect their debt, which the stay should prevent.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that, on the controlling federal-level standard, whether the City's conditional refusal — requiring upfront payment or plan confirmation — violated other subsections of § 362(a) (such as § 362(a)(4) — acts to perfect or enforce a lien — or § 362(a)(6) — acts to collect a prepetition debt) was not decided. In one of the consolidated client matters, the trial-level bankruptcy review found violations of those subsections; the intermediate appellate review and federal-level review did not reach those theories. The client's intuition that conditioning return on payment is 'clearly collection' therefore has live doctrinal support under § 362(a)(4)/(a)(6), even though it is foreclosed under § 362(a)(3) alone.

facts.client_belief: Reading § 542 as the only way to get my car back seems absurd — it requires a full lawsuit (adversary proceeding) that can take over 100 days. I shouldn't have to wait that long when my car is being held hostage.
facts.court_record: Concurring reasoning in the controlling holding acknowledges that § 542(a) turnover proceedings, typically treated as adversary proceedings under Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 7001(1), average over 100 days. Some bankruptcy forums allow turnover by motion rather than adversary proceeding where the creditor receives adequate notice. The opinion encourages expedited procedures but leaves gap-filling to rule drafters and policymakers. The client's intuition that a 100+ day adversary proceeding is absurd in this context is correct as a policy matter and is reflected in the concurring reasoning, but it does not bypass the procedural framework altogether.

facts.client_belief: My car was worth around $4,300 and already serving as collateral on a $7,300 debt. The City knew this car wasn't worth much to them sitting in the impound lot — they were just being difficult, and that should make turnover a slam-dunk.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that, in the client's matter, the vehicle was worth approximately $4,300 and was already encumbered by a debt of approximately $7,300. Under § 542(a), turnover is not required for property of 'inconsequential value or benefit to the estate.' Whether this vehicle meets that threshold is a fact-specific inquiry. Returning the vehicle would benefit all parties, including the City, by enabling the client to earn income and make plan payments — but the client's confidence that the value differential makes turnover a 'slam-dunk' overstates how the inconsequential-value exception is actually applied: the City can press it as a threshold defense to the turnover petition, not the other way around.

facts.client_belief: This City policy of holding cars until fines are paid is part of a broader system that traps low-income people in debt. I thought the whole point of Chapter 13 was to give people a fresh start, so the law should bend to that purpose.
facts.court_record: Concurring reasoning in the controlling holding acknowledges the policy concern: the impound-and-hold practice disproportionately burdens low-income communities and communities of color, and the Bankruptcy Code's fresh-start purpose is frustrated by prolonged vehicle retention. The client's intuition that the law should bend to that purpose, however, is mistaken: the controlling holding declines to expand § 362(a)(3) on policy grounds, leaving any structural fix to legislative reform and to expedited § 542 procedures. The fresh-start narrative is real but is not, on this record, a doctrinal lever to reach the City's retention.

expected_inquiries: Ask the client for the specific types of violations at issue, the dates the fines were assessed, the total amount owed to the City, and whether the City had obtained a court judgment or administrative order on the debt before impounding the vehicle.
Ask whether the client had retained counsel when filing the petition, whether a demand letter or motion for turnover was filed, and whether any adversary proceeding has been initiated under § 542.

Ask the client whether the City took any additional action after the bankruptcy filing — such as selling the vehicle, transferring it, or applying storage fees — because affirmative acts of that nature may still violate § 362(a)(3) even under the controlling narrower reading.

Gather all written communications from the City regarding the conditions for return of the vehicle (e.g., requirements to pay upfront or await plan confirmation), as these may support an argument that the retention was not purely passive.

Document the client's commute, employment situation, and income source in detail — including distance to work, availability of public transit, and whether job loss has already occurred or is imminent — to support a showing of necessity and irreparable harm in any motion for expedited turnover.

Confirm which judicial district the client's case is in and identify the applicable bankruptcy court's local rules and any standing orders regarding § 542 turnover proceedings, including whether motions or adversary proceedings are required.

Ask whether the client received any notice from the City after the bankruptcy filing regarding a scheduled auction, lien sale, or other disposition of the vehicle, and whether the City continued accruing storage or impound fees post-petition.

Obtain all written communications in which the City stated its conditions for returning the vehicle, including any form letters, notices of impound fees, or correspondence from the City's legal department, to document the collection demand.

Ask the client's bankruptcy attorney whether a motion for expedited turnover has been filed or considered, and whether the bankruptcy court has any local rules or standing orders that permit abbreviated turnover procedures for vehicles.

Obtain an independent appraisal or Kelley Blue Book valuation of the vehicle, documentation of the outstanding lien balance, and evidence of the vehicle's necessity to the client's employment (e.g., employer letter, commute records) to use in the turnover proceeding.

Ask the client whether they are interested in participating in any class-action, public-interest, or advocacy efforts related to the City's impound practices, and flag that organizations such as the ACLU have submitted amicus briefs on this issue that may provide litigation support resources.

Ask the client whether they are interested in participating in any class-action, public-interest, or advocacy efforts related to the City's impound practices, and flag that organizations such as the ACLU have submitted amicus briefs on this issue that may provide litigation support resources.
memo_expectations: Analyze whether the City's refusal to return the impounded vehicle, combined with conditioning return on upfront payment or plan confirmation, constitutes an affirmative act to collect a prepetition debt in violation of § 362(a)(6) or an act to enforce a lien under § 362(a)(4) — theories that the controlling federal-level holding expressly left open.

Evaluate whether the debtor can satisfy the prerequisites for turnover under § 542(a), including demonstrating that the vehicle is property the trustee could use under § 363, that it is not of 'inconsequential value or benefit to the estate,' and that the debtor can provide adequate protection of the City's secured interest.

Assess the vehicle's value relative to the outstanding City debt and any senior lien to determine whether the estate has equity in the vehicle and whether the 'inconsequential value' exception to § 542(a) is available to the City.

Research the applicable bankruptcy court's local rules and standing orders to determine whether § 542 turnover can be sought by emergency motion rather than a full adversary proceeding, and if so, what showing of urgency and notice to the creditor is required.

Determine whether any additional City conduct post-petition — continued accrual of storage fees, threats of auction, or formal lien enforcement — independently violates § 362(a)(3), (a)(4), or (a)(6) under the controlling narrower interpretation; the practical-hardship narrative is most useful in supporting expedited turnover under § 542(a), not in expanding the stay itself.

Identify whether any other § 362(a) subsection (particularly §§ 362(a)(4) and (a)(6)) can support a damages claim under § 362(k) for willful stay violation, given the City's apparent awareness of the bankruptcy filing and its continued conditional retention.

Research the applicable bankruptcy forum's local rules and standing orders to determine whether § 542 turnover can be sought by emergency motion rather than a full adversary proceeding, and if so, what showing of urgency and notice to the creditor is required.

opening: Hi, I'm X, Executive Director of X Association. I contacted your office about a regulatory dispute — my organization is challenging a federal agency's authority to impose restrictions on our members, and I was hoping you could help us understand our options.

facts.client_belief: The Federal Health Agency imposed a nationwide eviction moratorium and kept extending it even after Congress's own moratorium expired and Congress chose not to renew it. We believe the Federal Health Agency simply had no authority to do that.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that Congress enacted a 120-day eviction moratorium in the Federal Relief Act for federally backed properties, which expired in July 2020 without renewal, and that the Federal Health Agency then imposed its own nationwide moratorium under § 361(a) of the Public Health Service Act and subsequently extended it multiple times. The controlling federal-level reasoning has found the client 'virtually certain to succeed' on the argument that the Federal Health Agency exceeded its statutory authority.

facts.client_belief: The statute the Federal Health Agency relies on — § 361(a) — is an old public health law about fumigation and pest control. There is no way that language authorizes a sweeping nationwide eviction ban; this should be an obvious win.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that § 361(a) authorizes measures such as inspection, fumigation, disinfection, sanitation, pest extermination, and destruction of contaminated animals or articles, and that those examples directly target disease itself, whereas an eviction moratorium affects the spread of disease only indirectly.
