The client's intuition that this is an 'obvious win,' however, somewhat overstates the doctrinal posture: the second-sentence-limits-the-first reading was contested in the doctrinal dissent, and the Government argued the first sentence's general grant of authority is independent of the specific examples. The client's reading prevailed under the corrected federal-level standard, but it required active doctrinal work to establish.

facts.client_belief: The government claims the first sentence of § 361(a) gives the Federal Health Agency unlimited authority to do whatever it judges necessary to prevent disease spread, including banning evictions. That can't be right — the examples in the second sentence have to mean something.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the second sentence of § 361(a), listing specific enforcement measures, can be read to inform and limit the first sentence's grant of authority rather than expand it. Reading both sentences together, it is 'a stretch' to read § 361(a) as conferring authority over evictions. Doctrinal authority on the other side reads the second sentence as expanding rather than limiting the first; the client's intuition that 'the examples have to mean something' captures the operative interpretive instinct, but the dueling readings are textual not obvious.

facts.client_belief: Even if there is some ambiguity in the statute, an agency shouldn't be able to claim this kind of massive power — covering 80% of the country and affecting millions of tenants — without Congress clearly authorizing it. With that scope, the major-questions doctrine has to apply automatically.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that, when an agency claims authority of 'vast economic and political significance,' Congress must speak clearly under the major-questions doctrine. The moratorium covered at least 80% of the country and between 6 and 17 million tenants at risk of eviction; Congress provided nearly $50 billion in emergency rental assistance as a proxy for its economic scale. The client's intuition that the major-questions doctrine applies 'automatically' at this scale, however, slightly overstates the framework: the doctrine is a triggered canon, not a per-se rule, and the Government can argue (and did) that the underlying public-health emergency justifies a broader reading even at this scale. The client's instinct prevailed under the corrected federal-level standard but required scope-evidence development to win.

facts.client_belief: This moratorium has never been done before under this statute. The Federal Health Agency has had § 361(a) since 1944 and never previously used it for anything remotely like an eviction ban — that alone should be enough to defeat their authority claim.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that, since § 361(a)'s enactment in 1944, regulations promulgated under it had generally been limited to quarantining infected individuals and prohibiting importation or sale of disease-carrying animals, and that no prior regulation approached the scope of the eviction moratorium. The client's intuition that decades of non-use is by itself dispositive, however, overstates the doctrine. The unprecedented nature of the claim is 'weighty evidence' against the Government's interpretation, but it is not categorically dispositive — the Government argued that the COVID-19 emergency was itself unprecedented and justified novel use of the statute. The unprecedented-use argument prevailed but as one input into the major-questions analysis, not as a standalone bar.

facts.client_belief: The government also imposed criminal penalties — up to $250,000 and a year in jail — for violating the moratorium. That makes the case for invalidation even stronger.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the Federal Health Agency's moratorium imposed criminal penalties of up to $250,000 and one year in jail for violations. The corrected federal-level reasoning cited this as further evidence that § 361(a) — described as a 'wafer-thin reed' — was an insufficient basis for such sweeping authority. The client's intuition that criminal penalties categorically strengthen the invalidation case is correct as a matter of doctrinal weight, but it is one of several inputs (statutory text, scope, federalism, congressional silence) — not by itself dispositive.

facts.client_belief: Landlord-tenant law is state law. The federal government is stepping into an area that has always belonged to the states without any clear congressional authorization — that should automatically defeat the moratorium.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the moratorium intruded into landlord-tenant relations, an area traditionally governed by state law. Established federal authority requires 'exceedingly clear language' when Congress wishes to significantly alter the balance between federal and state power, and the moratorium's intrusion into state-law property rights reinforced the major-questions concern. The client's intuition that federalism intrusion 'automatically' defeats the moratorium, however, overstates the doctrine: the federalism canon is one input that strengthens the major-questions analysis, but Congress can authorize federal intrusion into traditional state domains if it does so with sufficient clarity — the question is whether it did so here, not whether the intrusion is categorically forbidden.

facts.client_belief: Our members are landlords who can't evict tenants who aren't paying rent, and there's no guarantee we'll ever recover the lost rent. The government keeps saying the $46 billion in rental assistance fixes our harm, but that money isn't reaching us.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that depriving the client and its members of rent payments with no guarantee of eventual recovery constitutes irreparable harm, and that preventing eviction of breaching tenants interferes with a fundamental element of property ownership — the right to exclude. The doctrinal dissent noted Congress appropriated $46.5 billion in rental assistance and that the moratorium required tenants to make partial payments to the extent possible, arguing this mitigated landlord harm. The client's intuition that the rental-assistance program does not actually reach landlords on the ground is a real factual concern but is contested; if the program is in fact disbursing funds, the irreparable-harm narrative weakens.

facts.client_belief: The government argues that vacating the stay would hurt tenants who might spread COVID-19 if evicted. But that public interest argument doesn't override the fact that the Federal Health Agency acted unlawfully.
facts.court_record: It is acknowledged at the federal level that there is a strong public interest in combating COVID-19, but 'our system does not permit agencies to act unlawfully even in pursuit of desirable ends' (Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer). It was further noted that Congress had been on notice that any extension would require new legislation yet failed to act. The client's intuition that the public-interest argument cannot 'override' an unlawful action is therefore correct as a doctrinal matter — but the operative question is whether the action was unlawful, which the public-interest framing does not by itself answer.

facts.client_belief: When the trial-level review granted us summary judgment and found the moratorium unlawful, the government asked for a stay. The lower review said there was at least a 'serious legal question' and granted the stay, but we think that standard was wrong.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the trial-level review granted summary judgment in the client's favor but stayed its order, applying a 'serious legal question' standard, and that the next-level appellate review agreed and also declined to vacate the stay. The corrected federal-level standard applied the four-factor stay analysis under Nken v. Holder and found all factors supported the client — particularly that the client had a 'substantial likelihood of success,' not merely a serious legal question.

facts.client_belief: The new moratorium issued after July 31 is basically the same as the old one — narrowing it to high-transmission counties doesn't make it lawful.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the Federal Health Agency allowed the moratorium to expire on July 31, 2021 and reimposed it three days later, and that, apart from slightly narrowing geographic scope to counties with substantial or high transmission, the new moratorium is 'indistinguishable from the old.' Doctrinal authority on the other side argues the modifications were meaningful and the new order was substantially more tailored. The client's intuition that geographic narrowing alone does not cure the statutory-authority defect is correct as a doctrinal matter, but the substantiality of the modifications was contested, not obvious.

facts.client_belief: At least five members of the reviewing body had already signaled they believed the Federal Health Agency lacked authority — four would have vacated the earlier stay outright, and one separate concurring vote said the moratorium exceeded statutory authority. The lower review should have taken that as a clear signal.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that an earlier round of federal-level review of the application to vacate was accompanied by four members of the reviewing body stating they would vacate, and one separate concurring vote concluding that the moratorium exceeded statutory authority but allowing the stay for the short remaining period. The trial-level review on remand relied on those signals to conclude the Government was unlikely to succeed on the merits, though it felt bound by appellate precedent. The corrected federal-level standard ultimately agreed on the merits.

facts.client_belief: The government's interest in maintaining the moratorium has weakened — vaccine distribution has improved, rental assistance has had more time to roll out, and the original equitable justifications for a stay no longer apply.
facts.court_record: The corrected federal-level reasoning found that the Government's interest in the stay had diminished since it was originally entered: three additional months had passed for distribution of rental-assistance funds, whatever interest in orderly administration of those programs had since decreased, and Congress failed to legislate an extension despite notice that the moratorium's end would require new legislation.

expected_inquiries: Ask the client to provide documentation of the specific financial losses attributable to the moratorium, including unpaid rent ledgers, tenant-by-tenant arrears, and any partial payments made under the moratorium's directive.

Ask whether the client or its members have applied for or received federal rental-assistance funds, and in what amounts, so counsel can accurately characterize the net harm in any future equitable proceedings.

Ask whether any of the client's members have already obtained state-court eviction judgments that remain unenforceable due to the moratorium, to identify the strongest candidates for demonstrating concrete irreparable harm.

Ask whether the client has standing to assert its members' injuries in a representative capacity and whether individual landlord members are prepared to submit declarations supporting the irreparable-harm showing.

Ask the client to identify which specific counties covered by the moratorium experienced 'substantial or high' transmission levels at the time of filing, and obtain the Federal Health Agency transmission-rate data to assess the geographic scope of the contested order.

Ask whether any member intends to pursue damages claims against the government and, if so, whether a Tucker Act or other monetary-relief vehicle has been explored as a complement to the equitable relief obtained.

Advise the client that, because the corrected federal-level standard vacates the stay and renders the trial-level summary judgment enforceable, the next step is to monitor whether the Government files a renewed regulatory action and whether Congress moves to enact new moratorium legislation.
Ask the client to identify any pending or anticipated Congressional legislation that could moot the case or require revision of litigation strategy.

Ask whether any member intends to pursue damages claims against the government and, if so, whether a Tucker Act or other monetary-relief vehicle has been explored as a complement to the equitable relief obtained.

Ask whether any member intends to pursue damages claims against the government and, if so, whether a Tucker Act or other monetary-relief vehicle has been explored as a complement to the equitable relief obtained.
memo_expectations: Analyze whether § 361(a) of the Public Health Service Act, read in its entirety, grants the Federal Health Agency authority to impose an eviction moratorium, applying the canon that specific examples in a statute inform and limit the scope of a general grant.

Apply the major-questions doctrine to assess whether the Federal Health Agency's claimed authority is the kind of vast economic and political power that requires clear congressional authorization, and evaluate whether such authorization exists.

Assess the client's likelihood of success on the merits under the four-factor Nken v. Holder stay standard, distinguishing the 'serious legal question' threshold applied at the lower-level review from the 'substantial likelihood of success' standard required at the federal level.

Analyze the irreparable-harm prong, including the right-to-exclude theory under Loretto, the absence of a guarantee of full rent recovery, and whether congressional rental-assistance appropriations adequately compensate landlords.

Evaluate the federalism dimension — the landlord-tenant relationship as a traditional domain of state law — and whether the moratorium's intrusion into state police powers requires exceedingly clear federal authorization under Cowpasture River.

Examine the precedential scope of the decision for future agency actions: does the ruling limit only eviction moratoria under § 361(a), or does it signal a broader limit on the Federal Health Agency rulemaking under the major-questions doctrine?

Consider the implications of the Federal Health Agency's failure to seek express congressional reauthorization after the first moratorium expired and whether that legislative gap reinforces or undermines the major-questions analysis.
Assess the dissent's statutory interpretation — that § 361(a)'s second sentence expands rather than limits the first — and prepare counterarguments for any further proceedings or related litigation.
Brief the unlawful-means-no-matter-the-end principle and prepare to rebut any future agency claim that public-interest urgency dispenses with the major-questions clear-statement requirement.

opening: Hi, I'm X. I spoke with your office about a consumer protection issue related to a foreclosure on my home — I was hoping you could help me figure out my rights.

facts.client_belief: I bought a home in the State back in 2007 with a loan of just under $330,000, using the property as collateral. A couple of years later I fell behind on payments.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client purchased a home in the State in 2007 with a just under $330,000 loan secured by the property as a mortgage/deed of trust, and that he defaulted approximately two years later, around 2009.

facts.client_belief: In 2014, a law firm we'd never heard from showed up out of nowhere and sent me a letter saying they were hired to start a foreclosure. They even said in the letter that they were complying with the FDCPA — so they must be debt collectors under that law.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the lender retained outside counsel in 2014 to carry out a nonjudicial foreclosure as its agent, and that the firm's letter disclosed the outstanding loan amount, identified the lender as the creditor, and purported to provide notice under both the FDCPA and the State law. Under the corrected federal-level standard, however, a business engaged in no more than nonjudicial foreclosure proceedings is NOT a 'debt collector' within the primary definition of the FDCPA, except for the limited purpose of § 1692f(6). The firm's own label of FDCPA compliance in the letter has no legal effect on whether it actually qualifies as a debt collector — voluntary recitation does not create coverage.

facts.client_belief: I sent the firm a letter invoking my rights under the FDCPA — specifically the part that says a debt collector has to stop collecting and verify the debt if I dispute it. They completely ignored that and just filed the foreclosure anyway.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client invoked § 1692g(b), which requires a 'debt collector' to cease collection activity and provide debt verification upon a consumer's written dispute. Under the corrected federal-level standard, the firm is not a 'debt collector' under the primary FDCPA definition for purposes of nonjudicial foreclosure, so § 1692g(b)'s verification requirement did not apply. The firm's initiation of the nonjudicial foreclosure after receiving the client's dispute letter was therefore not a violation of § 1692g(b). The client's intuition that invoking § 1692g(b) creates the protections it normally provides therefore overlooks the threshold coverage question — the protections never attached.

facts.client_belief: the firm filed a 'notice of election and demand' with the county public trustee even after I disputed the debt. That notice even said they were going to sell my property to pay the debt — that's clearly debt collection, not just a security-interest enforcement.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the firm filed a notice of election and demand with the county public trustee as required under the State's nonjudicial foreclosure statute, and that nonjudicial foreclosure is, in an ordinary sense, a means of collecting a debt — an indirect attempt to collect on a consumer's obligation. Under the corrected federal-level standard, however, the limited-purpose definition of § 1692a(6) carves security-interest enforcers out of the primary 'debt collector' definition, so the notices required to carry out a nonjudicial foreclosure are excluded as the 'legal means required' to enforce a security interest. The client's intuition that 'this is clearly debt collection' captures the ordinary-language sense but conflicts with the doctrinal carve-out for security-interest enforcement.

facts.client_belief: Even if they're some kind of limited debt collector, the FDCPA's venue provision — the part about legal actions to enforce interests in real property — only makes sense if people who enforce real-property security interests are covered by the whole Act.
facts.court_record: Under the corrected federal-level standard, the client's argument that the venue provision implies coverage of security-interest enforcers is foreclosed. The venue provision (§ 1692i(a)) merely specifies where a debt collector must sue if it brings a legal action to enforce a real-property security interest; it does not independently define who is a debt collector. The provision still has practical effect for entities that qualify as debt collectors on other grounds (e.g., credit-card collectors) who also happen to file real-property enforcement actions. Here, the only basis alleged for calling the firm a debt collector was its role in nonjudicial foreclosure, which has been excluded.

facts.client_belief: Okay, even if they're not a regular debt collector, the law still has a special provision — § 1692f(6) — that applies to security-interest enforcers. So at a minimum they can't threaten to take my property when they don't actually have the right to do so.
facts.court_record: It is undisputed that the firm, as a security-interest enforcer, is subject to § 1692f(6), which prohibits taking or threatening nonjudicial action to dispossess property when there is no present right to possession, no present intention to take possession, or the property is exempt. The corrected federal-level standard expressly affirmed this limited coverage. Whether the firm actually violated § 1692f(6) was not decided.

facts.client_belief: The foreclosure letters the firm sent me were terrifying — they made it crystal clear that I'd lose my home unless I paid up immediately. Any normal homeowner reading those letters would think someone was trying to collect a debt from them.
facts.court_record: The corrected federal-level standard acknowledges the gravity of foreclosure notices to homeowners, but holds that notices required as antecedent steps under state nonjudicial foreclosure law are excluded from FDCPA coverage along with the foreclosure process itself. The reasoning is that excluding 'the enforcement of security interests' must also exclude the legal means required to do so. The standard left open whether conduct related to, but not required for, security-interest enforcement could transform a foreclosure agent into a debt collector under the primary definition. The client's intuition that 'any normal homeowner reading those letters would think someone was trying to collect a debt' is correct as a matter of consumer perception but does not change the doctrinal carve-out — perception does not control coverage.

facts.client_belief: I'm worried that the corrected federal-level ruling basically lets creditors and foreclosure firms get away with any abusive behavior — like harassing phone calls in the middle of the night — just by calling it 'security-interest enforcement.'
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the corrected federal-level standard expressly rejects the broader concern that creditors and foreclosure firms can avoid all FDCPA liability by relabeling abusive conduct as 'security-interest enforcement.' The FDCPA exclusion applies only to conduct that constitutes nonjudicial foreclosure proceedings as required by state law. 'Enforcing a security interest does not grant an actor blanket immunity from the Act.' Abusive conduct not required for security-interest enforcement — such as repetitive nighttime phone calls — may still trigger FDCPA liability. Concurring reasoning further stressed this limitation.

facts.client_belief: There's a circuit split on this issue — other federal circuits found that foreclosure firms are covered by the FDCPA. Doesn't that mean I have a stronger argument?
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that intermediate appellate authority on the question presented was previously split — some appellate courts had held that nonjudicial foreclosure agents are debt collectors for all FDCPA purposes, while the corrected federal-level standard has now held the opposite. Prior intermediate appellate precedents favorable to homeowners (e.g., Kaymark, Glazer, Wilson) have been expressly abrogated. The client's intuition that the prior circuit split makes his argument 'stronger' captures the historical posture but is now obsolete: the split has been resolved against the client's position.

facts.client_belief: I at least want an injunction or some kind of relief to make them stop and to protect other homeowners in the same situation.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the matter was resolved on the merits of the FDCPA coverage question, with the corrected federal-level standard affirming the dismissal. No injunctive relief was sought or considered at the federal-level review. State law provides protections against abusive nonjudicial foreclosure practices (notice requirements, public-trustee oversight, limited court supervision), and Congress retains the power to expand FDCPA coverage if it chooses. The client's intuition that an injunction is the natural remedy overstates what is doctrinally available on this record — an FDCPA-vehicle injunction depends on FDCPA coverage, which has been negated.

facts.client_belief: I thought that because the firm voluntarily put 'FDCPA compliant' language in their letter, and because the repo-man cases suggested security-interest enforcers can be covered, there was solid legal basis to bring a full FDCPA suit.
facts.court_record: Under the corrected federal-level standard, the 'repo man' argument that the limited-purpose definition was meant only to add coverage for personal-property repossessors not otherwise covered by the primary definition is rejected. Even repossession constitutes an indirect means of debt collection, so the limited-purpose definition would be superfluous under that reading. The text, legislative history, and concern over conflicts with state foreclosure schemes all support the narrower reading that excludes nonjudicial foreclosure agents from the primary definition. The client's intuition that the firm's voluntary FDCPA invocation plus the repo-man cases creates a 'solid legal basis' for a full FDCPA suit therefore relies on a textual theory that has been rejected.

expected_inquiries: Ask the client for the original loan documents, all correspondence from the lender or servicer after the default, and any records of payments made after the initial default.
Ask the client to provide all correspondence received from the foreclosure firm, including envelopes and any attachments, and note the exact language used regarding FDCPA compliance.

Ask the client whether the dispute letter was sent via certified mail with return receipt, whether any response was ever received from the firm, and whether the client has a copy of the letter and proof of delivery.

Ask the client to describe all contacts from the firm beyond the formal foreclosure filings — any phone calls, additional letters, or in-person contacts — and determine whether any of those were required under the State law or were voluntary collection efforts.

Ask the client whether the firm or the lender filed any separate lawsuit to obtain a deficiency judgment, made any demand for payment beyond the foreclosure notices, or engaged in any communication style that went beyond the standard the State foreclosure notice sequence.

Ask the client for documentary evidence of any defects in the foreclosure process: missed statutory notice periods, incorrect payoff amounts in the notice of election and demand, failures to send materials to the correct address, or errors in the public trustee filing.

Request a complete timeline and copies of every communication — letters, emails, voicemails, texts — the client received from the firm, and compare each against the State nonjudicial foreclosure statute's required notice sequence to isolate any non-required contacts.

Ask the client to document any contacts from the firm that felt harassing or abusive, including the method (phone, letter, in-person), time of day, frequency, tone, and content, and whether any of those contacts referenced collecting money rather than the foreclosure process specifically.

Ask whether the client has any claims under state consumer protection statutes (e.g., CCPA, C.R.S. § 6-1-101 et seq.) and whether any state court cases or attorney general guidance have addressed abusive nonjudicial foreclosure practices.

Ask whether the client has already lost the home through completed foreclosure sale or whether the sale is still pending; the remedies available differ substantially depending on whether the foreclosure has been completed.

Identify any specific conduct beyond the firm's required state-law foreclosure actions that could support a § 1692f(6) claim or a state-law analogue, including communications outside the standard notice sequence.

Identify any specific conduct beyond the firm's required state-law foreclosure actions that could support a § 1692f(6) claim or a state-law analogue, including communications outside the standard notice sequence.
memo_expectations: Confirm the exact default date and any subsequent forbearance agreements, loan modifications, or partial payments, as these affect the outstanding balance, the accrual of fees, and the timeline of any statutes of limitations.

Analyze whether the firm's voluntary invocation of the FDCPA in its correspondence constitutes a contractual or estoppel-based waiver of the statutory exclusion, and research whether any circuit has accepted this argument post-the client.

Analyze whether any state-law analogue to § 1692g(b) under the State's consumer protection statutes applies to nonjudicial foreclosure agents, and whether the firm's conduct in proceeding without verification gives rise to a claim under state law even if the federal FDCPA claim fails.

Distinguish between acts required by state law to complete a nonjudicial foreclosure (excluded from FDCPA coverage) and any additional communications or conduct by the firm that went beyond state-law requirements, which might still be subject to the FDCPA or § 1692f(6).

Assess whether any other activity of the firm — beyond the nonjudicial foreclosure steps — could independently bring it within the primary 'debt collector' definition, thereby making § 1692i applicable, and identify what discovery would be needed to develop that record.

Evaluate whether the firm's conduct satisfies the elements of a § 1692f(6) violation — specifically whether there was a 'present right' to possession at the time each notice or filing was made — and whether the State's nonjudicial foreclosure statute was strictly followed at every step.

Identify which specific communications from the firm were required by the State law and which were not; any voluntary communications that went beyond the statutory script may still fall within the primary FDCPA definition and warrant further analysis.

Analyze each instance of the firm's alleged abusive conduct to determine whether it was a required step under the State law; if not, develop the argument that such conduct independently triggers the primary 'debt collector' definition or violates § 1692f(6).

Reset the client's expectations: the prior intermediate appellate authority favorable to homeowners is no longer controlling; the operative federal-level standard treats nonjudicial foreclosure agents as outside the primary FDCPA definition.

Identify state-law remedies (the State statutory protections, public-trustee oversight) and consider whether any state-law cause of action could provide injunctive or declaratory relief in lieu of an FDCPA-based federal injunction.

Counsel the client that the 'repo man' theory and the voluntary-invocation theory have both been rejected; if any FDCPA-style claim remains viable, it must be grounded in conduct beyond what state foreclosure law required, and analyzed under § 1692f(6) rather than the primary definition.

opening: Hi, I'm X, Tribal Council Chair of X Tribe. I reached out because I'm involved in a property boundary dispute with a neighboring landowner, and I'm trying to understand my legal options — I was hoping you could help.

facts.client_belief: We bought about 40 acres of land in 2013 — a site where tribal members who died of smallpox are buried. We've been trying to restore our connection to that land.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that, in 2013, X Tribe (a federally recognized Indian tribe) purchased approximately 40 acres of land in a standard market transaction, and that the client then commissioned a boundary survey with the intention of asking the federal government to take the land into trust as part of the adjacent reservation.

facts.client_belief: After we got a survey done, it showed the boundary fence between our land and the neighboring landowners is in the wrong place — about an acre of our property is on their side of the fence. We told them we planned to tear down the fence and put it in the right spot. We figured straightforward enforcement of our property right wouldn't expose us to anything.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the client's survey indicated approximately one acre of its purchased property lay on the neighboring landowners' side of the existing barbed wire fence, and that the client notified the neighboring landowners of its intent to remove the fence, clearcut the intervening acre, and construct a new fence on the surveyed boundary. The client's intuition that announcing its planned exercise of property rights is exposure-free, however, overstates the legal posture: by giving notice of intent to alter the disputed boundary, the client invited a quiet title action that has now resolved against the client at the state-appellate level on immunity grounds — and the immovable-property exception remains live for review on continued review. Pre-action notice is sometimes prudent, but it can also surface contested boundaries on terms the client did not choose.

facts.client_belief: The neighboring landowners filed a quiet title action against us in state court, claiming adverse possession and mutual acquiescence. They say they've treated that acre as their own for years and that the previous owner of our land accepted their claim. That's an obvious stretch — they're just trying to keep land that isn't theirs.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the neighboring landowners filed a quiet title action in state court invoking adverse possession and mutual acquiescence, and that they presented evidence that the fence had stood in the same location for many years, that they had treated the disputed acre as their own, and that the prior owner of the client's tract had accepted their claim to the land on their side of the fence. The client's intuition that adverse possession and mutual acquiescence are 'obvious stretches,' however, understates the substantive merits: long, open, and notorious occupation of the disputed acre under color of an established fence is the standard fact pattern for adverse possession in the State, and prior-owner acquiescence is a recognized doctrine. The substantive merits are real even if the immunity defense initially deflects them.

facts.client_belief: We asserted sovereign immunity to get out of this lawsuit. We're a federally recognized tribe with common-law immunity from suit, just like any sovereign government.
facts.court_record: Indian tribes possess common-law immunity from suit traditionally enjoyed by sovereign powers. The X Tribe (a federally recognized Indian tribe) asserted this immunity as a complete defense. The existence of tribal sovereign immunity as a general doctrine is undisputed; its application to this specific lawsuit is the central disputed question.

facts.client_belief: The higher-level state review ruled against us, saying sovereign immunity doesn't apply in 'in rem' proceedings to quiet title in land. They relied on a federal-level the prior ruling decision for that principle.
facts.court_record: It is not in factual dispute that the higher-level state review rejected the client's immunity claim, reasoning that sovereign immunity applies only to in personam jurisdiction over a tribe, not to in rem proceedings where a court quiets title in a parcel of land, and that the higher-level state review cited a prior federal ruling on tribal land and Bands of the prior ruling Nation (1992) as establishing this distinction for tribal immunity.

facts.client_belief: The higher-level state review was right to rely on the prior ruling — that case clearly established that courts have subject-matter jurisdiction over in rem proceedings even when a tribe claims sovereign immunity.
facts.court_record: Under the corrected federal-level standard, the prior ruling did not address the scope of tribal sovereign immunity at all. the prior ruling resolved only a statutory interpretation question about the Indian General Allotment Act of 1887 — specifically whether in rem (property) taxes on fee-patented land within reservations were still authorized under § 6 of that Act, as distinguished from in personam transaction taxes barred by Moe. the prior ruling said nothing about sovereign immunity doctrine. The client's intuition that the higher-level state review's reliance on the prior ruling was solid therefore overlooks the prior ruling opinion's actual scope.

facts.client_belief: As a tribe, our sovereign immunity protects us from all suits, including in rem quiet title actions. The nature of the proceeding — whether it targets the land rather than us directly — shouldn't matter.
facts.court_record: Under the corrected federal-level standard, the question of whether the in rem nature of a quiet title action, by itself, defeats tribal sovereign immunity has been expressly left undecided. The earlier higher-level state ruling (which had ruled based on the prior ruling) has been vacated and remanded. The client's intuition that the in rem / in personam distinction is irrelevant to immunity captures one possible doctrinal answer, but the question remains formally unresolved on continued review.

facts.client_belief: The neighboring landowners argued at the federal-level review that a common-law 'immovable property' exception to sovereign immunity should apply here — that when a tribe buys land outside its reservation like a private party, it can't claim immunity in a suit about that land. That argument should fail because tribal immunity is unique.
facts.court_record: The neighboring landowners argued that, at common law, sovereigns have no immunity from actions involving immovable property located in another sovereign's territory, and that a prince acquiring property in a foreign state assumes the character of a private individual (Schooner Exchange v. McFaddon, 1812). Under the corrected federal-level standard, this argument was not ruled on because it emerged late in the matter — only in the federal government's amicus position after the client's opening brief was filed — and was remanded for the higher-level state review to address in the first instance. The client's intuition that the immovable-property argument 'should fail because tribal immunity is unique' overstates the doctrinal posture: the question is genuinely live on continued review.

facts.client_belief: Tribal immunity is special and different from state or foreign sovereign immunity. Courts can't just import exceptions from those other immunity frameworks and apply them to tribes — it doesn't work that way.
facts.court_record: Under the corrected federal-level standard, tribal sovereign immunity 'is not coextensive with that of the States.' However, established federal authority has also refused to extend tribal immunity beyond what common-law sovereign immunity principles would recognize, and has declined to make tribal immunity broader than state or federal immunity. Whether tribal immunity is broader or narrower on the immovable-property question was expressly left for the higher-level state review on continued review. The client's intuition that 'tribal immunity is special' captures a real doctrinal recognition but does not by itself foreclose application of the immovable-property exception — that question is open.

facts.client_belief: If the neighboring landowners don't like the boundary, their remedy is to negotiate with us — now that courts have made clear we have immunity, we can work things out through discussions.
facts.court_record: Concurring reasoning at the federal-level review noted that forcing the neighboring landowners to 'negotiate' from a position where they have no legal recourse is not a meaningful remedy. The concurring reasoning also rejected an alternative suggestion that the neighboring landowners should deliberately trespass on the disputed land to induce the client to file suit and thereby waive immunity, characterizing that approach as requiring private individuals to 'pick a fight' to vindicate their interests. The client's intuition that immunity simply forces the neighboring landowners to 'work things out through discussions' therefore understates the asymmetry concern that the concurring reasoning highlighted.

facts.client_belief: The federal government agreed with our position that the political branches, not courts, should determine when tribes can be sued over off-reservation land purchases.
facts.court_record: The federal government filed an amicus position supporting the client on the immunity question, but also proposed the alternative remedy of inducing the client to file suit by trespassing — a suggestion the concurring reasoning found unsatisfactory. The position that the political branches hold primary responsibility for foreign sovereign immunity was addressed in the dissenting reasoning, which found it inapplicable to the distinct context of tribal immunity over domestic real property. The client's intuition that political-branch deference applies as cleanly to tribal immunity as to foreign sovereign immunity is therefore contested under the dissenting reasoning.

facts.client_belief: The whole point of getting continued review was to resolve whether in rem jurisdiction defeats tribal sovereign immunity. The federal-level review should have answered that question definitively.
facts.court_record: Dissenting reasoning at the federal-level review urged that the matter should have been resolved by addressing the immovable-property exception, characterized as 'hornbook law' that clearly applies to tribal immunity just as it does to state and foreign sovereign immunity. The corrected federal-level standard declined to address the exception because it had not been raised below and appeared only in an amicus position late in the proceedings. The client's intuition that the federal-level review 'should have answered the question definitively' captures the dissenting reasoning's view but conflicts with the procedural-preservation concern that drove the majority outcome.

facts.client_belief: We purchased this land in a regular market transaction in 2013. That should be irrelevant to our immunity — how we bought it doesn't change our status as a sovereign.
facts.court_record: Concurring reasoning at the federal-level review noted that the client purchased the land in a standard market transaction, not in trust, and not on the existing reservation. This makes the immovable-property exception particularly pertinent: the exception applies specifically when a sovereign acquires property in another sovereign's territory in the manner of a private individual. The client's intuition that 'how we bought it doesn't change our status as a sovereign' therefore understates how acquisition method affects the immovable-property analysis — the non-trust, off-reservation character of the purchase is a central question left for continued review.

expected_inquiries: Ask the clients for the complete chain of title to the 40-acre parcel — deeds, title insurance commitments, and any title reports — to verify the client's claimed boundary and identify any recorded easements or encumbrances.

Obtain and review the boundary survey commissioned by the client, including the surveyor's methodology, field notes, and any comparison with prior surveys of the neighboring landowners' parcel, to assess the factual strength of the boundary claim.

Ask whether the client has submitted or intends to submit a fee-to-trust application to the Bureau of Indian Affairs, and advise on the timing implications: trust acquisition might affect state-court jurisdiction but could also create new procedural complexities.

Inquire about the history of the fence — who built it, when, and whether any prior owner of the client's tract ever asserted or relinquished a claim to the disputed acre — to evaluate the strength of the neighboring landowners' mutual acquiescence defense.

Confirm that the client has not taken any self-help action (e.g., begun clearing trees, moved or cut the fence) that could constitute trespass and expose the client to counterclaims or be used to justify an emergency injunction in state court.

Ask about the client's communications with the neighboring landowners before and after the survey was completed, including any written correspondence, to identify statements that could be construed as admissions or that might affect waiver or estoppel arguments.

Advise the client that, on continued review, the higher-level state forum will address the immovable-property exception; assess the risk that the forum will hold the exception applicable and recommend whether to pursue a negotiated resolution with the neighboring landowners while continued review proceeds.

Research whether any state statute or court rule expressly addresses suits against Indian tribes over off-reservation fee land, and determine whether the state has consented to suit or established any alternative dispute-resolution mechanism.

Research whether any Washington state statute or court rule expressly addresses suits against Indian tribes over off-reservation fee land, and determine whether the state has consented to suit or established any alternative dispute-resolution mechanism.
memo_expectations: Analyze whether the 'immovable property' common-law exception to sovereign immunity applies to Indian tribes and, if so, whether it defeats the client's immunity in this quiet title action over non-trust, off-reservation land.

Assess the significance of the corrected federal-level standard's holding that a prior federal ruling on tribal land addressed only the Indian General Allotment Act, not tribal sovereign immunity, and identify which prior lower-court decisions must be distinguished on continued review.

Evaluate the adverse possession and mutual acquiescence claims on their substantive merits under the State law, including the period of adverse use, the nature of the neighboring landowners' possession, and the prior owner's alleged acquiescence to the fence line.

Analyze whether the client's stated intention to remove the fence and clearcut the disputed acre creates any independent causes of action (e.g., trespass, anticipatory interference with property rights) that might themselves trigger a waiver of immunity or provide an alternative litigation path.

Examine the federal trust-land acquisition process under 25 U.S.C. § 5108 and 25 C.F.R. § 151.4, and advise on whether initiating or completing that process would affect the state court's jurisdiction over the boundary dispute.

Assess whether any existing statutory waivers of tribal immunity (e.g., under the Indian Land Consolidation Act or other federal statutes) could apply to a quiet title action over fee-simple off-reservation land purchased by a tribe.

Review the historical record of the fence's location, the survey methodology, and any prior recorded deeds or plats to determine whether the client's boundary claim is factually sound, independent of the immunity question.

opening: Hi, thanks for meeting me. I'm X. I'm dealing with a federal criminal matter and I was hoping you could help me understand where I stand.

facts.client_belief: I've lived at our family house on the family residence since 2011 — it's the place I grew up in, and since my mom passed in 2017, my girlfriend, my son, my stepfather and I have been the ones living there.
facts.court_record: The client has resided at the family residence since 2011. After the mother's death in 2017, the household consisted of the client, his son, his girlfriend, and his stepfather. The residency facts are not in dispute and are supported by multiple witnesses, including the client's own statements to detectives.

facts.client_belief: Yeah, I put a keypad lock on the back room — I use it as my office for my electrical company. I keep my business paperwork, computer and files in there.
facts.court_record: The client installed a keypad lock on a back bedroom of the residence and uses that room as an office for his electrical contracting business. The office contains business signage, files, and computers. This is not in dispute.

facts.client_belief: The cops say I was at some motel shooting on November 28th — two days later they pulled me over in my work van and hauled me in. I'm not trying to pretend they didn't arrest me.
facts.court_record: On November 28, 2020, a shooting and suspected abduction occurred at a motel. Two days later, officers conducted a traffic stop on the client's white work van and took him into custody in connection with that incident. The fact of the arrest and its temporal connection to the motel incident is not in dispute.

facts.client_belief: My stepfather couldn't have let them into the house — he had moved out a week before. He wasn't living there anymore, so he had no business opening my door for the cops.
facts.court_record: The stepfather retained common authority over the residence sufficient to consent to a warrantless search under the co-occupant doctrine. Although he had moved his bed to the sister's home days earlier, he kept his key; the overwhelming majority of his possessions — furniture, clothing, even his dogs — remained in the home; and he testified that his departure was intended to be temporary. The client's belief that a brief departure strips a co-occupant of authority misunderstands the Matlock standard of joint access or control for most purposes.

facts.client_belief: Look, I already told the detectives at the station — no, you can't search my house. My refusal should have killed the whole thing. They can't just go find somebody else to say yes after I said no.
facts.court_record: The client's refusal of consent at the police station is ineffectual under the controlling co-occupant consent precedent because he was not physically present at the premises when the stepfather consented. A co-occupant's objection to a search does not vitiate another co-occupant's consent when the objector is not physically present. That the client's absence was caused by his arrest does not change the analysis, because the arrest was objectively justified.

facts.client_belief: I had to push him out — he was disrespecting me over the car, it got physical. If I made him leave, then legally he's not a co-owner of that house anymore, right? He can't come back and sign me up for a search.
facts.court_record: The client struck the stepfather in the face, breaking his nose, which caused the stepfather's temporary departure. Under controlling circuit precedent, one occupant cannot force a co-occupant out through physical violence and then claim the victim has lost common authority over the residence. Courts will not condone and reward violent, abusive behavior. The client's belief that his own violence stripped the stepfather of authority is legally backwards — it strengthens, rather than weakens, the stepfather's authority.

facts.client_belief: Before any of this went down, my stepfather signed the house over to my sister — there's a quitclaim deed. So by the time the cops came, he didn't even own the place anymore. He couldn't consent to anything.
facts.court_record: Under the applicable state law, the quitclaim deed was legally effective upon execution, not upon recording. However, this cuts against the client in two ways. First, the consent rested on common authority — mutual use and control — not on legal title; so even a valid transfer does not defeat the stepfather's consent as a co-possessor. Second, the sister, as the true titleholder post-execution, also gave consent, providing an independent basis for the search. The client's belief that an unrecorded deed created a gap in authority is legally mistaken.

facts.client_belief: I wasn't even at the house when they searched it — I was sitting in a jail cell. You can't say I possessed drugs I wasn't anywhere near.
facts.court_record: Physical absence at the time of search does not defeat possession. The law recognizes constructive possession, which requires only dominion and control over the premises where the contraband is concealed. Multiple facts establish the client's control: he resided at the property; his distinctive clothing (with his DNA) was found there; and the contraband was in a room to which he controlled access via a keypad lock. The client's I-wasn't-there theory misunderstands the doctrine of constructive possession entirely.

facts.client_belief: The back room with the meth? That had a keypad lock — anybody in the house could have put stuff in there. Just because there's a lock doesn't mean it's mine.
facts.court_record: The keypad-locked office is in fact strongly probative of the client's exclusive control, not against it. A keypad lock controls who can enter; those with the code are selectively admitted. Combined with the business signage, the business records, and the altered movie poster bearing the client's own face in place of Tony Montana, the room is personalized to the client. The client's framing — that a lock makes the room accessible to others — inverts the ordinary evidentiary inference.

facts.client_belief: That poster with my face on a movie-kingpin poster — it's a joke, a birthday gift from my buddies. It's just decoration. They're going to use a poster to convict me of drug dealing?
facts.court_record: The altered movie poster is not barred under Rule 403. While the underlying film depicts a drug kingpin, the violence is not shown on the poster itself. The probative value is not in the content of the film but in the personalization — the client's face superimposed on the kingpin's — which, like the business signage and documents in the same room, tends to establish control over the locked space where the methamphetamine was found. The client's it's-a-joke framing does not neutralize its evidentiary weight.

facts.client_belief: There's this YouTube music video of me and my friends rapping at the house — there's guns and stuff in the background but it's a music video, it's fake, it's art. It shouldn't be used against me.
facts.court_record: The music video is admissible under Rule 404(b) as other-acts evidence going to knowledge, intent, and absence of mistake — not as character evidence. Unlike cases where the defendant did not appear in the video, the client appears in this one; his hands are shown holding a plate of suspected narcotics; the filming location is the same property where the firearms and methamphetamine were found; and firearm magazines are visible. A limiting instruction mitigates prejudice. The it's-just-art framing does not overcome the probative value.

facts.client_belief: The motel shooting and the guns in my house are two separate things. They shouldn't be able to mix that stuff up and throw it all at the jury together.
facts.court_record: Evidence of the motel incident is admissible as intrinsic to the firearm charges — it is inextricably intertwined with the charged offenses. Surveillance video depicts a suspect resembling the client wielding a small firearm similar to one later found in the home; the suspect's partner discharged the other charged firearm; the occupational license number on the getaway van traces to the client's company. The incident is the first link in the chain explaining how detectives identified the client and obtained the evidence. Separation is not legally available.

facts.client_belief: I own the electrical company — a lot of people drove that white work van. Just because the van is tied to my company doesn't mean I was the one at that motel.
facts.court_record: The van's occupational license number tracing to the client's company is only one of several corroborating facts. Surveillance footage depicts a man matching the client's description (very short and stocky). Items found at the residence — a distinctive a distinctive baseball cap, distinctive sneakers, an olive-green shirt, rubber-coated gloves — match the clothing worn by the shorter suspect in the video. DNA from the baseball cap matches the client. The aggregate linkage does not fail merely because other employees had access to the van.

facts.client_belief: That hat they say has my DNA — lots of people could've worn that hat. I share the house. DNA on a hat doesn't prove I was the guy at the motel.
facts.court_record: DNA on the baseball cap, found in the client's bedroom, combined with the cap matching the distinctive cap worn by the shorter suspect in the motel surveillance video, is powerful identification evidence. The client's anyone-could-have-worn-it argument is weakened by (a) the cap's discovery in his bedroom, (b) the matching distinctive sneakers and olive shirt found with it, and (c) the short, stocky physical description matching the client. Arguing DNA contamination or cross-transfer faces a steep evidentiary uphill battle.

facts.client_belief: The drugs they found were a small amount — my girlfriend and I both use meth, it was for us. Thirty grams is not a lot, it's personal use.
facts.court_record: Thirty-one grams of 93-percent-pure methamphetamine is inconsistent with personal use and consistent with distribution. Distribution intent can be inferred from quantity alone, but here the inference is reinforced by the presence of distribution paraphernalia: numerous small plastic baggies, spoons, a measuring cup, and digital scales — described by investigators as basically everything that someone would need to sell or distribute narcotics. The personal-use defense will face significant headwinds on these facts.

facts.client_belief: The indictment says mixture of methamphetamine — that means they're going to treat it like regular meth. The purity doesn't matter to my sentence.
facts.court_record: The purity profoundly affects the sentencing exposure. At 93 percent purity, the substance qualifies as ice (which requires at least 80 percent pure d-methamphetamine hydrochloride) under U.S.S.G. section 2D1.1. Even where the indictment charges a mixture, the sentencing court determines the base offense level by the actual substance proven at trial. Twenty to 35 grams of ice carries a base offense level of 26, whereas the same quantity charged as a mixture would carry a level of 18 — a dramatic difference. The client's assumption that the indictment's label governs the sentence is a critical error.

facts.client_belief: I have a felony from years ago — but I've been fine, paying taxes, running my business. That old conviction shouldn't stop me from having a gun in my own house.
facts.court_record: The client's prior felony conviction is a stipulated, dispositive element of 18 U.S.C. section 922(g)(1) — felon in possession of a firearm — and his knowledge of that felony status is also stipulated. Time elapsed since the prior conviction, good conduct, and business operation are legally irrelevant to the elements of the offense, though they may bear on sentencing. Unless civil rights have been formally restored in a manner that removes the predicate (a high bar), the client remains a prohibited person. The my-own-house framing has no legal effect — the statute covers possession anywhere.

facts.client_belief: They charged me with two separate gun counts — one for each pistol. But if I had both guns at the same place at the same time, isn't that just one thing? You can't charge me twice for that, right?
facts.court_record: Under controlling circuit precedent, simultaneous possession of several firearms constitutes only one offense under section 922(g). There is a legitimate multiplicity issue; the proper remedy is a motion to dismiss one of the redundant counts. This is a real, winnable procedural point — but it does not defeat the case. The client will still face a single section 922(g) conviction and the separate section 841(a)(1) methamphetamine count. The client's instinct that something is wrong is correct, but mischaracterizes the issue as double jeopardy in the constitutional sense when the technical doctrine is multiplicity.

expected_inquiries: Ask the client to describe, in detail, the exact words he used when he refused consent at the police station, and whether any officer was present who could testify to that refusal.
Ask for the full timeline of the stepfather's move-out: exact date, what was moved, what stayed behind (furniture, clothes, pets), who has keys, and any text messages or recordings about the move.
Ask the client to confirm the existence and terms of the quitclaim deed to his sister, including the execution date, notary, witnesses, and whether it has been recorded with the county.
Ask the client to walk through every person who had the keypad code to the back office, whether any of them used the office, and exactly what was stored there besides the items the government seized.
Ask about the client's documented history of methamphetamine use — medical records, rehab admissions, prescriptions, prior statements to providers — to support a possible personal-use theory.

Ask the client about the white work van: who else drove it, who had access to the company's occupational license number, and whether any employees wore clothing similar to that seen on the surveillance footage.

Ask about the prior felony conviction referenced in the section 922(g) charge — the date, jurisdiction, whether civil rights have been restored, and whether any collateral attack on that predicate is possible.

Ask to see all of the government's discovery: the surveillance footage, the DNA report on the baseball cap, the DEA chemist's report on the purity, and any cell-site location data placing the client at or away from the motel.
Ask the client to identify every person who appears in the YouTube music video, who filmed it, who posted it, and whether firearms and baggies shown were real or props.
Ask the client whether he has ever made any recorded statement to law enforcement about the firearms or the methamphetamine — including post-arrest statements, jail calls, or statements to cellmates.
Ask whetherre are any co-defendants or uncharged co-conspirators (e.g., the girlfriend in the van, the partner at the motel), and explore cooperation exposure or benefits.
Ask about the client's financial situation and assets traceable to the electrical business vs. suspected drug proceeds, to prepare for potential forfeiture and to evaluate retainer structure.

Ask the client for a full roster of employees who had access to the white work van on November 28, 2020, including their physical descriptions and typical work attire, and ask whether any of them wore clothing similar to the items recovered at the residence.

Ask the client about his and his girlfriend's documented history of methamphetamine use — medical records, prior rehab admissions, prescriptions, or statements to healthcare providers — and ask for a realistic estimate of their combined daily consumption to probe the plausibility of a personal-use claim for 31 grams.

Ask the client whether he has any information about the drug's source or supply chain, and inquire whether an independent expert could contest the DEA forensic chemist's purity determination or the methodology used to classify the substance as ice rather than a mixture.

Ask the client for the exact date, jurisdiction, offense, and sentence of the prior felony conviction; ask whether he was represented by counsel at that proceeding; and ask whether he has ever received documentation from a court, governor, or parole authority restoring his civil rights or his right to possess firearms.

Ask the client to confirm that both charged firearms (a 9mm pistol found in the bedroom and a .380 pistol found in the bathroom) were possessed simultaneously at the same property, and ask whether government has indicated any position on a motion to dismiss one of the redundant § 922(g) counts.

Ask the client to confirm that both charged firearms (the Taurus 9mm found in the bedroom and the Springfield Armory .380 found in the bathroom) were possessed simultaneously at the same property, and ask whether the government has indicated any position on a motion to dismiss one of the redundant § 922(g) counts.

Analyze the effect of the client's prior refusal of consent at the police station, and whether his physical absence from the premises at the time of the stepfather's consent removes him from the protections of the governing co-occupant consent precedents.

Assess the doctrine of constructive possession for the methamphetamine found in the locked back office, including the evidentiary weight of the keypad lock, business signage, personalized movie poster, and DNA on the hat.

Evaluate whether quantity (31 grams at 93 percent purity) and the presence of baggies, scales, and spoons establish intent to distribute as opposed to personal use, and the viability of a personal-use defense given the client's claimed addiction.

Analyze the admissibility of the modified altered movie poster and the YouTube music video under Rule 404(b), and the strategic cost of seeking their exclusion vs. their likely admission.

Assess the viability of a motion to suppress based on challenging the stepfather's authority through the theory that the client's own violence did not preserve common authority — and the weak precedent posture for that argument .

Analyze whether aggregation of circumstantial evidence — the occupational license number on the van tracing to the client's company, his physical description (very short and stocky), the distinctive clothing match (the distinctive cap, distinctive sneakers, olive shirt, rubber-coated gloves), and the DNA on the cap — is sufficient to identify the client as one of the motel suspects, and evaluate the strength of an alternative-suspect or multiple-employees-had-van-access defense.
