Identify all sentencing objections that must be preserved on the record to secure de novo review on appeal, including objections to the career offender designation, the reckless endangerment enhancement, the reliance on prior PSRs, and any failure to apply the pending-amendment principle.

opening: Hi, thanks for taking this. I'm X. I'm facing federal charges tied to a violent offense, and I'd like to get your view on where I stand.

facts.client_belief: Yeah — I'm the one who did it. I killed her back in 2002. I pled to it in the state court right after and I've been serving a life sentence ever since. I'm not trying to pretend I didn't do it.
facts.court_record: The client has admitted, both contemporaneously in the 2002 state-court plea and in his own trial testimony, that he caused the decedent's death in 2002. He pleaded guilty in state court and was sentenced to life imprisonment. The fact of the killing and the fact of the prior state plea are not in dispute.

facts.client_belief: The reason this thing is being reopened is that whole Supreme Court ruling a few years back about tribal land in the State. The state court turned around and said they never had the authority to handle my case in the first place, and tossed the conviction.
facts.court_record: Following a 2020 Supreme Court decision on Indian-country jurisdiction, portions of the State were held to be Indian country for Major Crimes Act purposes. Because the client is an enrolled member of a federally recognized tribe and the offense occurred within reservation boundaries, the state lacked jurisdiction to prosecute; the state-court judgment was vacated on post-conviction relief. The vacatur and the jurisdictional basis for it are not in dispute.

facts.client_belief: I'm a member of a tribe — federally recognized — and it happened inside the reservation. So now I'm sitting in federal court on it. That's the whole reason the feds picked it up.
facts.court_record: The client is an enrolled member of a federally recognized tribe, and the offense occurred within the boundaries of the reservation. Under the Major Crimes Act, 18 U.S.C. § 1153, exclusive federal jurisdiction attaches to the charged offenses for tribal members whose conduct falls within enumerated categories, including murder. The tribal membership and locus of offense are not in dispute.

facts.client_belief: Hold on — I already served twenty-plus years on a life sentence for this. How can they hit me with it all over again? They already got their pound of flesh out of me. That's got to be double jeopardy.
facts.court_record: Double jeopardy does not bar the federal prosecution here. The state-court judgment was vacated for lack of jurisdiction — that is, the state conviction is a legal nullity, not a valid prior conviction. The dual-sovereignty doctrine further permits successive state and federal prosecutions for the same conduct even where a valid state conviction existed. The time the client spent in state custody may be relevant to credit calculations or sentencing mitigation, but does not bar retrial. The client's 'already did my time' framing does not survive the jurisdictional nullification.

facts.client_belief: After I got arrested, my lawyer back then went and talked to the D.A. He came back and told me if I led the cops to where she was, they wouldn't seek the death penalty. That was a deal. So the fact I showed them where the body was — that's all part of plea talks. They can't use any of that against me.
facts.court_record: Under Federal Rule of Evidence 410(a)(4), statements made during plea discussions with an attorney for the prosecuting authority are inadmissible if the discussions did not result in a plea that was not later withdrawn. Two elements are critical here: (a) the statements must be made during plea discussions, and (b) they must be made with the prosecuting attorney. The client's statements directing officers to the body were made to law-enforcement officers, not to the prosecutor. The client's counsel may have discussed terms with the prosecutor separately, but Rule 410 generally does not reach the defendant's own statements to police. The 'part of plea talks' framing does not fit the rule's text.

facts.client_belief: But I thought we had a deal. I believed that when I told them where she was, it was in exchange for them not seeking death. That was my understanding. That has to count for something.
facts.court_record: Some courts recognize a subjective-belief exception to the general rule, under which Rule 410 may protect a defendant's statements when he reasonably believed he was speaking during plea negotiations. To qualify, the client bears the burden of establishing both that his subjective belief was genuine and that it was objectively reasonable in the circumstances. A belief based solely on the client's own counsel's characterization — without direct communication from the prosecutor or any conduct by the prosecutor inducing reliance — is typically insufficient. Critically, the controlling circuit has not definitively adopted the subjective-belief exception: in controlling precedent, the court applied the plain-language prosecuting-authority requirement without reaching the exception, and in this case the court of appeals likewise declined (in footnote 11) to resolve whether exception exists because the client failed the threshold prosecuting-authority requirement regardless. The client's subjective-belief theory therefore faces both a threshold circuit-law uncertainty and a steep evidentiary burden on these facts.

facts.client_belief: The police took me there themselves — they drove me, they led the caravan. So the officers were basically negotiating the deal with me. That means what I told them about the location is off-limits.
facts.court_record: The exception for statements to officers who have express authority to negotiate a plea is narrow and rarely applied. It requires affirmative evidence that the prosecuting office delegated plea-negotiation authority to specific officers in a specific manner. Mere presence during a body-recovery trip — even in a caravan — does not establish such delegation. The physical participation of officers in transport does not transform the investigative act into a plea negotiation. The client's theory does not match the cases that have applied the exception.

facts.client_belief: Even if they do get to use what I said about the body — they shouldn't get to use any of the evidence they found once they got there. Without me pointing the way, there would be no body, no tarp, no bullets, nothing. It's all a chain from that one statement.
facts.court_record: The derivative-evidence argument (a 'fruit of the poisonous tree' theory for Rule 410 violations) is legally unsupported. Rule 410's text addresses statements themselves, not downstream evidence derived from those statements. Unlike the Fifth Amendment exclusionary rule in the confession context, Rule 410 does not contain a suppression-of-derivatives mechanism. Even if the statements themselves were excluded, physical evidence recovered from the body site would remain admissible. The client's 'chain from one statement' framing has no legal foundation in Rule 410 doctrine.

facts.client_belief: I looked at the pool of people they're pulling jurors from — and seven of them come from the same little town. That can't be random — there's got to be something going on with how they put that pool together.
facts.court_record: A Jury Selection and Service Act challenge requires strict compliance with procedural prerequisites under 28 U.S.C. § 1867, including a sworn statement of facts attached to the motion and timely filing (before voir dire or within seven days of discovering grounds). A substantive fair-cross-section claim under the controlling fair-cross-section precedent requires proof of (1) distinctiveness of the excluded group, (2) unreasonable underrepresentation, and (3) systematic exclusion. Statistical clustering by town of residence is not, by itself, evidence of systematic exclusion of any cognizable group. Random selection frequently produces clusters. The client's intuition about the seven jurors from one town, without more, does not state a viable claim.

facts.client_belief: From what me and my family can see, there's no members of distinctive demographic groups in the pool at all. That's a pattern. That proves the pool isn't a fair slice of the community, and I should be able to get this whole thing knocked out before we start.
facts.court_record: A fair-cross-section claim under the controlling precedent based on lay observation — the client's and his family's visual impression of who was in the jury pool — is almost never sufficient. Courts require reliable statistical evidence (typically drawn from the district's jury plan documents, voter rolls, and published demographic data) showing both the absolute disparity and the systematic mechanism producing it. 'Visual observations' by family members, however sincere, are not probative of systematic exclusion in the Jury Act sense. The claim also requires procedural compliance — the same sworn-statement requirement governs both procedural and substantive challenges.

facts.client_belief: I plan to raise this jury issue before they start questioning the jurors, and a couple more times if I need to once the trial starts. I'll put it on the record. That should be enough to preserve it in case I have to appeal later.
facts.court_record: Preservation requires not just raising the issue but doing so in the procedurally correct vehicle. Under 28 U.S.C. § 1867(a) and (d), a Jury Act motion must be filed before voir dire (or within seven days of discovering the grounds) and must include a sworn statement of facts. Motions without sworn statements are procedurally barred. Motions raised first during trial — after voir dire — are untimely on their face. A post-trial filing may still fail on timeliness and on merits if the underlying motions were procedurally defective. Merely 'putting it on the record' does not cure the procedural defects.

facts.client_belief: One of my earlier federal lawyers — the one who withdrew — I'm sure he told the government stuff he shouldn't have. They worked out something and he handed over information about me. I want to see every email and message between them, and I heard the discovery rules say I should get that.
facts.court_record: Rule 16(a)(1)(E) governs pretrial discovery of documents material to preparing the defense, to be used in the government's case-in-chief, or obtained from or belonging to the defendant. Communications between the government and prior defense counsel do not ordinarily fall within any of these categories. If the client's real concern is ineffective assistance or privilege breach by prior counsel, that is typically a post-conviction matter (under 28 U.S.C. § 2255) rather than a Rule 16 production issue. The district court may review the communications in camera and make findings, but a motion to compel production to the defense as a Rule 16 matter faces a legal mismatch between the theory and the rule.

facts.client_belief: She came at me with my own gun. I was protecting myself. That's self-defense, plain and simple. That's a complete defense to this charge.
facts.court_record: A self-defense theory is a defendant's right to raise, but it faces several difficulties on these facts. First, proportionality: the decedent's alleged use of a firearm against the client may support initial defensive force, but the client's post-altercation conduct — transporting the body to a gravel pit, placing it in a shallow grave in a tarp, and firing multiple close-range shots to the head — is very hard to reconcile with self-defense. Second, opportunity to retreat and to call for help: the facts suggest both were available after the initial altercation. Third, the existence of the journal-centered motive evidence complicates the 'spontaneous fear' narrative. A self-defense instruction may be available, but a complete acquittal on it is unlikely.

facts.client_belief: After she wasn't moving, I wrapped her up and moved her because I panicked. The shots to the head later on — I can't even explain those, I wasn't in my mind. None of that takes away from the fact that she came at me first.
facts.court_record: The jury will evaluate the entire sequence of conduct, not just the initial altercation. Post-offense concealment, transportation, burial, and additional shots fired at close range are all powerful evidence of consciousness of guilt and of a premeditated or deliberate character to the act — directly relevant to first-degree murder. 'Panic' as an explanation for post-altercation conduct becomes less credible the longer the sequence lasts and the more discrete, goal-directed acts it involves. The jury is unlikely to separate the initial event from the later conduct when weighing culpability.

facts.client_belief: About a year after it all happened, I was being interviewed by an FBI agent on something completely unrelated. I said something about killing her. That was informal. They're going to try to use that — but it shouldn't come into this case.
facts.court_record: Spontaneous volunteered statements about a prior homicide, made to an FBI agent in the course of an interview, are generally admissible as statements of a party opponent under Federal Rule of Evidence 801(d)(2) and are typically not suppressible unless a Fifth Amendment or Sixth Amendment violation occurred in obtaining them. The client's framing of the interview as 'informal' or 'unrelated' does not establish any such violation. Unless the client was in custody on an unwarned charge and was interrogated, the statement will likely come in.

facts.client_belief: My old lawyer — the one who led the police to the body back then — I hear the government wants to put him on the stand. That has to violate what he and I had — he was my lawyer. They can't make him talk about our case.
facts.court_record: Prior defense counsel may be called to testify to non-privileged matters, including their own observed conduct (leading officers to a location), their own conversations with third parties (such as the prosecutor), and — critically — matters as to which privilege has been waived, including by the client placing the representation at issue. The client's direct testimony about what counsel said to him, or about the alleged 'deal,' may itself waive the privilege as to that subject. The attorney-client privilege is narrower than many defendants assume, and it rarely prevents former counsel from testifying about the events the defendant himself places in dispute.

facts.client_belief: I'm a tribal member and this happened on the reservation. The way I always figured it, if something happens on reservation land, that's tribal territory — the tribe handles it, not the federal government. I never thought Washington could come in and charge me under federal law for something that went down inside the reservation.
facts.court_record: Under the Major Crimes Act, 18 U.S.C. § 1153, federal courts have exclusive jurisdiction over enumerated major crimes (including murder) committed by Indians in Indian country. Tribal courts generally do not have jurisdiction over these enumerated federal offenses, and for the most serious crimes their sentencing authority is statutorily limited. The tribal-court-instead-of-federal-court intuition misunderstands how concurrent tribal-federal jurisdiction has been allocated by Congress. The federal forum is not an option to opt out of.

facts.client_belief: The limitations period has got to apply. This happened in 2002. You can't come at me in 2021 — almost twenty years later — on something this old. That's past the deadline.
facts.court_record: There is no federal statute of limitations for murder. 18 U.S.C. § 3281 provides that indictments for offenses punishable by death may be found at any time, and the federal murder statute carries that exposure. The felony-murder / firearm-caused-death count under 18 U.S.C. § 924(j)(1) is tied to the underlying untimed murder predicate and is similarly not time-barred. A separate § 924(c) firearm count may be subject to a limitations challenge, but the core counts are not. The client's limitations intuition is correct for some federal offenses but not for murder.

expected_inquiries: Ask the client for a precise, minute-by-minute account of the original 2002 events — the altercation with the decedent, every location visited, every person spoken to, and every statement made to any law-enforcement officer or prosecutor from the day of the disappearance forward.

Ask the client to describe the conversations between his original attorney and the prosecutor: who said what, in what order, whether any written record exists, and whether client himself ever spoke directly with any prosecutor.

Ask whether client has a written record of his tribal enrollment, whether his enrollment was current in 2002, and whether decedent was also a tribal member — these facts drive Major Crimes Act jurisdiction.

Ask for every document relating to the state-court plea and the state-court vacatur order — including the original plea agreement, sentencing transcript, and the post-conviction relief petition that led to the vacatur.
Ask the client to describe the journal he says he took from the decedent's car, what it said, where it is now, and whether any contemporaneous copy or photograph exists.
Ask the client to describe the firearm used: how long he had owned it, where it was stored, who else knew about it, and whether he had any prior training or prior incidents involving it.

Ask about the FBI interview 'about a year after the murder' at which the client reportedly said he killed the decedent: the setting, what he was in custody for at the time, whether he was Mirandized, whether counsel was present, and whether a recording or report exists.

Ask for a complete list of every attorney who has represented the client on this matter since 2002 — state and federal — and whether client has ever discussed the facts of the offense with any of them.
Ask about prior counsel specifically: what the client told him, what he believes prior counsel disclosed to the government, and what specific prejudice he claims to have suffered.

Ask the client to identify every lay observation about the jury pool he relied on for the fair-cross-section argument — specifically how he and his family identified the purported absence of jurors from distinctive demographic groups.
Ask for complete records from any prior psychological or psychiatric evaluations, any diagnoses, any treatment, and any medications the client has received during his incarceration or earlier.
Ask about the client's tribal community ties and any potential tribal-court or tribal-community resources — these can matter for sentencing mitigation even where they do not affect jurisdiction.
Ask about the client's tribal community ties and any potential tribal-court or tribal-community resources — these can matter for sentencing mitigation even where they do not affect jurisdiction.
memo_expectations: Analyze the controlling Indian-country jurisdiction doctrine and the Major Crimes Act jurisdictional framework: why the state-court conviction was properly vacated for lack of jurisdiction, why the federal government now has exclusive jurisdiction over this offense, and why the federal prosecution is not barred by double jeopardy or by the earlier state proceedings.

Assess the statute of limitations exposure for each federal count: 18 U.S.C. §§ 1111 / 1153 murder in Indian country (generally no limitations period for murder) vs. 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) / § 924(j)(1) firearm counts, and why one firearm count may already be time-barred while the § 924(j)(1) count ties to the untimed murder predicate.

Evaluate admissibility under Federal Rule of Evidence 410(a)(4) of the client's statements directing officers to the victim's body, focusing on whether those statements were made 'during plea discussions with an attorney for the prosecuting authority' — with emphasis on the fact that the statements were given to law-enforcement officers, not the prosecutor.

Analyze the two Rule 410 exceptions applied in some circuits — (a) reasonable subjective belief that the defendant was speaking during plea negotiations and (b) officers with express authority to negotiate a plea — and the client's evidentiary burden to establish either one.

Analyze Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 16(a)(1)(E) and assess a motion to compel disclosure of communications between the government and prior defense counsel, distinguishing material sought for trial use vs. for an ineffective-assistance claim (which is typically the subject of post-conviction rather than pretrial discovery).

Assess a Jury Selection and Service Act challenge under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1861–1878: the strict procedural requirements for timeliness (motion before voir dire or within seven days of discovering grounds) and the non-negotiable sworn-statement requirement under § 1867(d).

Evaluate the substantive fair-cross-section challenge under the controlling fair-cross-section precedent: the client's evidentiary burden to show (a) the underrepresentation of a distinctive group, (b) that the underrepresentation is unfair and unreasonable relative to the community, and (c) systematic exclusion — and the insufficiency of lay 'visual observations' or cluster-of-jurors-from-one-town arguments.

Analyze a self-defense theory grounded in the client's account of being confronted with his own firearm: proportionality (the fatal force element), retreat / escape opportunities, and the effect of the client's subsequent conduct (transport of the body, burial, and gunshots to the head) on the overall credibility of the self-defense narrative.

Assess the anticipated cross-examination on the 'post-murder conduct': transportation of the decedent to a remote site, burial in a shallow grave wrapped in a tarp, and three close-range gunshots to the head — and why these facts are fatal to most self-defense theories even when the initial altercation is genuinely disputed.

Evaluate the risk posed by the prior counsel's potential trial testimony (the attorney who originally led law enforcement to the body) and the scope of any attorney-client privilege that survives — including the crime-fraud exception and any waiver arising from the client's own placing of privileged communications at issue.

Identify and preserve all objections for the trial record with specific legal grounds so that appellate review is de novo rather than plain-error or waived — including Rule 410 rulings, Jury Act rulings, Rule 16 rulings, and any evidentiary rulings on prior statements or testimony from prior counsel.

Model the sentencing exposure: murder under 18 U.S.C. § 1111 carries mandatory life imprisonment for first-degree, and the § 924(j)(1) count carries up to life — evaluate whether concurrent or consecutive structure is likely and whether any section 3553(a) mitigation realistically moves the outcome given the offense conduct.

Analyze Federal Rule of Evidence 801(d)(2)(A) party-opponent admissions doctrine and assess the admissibility of the client's spontaneous statement to an FBI agent approximately one year after the offense; determine whether interview was custodial (requiring Miranda warnings) or non-custodial, whether Sixth Amendment right to counsel had attached as to the murder charge at the time of the interview, and whether any colorable suppression motion exists — or whether statement comes in as a straightforward party admission regardless of the interview's informal character.

opening: Thanks for meeting with me. I'm X. I'm facing federal charges involving child pornography offenses, and I'd like to get your read on my situation.

facts.client_belief: Yeah — I have a 2015 federal case on this same kind of stuff. I was convicted, did my time, and I've been on supervision ever since. There's no argument about that part.
facts.court_record: The client has a 2015 federal conviction under 18 U.S.C. § 2252A(a)(1)/(b)(1) and § 2252A(a)(5)(B)/(b)(2) — both Chapter 110 offenses. He has stipulated to the fact, dates, and statutory sections of that prior conviction, and he was on supervised release from that conviction at the time of the current offense. These foundational facts are not in dispute.

facts.client_belief: My probation officer came by the transitional house I was living in for a surprise check. He ended up looking under my bed covers and there was a smartphone there. That's what kicked all of this off.
facts.court_record: During an unscheduled home visit at the client's transitional housing, the probation officer entered the client's bedroom and asked to review X's TV viewing history. While searching for the TV remote, X himself pulled back the covers on his bed, revealing a smartphone the officer had not previously known the client possessed. The phone's existence and location at discovery are not in dispute.

facts.client_belief: The phone had stuff on it — illegal material involving kids. I'm not going to sit here and pretend the jury got it wrong about what was on the phone. That's not the fight I want to pick.
facts.court_record: Forensic analysis of the phone revealed over one hundred images and two videos depicting minors, located in the cache files of an encrypted file-sharing application. The jury returned a special verdict finding beyond a reasonable doubt that the material depicted a minor under twelve years of age. The presence and legal character of the material on the device are not in dispute.

facts.client_belief: My landlord gave me the phone. I told my probation officer that and he didn't believe me. I've been saying it all along — I didn't buy that phone, I didn't order it, it came from the landlord.
facts.court_record: The client's account that the phone was provided by the landlord faces severe credibility issues at this stage. The client knew the phone's ten-digit passcode. He admitted six months of possession. The phone contained a Gmail account tied to the client's own first name, middle name, and birth year. The access logs for the illegal material fell within the six-month window of the client's admitted possession. The 'it came from someone else' narrative does not account for the control indicia that support possession. The narrative is no longer a live defense; its residual value at sentencing is limited.

facts.client_belief: The jury never decided my old case counts as one of the kinds of priors that triggers the ten-year minimum. Under the new Supreme Court case — the 2024 decision — a jury has to find that fact, not a judge. So the ten-year minimum shouldn't apply.
facts.court_record: Under the narrow the controlling prior-conviction precedent exception, a judge may find the fact of a prior conviction even when that finding increases the applicable penalty. a 2024 Supreme Court decision extended jury-finding requirements to the 'separate occasions' ACCA inquiry — but only because that inquiry requires additional post-conviction factfinding beyond identifying the offense of conviction. Here, determining whether prior offense was 'under this chapter' for § 2252A(b)(2) purposes requires only matching the statute-of-conviction number to Chapter 110 — a purely legal exercise. The client already stipulated to the statutory sections of the prior conviction. that decision is not a vehicle to escape the ten-year minimum here.

facts.client_belief: The government never mentioned my prior case in the original paperwork charging me. If the prior is what's triggering the big minimum, it should have been spelled out in the charges from day one so I knew what was coming.
facts.court_record: The Fifth Amendment does not require the government to allege a defendant's prior conviction in the indictment to trigger a recidivist mandatory minimum. the controlling prior-conviction precedent established that the prior conviction is a sentencing factor, not an element. Moreover, the indictment in this case cited the penalty provision § 2252A(b)(2) and identified the ten-year minimum on its face. The indictment is not defective. The 'should have been in the indictment' argument fails as a matter of established doctrine.

facts.client_belief: At trial, the probation officer sat up on the stand and told the jury he didn't believe my story about where the phone came from. That's not his job — he's not supposed to tell the jury whether to believe me. That alone should get my conviction knocked down.
facts.court_record: Even assuming the probation officer's opinion about the client's truthfulness was erroneously admitted, harmless-error review will likely defeat a new-trial remedy. The government's evidence of knowing possession was overwhelming: the concealed location of the phone, the client's knowledge of the passcode, the six-month possession admission, the client's own name and birth year tied to the associated Gmail account, and the access timestamps falling within his admitted possession window. The brief credibility opinion did not substantially sway the verdict. The 'new trial' remedy is not realistically available.

facts.client_belief: My probation officer didn't have a search warrant. He just walked right into my room and started going through my stuff — he had no right to do that without permission. Whatever he found in there shouldn't be allowed to be used against me.
facts.court_record: Supervised releasees typically consent, as a condition of release, to warrantless searches of their residence and effects by their probation officer, subject to reasonableness. Even absent express search conditions, the Supreme Court has upheld suspicionless searches of supervisees based on reduced expectations of privacy. Here, the officer's entry into the bedroom during a home visit and observation of the phone during a routine search for the TV remote falls well within standard supervision practice. The 'warrantless search' theory will not produce suppression.

facts.client_belief: I didn't unlock the phone for them — the officer did that, using a code I gave him. So I didn't turn over anything voluntarily. They shouldn't be able to use what they found once they got inside.
facts.court_record: A defendant's provision of a passcode to law enforcement when asked, especially in the supervised-release context, is routinely treated as consent to access the device's contents. The client did not refuse, did not assert any privilege, and by his own account provided the code. Even if some Fifth Amendment objection could theoretically be raised to being compelled to provide a passcode, it was not raised contemporaneously and is waived. Moreover, the phone's subsequent forensic analysis by a qualified agent produced independent evidence of possession and control. The 'he unlocked it, not me' distinction does not produce suppression.

facts.client_belief: The material was in the cache of some encrypted file-sharing app. I didn't put it there — the app could have downloaded it automatically. That's not knowing possession on my part.
facts.court_record: Cache files result from deliberate user interaction with content; they are not created by ambient software activity. The forensic record in this case reflects timestamped access to the specific files during the client's admitted possession window. Additional context evidence — privacy tools installed on the device, use of a privacy-focused search tool, and searches suggesting a desire to conceal device activity — reflects intentional conduct, not passive automatic behavior. The 'automatic download' theory is inconsistent with the forensic record and rarely succeeds even in cases where the record is thinner.

facts.client_belief: I took steps to be private online — using search tools that don't track you, encrypted apps, privacy settings. A lot of people do that for regular reasons. That shouldn't be used to prove I knew what was on the phone.
facts.court_record: Privacy tools are legitimately used by many people for many lawful reasons. In the context of this case, however, the combination of privacy tools with (a) the specific encrypted file-sharing application where the illegal material was cached, (b) web searches suggesting a desire to conceal device activity, and (c) the concealment of the device itself under the bed covers in violation of supervision conditions, produces a coherent pattern the jury was entitled to credit. Standing alone, a privacy tool proves little; in this aggregation, it contributes to knowledge and intent.

facts.client_belief: The jury also found 'beyond a reasonable doubt' that the pictures were of kids under twelve. But some of those kids look older than twelve. That finding was a stretch and it's what pushes my minimum to ten years.
facts.court_record: Age determinations in this context are frequently made by the trier of fact based on visual inspection, supplemented where appropriate by expert testimony. The special-verdict finding is reviewed for sufficiency-of-the-evidence on appeal, and reviewing courts view the evidence in the light most favorable to the verdict. Second-guessing the jury's age finding on appeal is a very steep climb. The under-twelve enhancement is the driver of the ten-year statutory minimum and is unlikely to be unwound.

facts.client_belief: I already completed sex-offender treatment on my last case. That should mean something — the court should see I've tried to address this, and give me a break on the lifetime supervision.
facts.court_record: Completion of prior treatment is a legitimate § 3553(a) mitigation consideration, but it has limited weight against the fact pattern of reoffense while still on supervised release. A sentencing court may reasonably view the completed treatment as evidence that treatment did not prevent reoffense, rather than as evidence of rehabilitation. Under U.S.S.G. § 5D1.2(b)(2), lifetime supervision is recommended for sex offenses, and the guidelines recommendation combined with recidivism on supervision typically produces lifetime supervision despite treatment history.

facts.client_belief: I'm going to be an older man when I get out. Lifetime supervision doesn't really make sense for someone my age when I'm released. There must be some way to argue against that.
facts.court_record: Age at release is a recognized § 3553(a) mitigation consideration, and courts have occasionally varied downward from lifetime supervision based on projected elderly release. However, the argument is weaker where the offense conduct is a repeat offense while already on supervision, the conduct involves material depicting very young minors, and the pattern suggests continued risk. Within-Guidelines lifetime supervision carries a rebuttable presumption of reasonableness on appeal, and meaningful variance requires concrete, individualized mitigation — not general observations about age.

facts.client_belief: I have diagnosed mental-health issues. That should be mitigation — the judge should be looking at my whole picture, not just the repeat conduct.
facts.court_record: Mental-health diagnoses and treatment are appropriate mitigation, and the court may (and typically does) include mental-health treatment as a special condition of supervised release. However, raising mental-health issues for the first time on appeal, without having developed the record at sentencing, will be procedurally barred from meaningful appellate review. The mitigation must be concretely presented below through records, evaluations, and treatment-provider testimony. The 'whole picture' argument depends entirely on the quality of the sentencing presentation.

facts.client_belief: I'm only being charged with possession. I didn't make it, I didn't sell it, I didn't share it with anyone. Possession is the mildest of these charges. I shouldn't be hit with the biggest hammer in the statute.
facts.court_record: Possession under § 2252A(a)(5)(B) carries a substantial penalty framework, and with the recidivist enhancement under § 2252A(b)(2) the mandatory minimum reaches ten years. While distribution and production carry higher ceilings, recidivist possession with the under-twelve enhancement is among the most aggravated forms of the possession offense. The legislative scheme treats repeat offenders who possess material depicting very young minors severely. The 'possession is the mildest' framing does not survive the statute's recidivism provisions.

facts.client_belief: I hear from my lawyer the judge is probably just going to run through the sentencing factors in a couple of paragraphs at most and call it a day. He's not going to address most of my mitigation arguments. That's not a real explanation for the sentence he's handing down — there's got to be grounds to push back on that.
facts.court_record: A sentencing court's explanation must be sufficient to show the factors were considered, but need not be a line-by-line recitation of every argument. Within-Guidelines sentences require less extensive explanation than outside-Guidelines sentences. A court is not required to explicitly address every mitigating argument, especially those raised only in passing or not raised at all at sentencing. Unpreserved procedural-reasonableness objections are reviewed for plain error, which is dramatically harder to win. Expecting a new sentencing based on brevity of explanation alone is unrealistic.

facts.client_belief: On top of this new sentence, they're going to revoke my supervision from the 2015 case and stack more prison time on. That just feels like I'm being punished twice for the exact same thing — how is that fair?
facts.court_record: Supervised-release revocation under 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e) and (g) is legally distinct from punishment for the new offense. Revocation penalizes the breach of trust inherent in violating the conditions of supervision; the new sentence punishes the new offense itself. The Supreme Court has specifically rejected the double-jeopardy theory as applied to this sequence. Consecutive structure for revocation time is the default, and courts routinely impose it. The 'double-counting' framing is inconsistent with the governing doctrine.

expected_inquiries: Ask the client to describe in detail the circumstances under which he obtained the phone: who gave it to him, what was said, whether any written record exists, and whether asserted donor can be located and interviewed.

Ask about every condition of his supervised release from the 2015 conviction — in particular, any condition requiring him to report new electronic devices, and any condition authorizing suspicionless or limited searches of his person or residence by the probation officer.
Ask the client whether he reviewed and signed the conditions of release, whether he understood them, and whether he was ever formally warned about unreported devices.
Ask for every document reflecting the probation officer's visits to the residence — visit logs, officer's notes, any recording, and any contemporaneous communications to or about the client.

Ask about the 2015 conviction in detail: the specific subsections charged, whether he was convicted after trial or plea, the sentence imposed, and the terms and completion status of any sex-offender treatment.
Ask about his participation in sex-offender treatment during supervision: the provider, the modality, discharge documentation, and whether provider will speak to the defense at sentencing.
Ask about any mental-health history: diagnoses, treatment providers, medications, hospitalizations, and any evaluations that exist or can be obtained before sentencing.

Ask about every Gmail account, social media account, cloud storage account, and file-sharing account the client has used, with usernames, approximate dates of use, and any two-factor-authentication credentials.
Ask about the client's technical familiarity with the applications found on the phone — the file-sharing and privacy tools — including how and from whom he learned about them.

Ask for the entire forensic report from the forensic extraction, including access logs, metadata, and any device-location or cell-tower data bearing on whether someone else could have been the operator.
Ask about his employment, family support, housing prospects, and any physical-health conditions — the § 3553(a) mitigation material that may modestly move the sentence within the available range.
Ask about his age, projected age at release under any likely sentence, and any health-related reasons that bear on the realistic need for lifetime versus a shorter supervised release term.

memo_expectations: Analyze the controlling prior-conviction precedent 'prior conviction' exception and its application here: the district court may find the fact of the prior conviction and match it to 18 U.S.C. § 2252A(b)(2)'s 'under this chapter' predicate without jury determination, because the prior offense was itself a federal Chapter 110 conviction to which the client has already stipulated.

Assess the scope of a 2024 Supreme Court decision and why it does not help here: that decision extended the jury-finding requirement to the 'separate occasions' ACCA inquiry because that inquiry required additional post-conviction factfinding, while the 'under this chapter' determination here requires only matching the statute-of-conviction number — a purely legal exercise.

Evaluate the Fifth Amendment / indictment challenge: why the government is not required to allege the prior conviction in the indictment to trigger the recidivist mandatory minimum, and why citation of § 2252A(b)(2) in the indictment together with the statutory minimum ten-year reference further defeats the claim.

Analyze the probation officer's opinion testimony about truthfulness (that he did not believe the client's account of how he obtained the phone): admissibility under Federal Rule of Evidence 701, the potential invasion of the jury's role under Rule 608(a), and the harmless-error analysis that applies when the opinion testimony was brief and the remaining evidence of possession was overwhelming.

Evaluate the procedural reasonableness of the potential lifetime term of supervised release: the district court's obligation to consider the § 3553(a) factors, the adequacy of the court's explanation for a within-Guidelines term, and the weight given to the client's recidivism while already on supervised release.

Analyze the substantive reasonableness of a lifetime supervised release term under § 3583(k) and U.S.S.G. § 5D1.2(b)(2), including the Congressional directive that lifetime supervision be available for sex offenses, the presumption of reasonableness attached to within-Guidelines sentences, and the limited purchase that age-at-release and prior-treatment-completion arguments have against the recidivism record.

Assess the constructive possession proof on the current offense: the phone found concealed under the bed covers, the passcode known to the client, the six-month possession admission, the Gmail account tied to the client's name and birth year, and the access timestamps within the possession window — each of which independently establishes knowledge and possession.

Analyze the privacy-defense argument (the phone was encrypted, the application was encrypted, searches used anonymizing tools): why evidence of deliberate concealment supports rather than undermines the knowledge element, and why the 'automatic download' theory fails against the specificity of the access pattern.

Evaluate the Fourth Amendment posture of the probation officer's discovery of the phone: the client's status as a supervised releasee typically authorizes warrantless searches of residence and effects by the probation officer under the conditions of release, and how that eliminates any suppression angle on the phone itself.

Model the combined exposure: the current 10-year mandatory minimum under § 2252A(b)(2) plus any consecutive time for the supervised-release revocation on the 2015 conviction, the lifetime supervised release, and the practical consequences of the sex-offender registration and residence restrictions.

Identify all sentencing objections the client must preserve on the record with specific legal grounds, including: mandatory-minimum application, recent-precedent-based jury-finding objection, any Rule 403 objection to probation officer credibility testimony, and procedural-reasonableness objections to the supervised-release term.

Evaluate realistic variance strategy under 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a): the limited purchase of a prior-treatment-completed argument against a recidivism fact pattern, the potential of documented mental-health mitigation, the limitations imposed by the 10-year statutory floor, and the reality that a within-Guidelines sentence is likely.

opening: Thanks for squeezing me in, man. I'm X. So the feds are coming at me on a meth-conspiracy thing, and honestly I just need somebody to tell me straight where I stand.

facts.client_belief: I knew they had a wire on my phone for months starting around February 2022 — that's how they built most of what they have on me. I'm not saying the tap didn't happen; it's on the record.
facts.court_record: In February 2022, a federal judge authorized a wiretap of the client's phone based on a task-force officer's affidavit. The wiretap ran for several months and intercepted calls and messages between the client and multiple associates. The existence of the wiretap and the volume of intercepted communications are not in dispute.

facts.client_belief: On February 22, 2022, I had my friend Y drive out of the apartment I had rented for her. She had some bags in the back of her car. She got pulled over. The police found drugs in her car. That happened.
facts.court_record: On February 22, 2022, the client instructed Y to transport bags from the client-provided apartment at a residential address (Apartment A). Her vehicle was stopped by local police (unrelated to the federal investigation), a K-9 alerted on the vehicle, and officers recovered 667.7 grams of 98% pure methamphetamine from a pink duffle bag in the backseat, along with approximately $2,800 in cash. The stop and the recovery of narcotics are not in dispute.

facts.client_belief: After they stopped Y, I knew they'd go search the apartment on Apartment A too. They found more of the same stuff there. I'm not fighting that part.
facts.court_record: Following Y's consent, officers searched Apartment A — which the client had provided for Y — and recovered an additional 222 grams of 100% pure methamphetamine. The presence of the additional methamphetamine at the apartment is not in dispute.

facts.client_belief: The whole wire was built on a social-media conversation where the agent said a water emoji meant methamphetamine. That's wrong — a water emoji has an obvious other meaning between a man and a woman. If they had it wrong there, the whole wiretap is dirty from the start.
facts.court_record: Under the controlling affidavit-challenge precedent, challenging the affidavit requires a preliminary showing of deliberate falsehood or reckless disregard for the truth — not merely an alternative interpretation. The officer's interpretation of the water emoji as methamphetamine is supported by context in the affidavit itself, including a separate intercepted call in which 'water' clearly referred to narcotics between the confidential source and her prior supplier. Even granting the client's alternative reading, a plausible alternative meaning is not the same as reckless falsity. Under the separate the affidavit-challenge standard step, the affidavit contains substantial independent support (toll records, confidential-source corroboration, pattern of contacts with known distributors) that would sustain probable cause even if the emoji interpretation were excised. The 'whole wire is dirty' framing does not produce suppression.

facts.client_belief: And on top of that — in one of the calls, the associate said she'd leave 'SIX' in the mailbox. The agent said that meant six thousand dollars of drug money. That was his guess. She could have meant anything.
facts.court_record: The officer's 'drug proceeds' interpretation of the 'SIX' reference is based on the full context of the investigation — including the relationship between the client and the associate, the pattern of prior transactions, and the timing of the delivery. In those terms, the question is not whether officer's interpretation is the only possible reading, but whether officer believed and appropriately accepted his interpretation as true. Training-and-experience-based interpretations of drug code are routinely sustained on that review even when alternative meanings are conceivable.

facts.client_belief: At trial, those same investigators are going to get up there and tell the jury what my calls 'really meant.' That's not their job — that's the jury's job. They shouldn't be allowed to translate my words for me.
facts.court_record: Under Federal Rule of Evidence 701, lay opinion testimony is admissible if it is rationally based on the witness's perception, helpful to the jury, and not based on specialized knowledge within Rule 702's scope. Monitoring officers who have reviewed hundreds of intercepted calls and have personal knowledge of the investigation can testify to their understanding of the calls — framed as 'the significance of the call to the investigation' or 'what this meant to the officer in the course of the investigation' — without invading the jury's role. The line is real but routinely policed. A categorical 'they can't interpret my words' objection will not succeed.

facts.client_belief: They're also going to put on a drug task force guy as an 'expert' to tell the jury what words like 'action' and 'zips' mean. That's fake expertise — he's just repeating street slang. That shouldn't count as expert testimony.
facts.court_record: Under Rule 702, an experienced narcotics investigator may testify as an expert on the structure of drug trafficking organizations, common code words, and typical operational patterns. Courts have routinely admitted such testimony where the witness establishes a sufficient foundation of training and experience. The critical limit is that the expert cannot simply tell the jury what the defendant meant on any specific call; he can testify to the general meaning of terms in the drug trade. A limiting instruction is typical. A motion in limine may narrow the testimony but is unlikely to exclude it wholesale.

facts.client_belief: The apartment where they found the second batch of drugs — that wasn't my place. It was my friend's. I just helped her out with rent. They're going to say I was 'running a stash house' out of her apartment. That's a stretch.
facts.court_record: The 'premises' enhancement under U.S.S.G. § 2D1.1(b)(12) requires that the defendant maintain the premises for the purpose of manufacturing or distributing a controlled substance. The client provided the apartment, stored distribution-quantity methamphetamine there, and used it as the logistical hub for the February 22 delivery. Under the controlling circuit precedent, control and purpose need not be exclusive; shared use does not defeat the enhancement. The 'just helped her with rent' framing is unlikely to defeat the two-level increase.

facts.client_belief: And they're going to call me the 'leader' of this whole thing because I connected a few people with each other. That's not leadership — I was working with my people, not over them. A leader enhancement is a four-level hit.
facts.court_record: The four-level leadership enhancement under U.S.S.G. § 3B1.1(a) requires the defendant to be an organizer or leader of criminal activity involving five or more participants or that was otherwise extensive. Relevant factors include decision-making authority, recruitment of accomplices, claims to larger shares of fruits, degree of planning, nature of participation, and control over others. The client's directions to Y to make deliveries, the provision of the apartment, and the coordination of buyers and suppliers fit several of these factors. 'Working with, not over' is not a legal distinction the guidelines recognize.

facts.client_belief: My old State A case from 2009 was state-court cocaine trafficking. That should not count as a 'serious drug felony' to jack up my mandatory minimum to fifteen years. Every state has its own laws — that shouldn't automatically match up.
facts.court_record: Under 21 U.S.C. § 802(57), a 'serious drug felony' is defined by reference to federal categories (§ 924(e)(2)(A)) that include controlled-substance offenses with maximum terms of ten or more years. The State A 2009 cocaine-trafficking conviction, if it carried that maximum and the client served more than twelve months (with release within fifteen years of the current offense), will typically qualify. The categorical approach requires close comparison of elements, but under the controlling circuit precedent the March 2009 the State A first-degree controlled-substance-trafficking statute encompassed the same substances related to cocaine as the contemporaneous federal Schedule II — cocaine appeared on both State A and federal Schedule II. The court has held the § 851 enhancement raising the minimum to fifteen years is warranted.

facts.client_belief: That same old cocaine case — they also want to use it to label me a 'career criminal,' which triples my time under the sentencing rulebook. You can't use the same prior case for two different hammers.
facts.court_record: Career offender status under U.S.S.G. § 4B1.1 and the § 851 statutory enhancement are not mutually exclusive; one old conviction can support both, and the two operate on different sentencing components (the guidelines range and the statutory floor, respectively). Moreover, career offender status under § 4B1.1 requires only two prior qualifying convictions, not just one, so the government's theory typically depends on additional priors or aggregation. The 'double use' intuition is not the law — the real question is whether priors qualify under each separate doctrine.

facts.client_belief: The amounts they're using to calculate my sentence — they're treating it as the pure kind, 'ice,' because the lab said ninety-eight or a hundred percent. That's a massive hit at sentencing. They should use the ordinary meth numbers, not the pure ones.
facts.court_record: Under U.S.S.G. § 2D1.1(c), pure methamphetamine or 'ice' (at least 80% purity) triggers significantly higher base offense levels than methamphetamine mixtures. At 98-100% purity, the substances here qualify as ice. Policy-based variance requests asking courts to use mixture guidelines rather ththe purity-based guidelines are legally permissible in some circuits, but are seldom granted and are reviewed for abuse of discretion. The client should not expect the sentencing court to adopt mixture treatment where the lab result is unambiguous.

facts.client_belief: My lawyer already warned me that on trial days, I'll be moved through the courthouse in shackles, and jurors could see that. The moment a juror sees you in chains, that's it — they've made up their minds. If that happens to even one juror, that by itself should stop the trial.
facts.court_record: Brief, inadvertent juror viewing of a defendant in restraints outside the courtroom does not automatically require a mistrial. The controlling question is whether actual prejudice resulted. Where the court promptly identifies the affected jurors, conducts individual voir dire, and obtains assurances of impartiality, the remedial process typically suffices. The 'as soon as they see chains, it's over' framing overstates the doctrinal position. A motion for mistrial may be filed, but without a showing of specific prejudice, it is unlikely to succeed.

facts.client_belief: Look, the two women they're using most — Y and Z — both cut deals to save themselves. They're testifying because the government is giving them lighter sentences. Their word, given under those circumstances, shouldn't be the thing that sends me away.
facts.court_record: Both Y and Z entered into plea agreements and testified as cooperating government witnesses. Under federal law and the controlling circuit precedent, accomplice testimony is not required to be corroborated; its credibility is exclusively the jury's domain. Defense counsel cross-examined both witnesses on their plea arrangements and specific inconsistencies — including Y's admitted prior falsehoods to law enforcement and difficulty recalling certain details from February 22, 2022 — placing those issues squarely before the jury. The jury's decision to credit their testimony receives substantial deference on appeal and does not give rise to a sufficiency defect.

facts.client_belief: A lot of what I said on those calls was exaggerated. I'd talk tough with my people, make things sound bigger than they were, and I was clearly not operating at the scale they're painting. A lot of this is just talk.
facts.court_record: A 'puffery' or exaggeration defense to recorded-call evidence is possible but very difficult on this record. The recorded calls here are corroborated by contemporaneous deliveries, the 667.7-gram courier seizure, the 222-gram apartment seizure, the cash transfer pattern, and cooperating-witness testimony. Where the calls predict and track actual transactions, the 'just talk' framing is easily refuted. Jurors tend to credit recorded statements, especially when they map onto subsequent events. This narrative risks undermining overall credibility if offered from the stand.

facts.client_belief: Nobody is ever going to testify that I personally handed drugs to anyone. There's no witness who can say they got something directly from my own hands. That's a big hole in their case.
facts.court_record: Neither possession nor distribution requires personal delivery by the defendant. Constructive possession — dominion and control over the contraband through others — is well-established. The client's directions to Y, the drugs coming from the client-provided apartment, and the client's instructions for the $2,900 payment are classic constructive-possession facts. For conspiracy, it is enough that the client agreed with others to distribute and an overt act was taken. The 'no hand-to-hand' framing is not a hole; it is outside the elements.

facts.client_belief: My old State A conviction has been off my record, I've paid my debt, I've worked since then. The courts shouldn't be piling a ten-plus-year-old prior onto my current case like it just happened yesterday.
facts.court_record: Time elapsed since a prior conviction does not eliminate its effect as a sentencing predicate unless the statutory lookback period has run. Under 21 U.S.C. § 802(58), the relevant period is fifteen years from release, measured to the commencement of the current offense. A 2009 conviction with custody extending into the early 2010s will easily be within that window. Character and rehabilitation evidence may support a § 3553(a) variance, but they cannot remove a qualifying prior from the enhancement analysis.

facts.client_belief: Realistically, I'm looking at probably fifteen years minimum — they've already told me that. That's a long time, but I can do it. That's my worst case.
facts.court_record: The 15-year statutory minimum is a floor, not a ceiling, and is almost certainly not the realistic sentence. Under the guidelines, after the career-offender overlay and the leadership and premises enhancements, the advisory range is approximately 360 months to life (30 years to life). The client's actual exposure is substantially greater ththe statutory floor. Judges most commonly sentence within or near the guidelines range. The 'minimum is my worst case' framing is a serious underestimate of exposure.
