Ask the client about his understanding and recollection of the courier delivery on February 22, 2022 — whether he had any awareness that Y had been stopped, whether any phones were destroyed or reset, and what he told any law enforcement in the hours and days after.

Ask the client to describe, in detail, every communication he had with W and Z — both on the phone and on social media — including the context of any emoji use, the topics being discussed, and any independent evidence of the nature of those relationships. Also ask specifically about the water emoji: when he used it, with whom, and what meaning he attached to it — this directly bears on any evidentiary-hearing proffer.

Ask about the client's relationship with each of the named co-conspirators (Y, X, V, Z, W): how each was recruited or encountered, their respective roles, and whether any of them are cooperating or likely to cooperate.

Ask the client to explain the apartment at a residential address (Apartment A): who leased it, who paid rent, who had keys, what was stored there, and what was his relationship to Y — this drives both the possession theory and the premises enhancement.

Ask the client to identify, by name and role, every person he directed, coordinated with, or recruited — including where and how drugs were stored, who picked up or dropped off, and who controlled the money — to assess whether five-or-more-participant threshold for the § 3B1.1(a) organizer/leader enhancement is met.

Ask the client for a complete timeline of the State A 2009 cocaine trafficking case: the specific statute of conviction, the plea or jury verdict, the sentence imposed, the exact dates of custody, and whether he has any written plea papers — this drives the career-offender and § 851 analyses. Also ask about every financial transaction the client made during the investigation period: bank accounts, cash purchases, money transfers, vehicle purchases, and any property — this shapes forfeiture exposure and contextualizes the $6,000 / $2,900 transfers.

Ask for every document from the State A case (indictment, judgment, plea transcript, sentencing transcript, jail credit records) to support a categorical-approach challenge to the prior as a qualifying predicate.

Ask for the client's complete history of substance use, treatment, mental health, and family circumstances — the § 3553(a) mitigation material that may move the court toward the lower end of the applicable guidelines range.

Ask the client to describe the courthouse lobby encounter: which entrance was used, how long defendants were in the lobby, which jurors he believes may have seen him, any direct eye contact, and any statements overheard — this shapes the actual-prejudice analysis and the voir-dire follow-up.

Ask the client to describe the courthouse lobby encounter: which entrance was used, how long defendants were in the lobby, which jurors he believes may have seen him, any direct eye contact, and any statements overheard — this shapes the actual-prejudice analysis and the voir-dire follow-up.
memo_expectations: Analyze the controlling affidavit-challenge precedent standard for challenging the wiretap affidavit: whether affiant's interpretation of the water emoji as meaning methamphetamine — and other code-word interpretations — was intentionally or recklessly false, and the high preliminary-showing burden (deliberate falsehood or reckless disregard, not mere ambiguity) the client must meet to earn an evidentiary hearing.

Assess the 'remaining probable cause' test under the affidavit-challenge standard: even if specific affidavit statements are set aside as problematic, whether affidavit contains sufficient other content — toll records, confidential-source corroboration, monetary transactions, pattern of contacts with known distributors — to independently support probable cause for the wiretap.

Evaluate the admissibility of law-enforcement lay opinion testimony under Federal Rule of Evidence 701 interpreting the content of intercepted calls: the foundational requirement that the officer be personally involved in monitoring and investigation, and the boundary between permissible 'what this meant in the investigation' testimony and impermissible 'telling the jury what the call said.'

Analyze Rule 403 / Rule 702 concerns about the drug-crime expert testimony on the structure of drug trafficking organizations and slang terminology ('action' for methamphetamine, 'zips' for ounces): the proper scope of such testimony and the limiting-instruction strategy to guard against the expert substituting for the jury.

Analyze the 'premises enhancement' under U.S.S.G. § 2D1.1(b)(12) for maintaining a premises for the purpose of manufacturing or distributing controlled substances: the two-level increase based on the apartment the client provided to Y, and the specific facts that support or undermine the 'primary use' requirement.

Evaluate the leadership/organizer enhancement under U.S.S.G. § 3B1.1(a): the four-level increase requires a showing that the client was an organizer or leader of a criminal activity involving five or more participants or was otherwise extensive — assess the strength of the evidence on each element.

Analyze the § 851 enhancement and whether prior State A cocaine trafficking conviction qualifies as a 'serious drug felony' under 21 U.S.C. § 802(57), triggering the enhanced 15-year mandatory minimum (and potentially life) under § 841(b)(1)(A).

Analyze the career-offender designation under U.S.S.G. § 4B1.1(a) and whether client's 2009 State A cocaine-trafficking conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under § 4B1.2(b) — applying the categorical approach to the State A statute and its divisibility.

Assess the actual methamphetamine ('ice') vs. mixture guidelines sentencing — under U.S.S.G. § 2D1.1(c), pure methamphetamine at 98-100% purity triggers far higher base offense levels than mixture — and the very limited prospects of a policy-based variance on this point.

Assess the courthouse lobby juror-encounter issue under the controlling shackling precedent: whether court's prompt remediation — separating potentially affected jurors, conducting individual voir dire, obtaining uncontroverted assurances of impartiality — satisfies the actual-prejudice standard for brief shackling exposure outside the courtroom; and whether any defendant retains a viable mistrial argument.

Identify all sentencing and trial objections the client must preserve with specific legal grounds, including: the affidavit-challenge ruling, suppression motion, Rule 701 objections to lay opinion testimony, Rule 403 objections to expert testimony, shackles objection, career-offender objection, § 851 objection, leadership-enhancement objection, and ice-vs.-mixture objection.

Evaluate the sufficiency of the evidence for conspiracy and possession with intent to distribute: the wiretap content, the pattern of deliveries, the 667.7 grams recovered from the courier's vehicle, the 222 grams from the client's apartment, and whether any part of the chain is meaningfully challengeable.

opening: Hi counsel, I'm X. As I mentioned on the phone, I've been indicted in federal court on some drug-related charges and I was hoping you could help me figure out where I stand.

facts.client_belief: I started doing driving work for a guy named Y back in 2019. He paid me between $500 and $1,200 a day depending on the run, and he'd also give me $1,500 to $2,000 upfront for hotels, food, and gas before every trip. I never got a paycheck on the books — it was all cash.
facts.court_record: The client worked as a long-haul courier for Y's operation from approximately 2019 through summer 2020. Payment structure of $500–$1,200 per day plus a $1,500–$2,000 per-trip advance paid exclusively in cash is consistent with the prosecution's documentary evidence and co-conspirator testimony, and is not meaningfully disputed.

facts.client_belief: In July 2020 I got pulled over on the interstate out in State A by a county deputy. He said I was speeding and following too close. A second officer showed up, they ran a dog around the van, the dog hit, they opened up the back, and they found the boxes with the marijuana plus some cash and vape cartridges.
facts.court_record: In July 2020 the client was stopped on an interstate in State A by a county deputy for a traffic violation. A K-9 alerted to the vehicle and a search recovered approximately 112 kilograms of marijuana, approximately $13,000 in cash, and approximately 1.24 kilograms of THC vape products and edibles. The traffic stop and the seizure quantities are established on the record and not disputed.

facts.client_belief: After that stop I was taken to the sheriff's office, but they ended up releasing me because federal the federal department said they weren't going to prosecute.
facts.court_record: Following the State A stop the client was detained at the sheriff's office and then released after the federal department declined to pursue federal prosecution at that time. Detention, release, and the initial the federal department declination are documented and not disputed.

facts.client_belief: Look, the federal department already told me they weren't prosecuting after State A. So I don't get how a whole year later the feds can come back and indict me for the same load of drugs — that has to be double jeopardy.
facts.court_record: The Double Jeopardy Clause of the Fifth Amendment attaches only after jeopardy has actually attached — typically when a jury is sworn or, in a bench trial, when the first witness is sworn. A charging-agency declination before any charges are filed is a prosecutorial discretion decision, not an adjudication on the merits, and does not bar later federal prosecution for the same conduct. The client's belief that the federal department's initial declination forecloses the present indictment is a legal misconception.

facts.client_belief: At most I'm on the hook for the 112 kilos they actually caught me with in State A. I shouldn't be lumped in with what everybody else in the whole operation moved — I only drove my own runs.
facts.court_record: Under federal conspiracy drug sentencing (including U.S.S.G. § 1B1.3 relevant conduct and Pinkerton conspiracy liability), a defendant is held accountable not only for the quantities he personally handled but for all reasonably foreseeable quantities of controlled substances distributed in furtherance of the jointly undertaken criminal activity. Because the client was one of several couriers in a single multi-state trafficking organization, a substantially larger aggregate drug quantity is potentially attributable to him. The client's belief that he faces only the seized 112 kg reflects a significant misunderstanding of conspiracy-scope attribution.

facts.client_belief: I was just a driver. I followed Y's instructions, picked up and dropped off where he told me, didn't plan anything, didn't recruit anybody. I don't see how 'just drove a van' can be the same thing as being in a conspiracy.
facts.court_record: A conspiracy under 21 U.S.C. § 846 requires only (i) an agreement between two or more people to violate the drug laws, (ii) the defendant's knowledge of that agreement, and (iii) his voluntary participation. A courier who knowingly transports controlled substances for a distribution organization, accepts payment, and follows operational directions is a participant in the conspiracy regardless of whether he held a leadership role. The 'just a driver' framing understates the legal sufficiency of the client's participation.

facts.client_belief: We never used any banks — Y paid me in cash, and I only ever carried cash in the van on the return trips. So I really don't see how a money laundering charge sticks to me — it was all just cash passed by hand, no wire transfers or bank accounts involved at all.
facts.court_record: The federal money laundering statute, 18 U.S.C. § 1956, defines 'financial transaction' broadly to include not only bank transactions but any disposition, delivery, or transfer of monetary instruments or funds — including hand-to-hand cash transfers, so long as the activity affects interstate commerce in some way. Handing drug-sale proceeds from a courier to a co-conspirator, or receiving an advance of drug proceeds to cover the expenses of a further trafficking trip, can satisfy the 'transaction' element. The client's cash-only understanding is a material legal misconception about what the statute reaches.

facts.client_belief: Even if moving the cash did count, I wasn't hiding anything. I just drove it from one place to another same way I drove everything else. That's not 'laundering' in any normal sense.
facts.court_record: There are two distinct theories under § 1956(a)(1): (A) promotional money laundering, which punishes transactions conducted with intent to promote the ongoing unlawful activity; and (B) concealment money laundering, which requires a purpose of hiding the source, nature, location, ownership, or control of the proceeds. Recent the controlling circuit authority (the line of cases tightening concealment-prong proof) makes domestic concealment charges hard to sustain on mere cash-courier facts — but the promotional prong is materially different: transporting cash proceeds to fund the next marijuana purchase or to pay drivers for the next delivery can itself promote the underlying distribution offense, even without any hiding. The client's intuitive definition of 'laundering' tracks only the concealment prong and misses the promotional theory the government is likely to pursue.

facts.client_belief: We used an encrypted messaging app that auto-deletes. The whole point was that nothing got saved. So the government shouldn't have much to hang on me besides what they physically caught in the van.
facts.court_record: Even where a messaging application deletes locally-stored content on a schedule, extraction of the physical device recovered from a co-conspirator can retain message content and metadata that was not yet purged, and co-conspirators who cooperate with the government testify directly about conversations they participated in. In this case, the organization's leader had his devices seized and analyzed, and multiple co-conspirators have reportedly agreed to testify. The client's assumption that encrypted-and-deleted communications equal no evidence is a significant evidence-assessment error.

facts.client_belief: The feds also charged me with having a gun during a drug crime. But the pistol they're talking about was in a backpack at the group's warehouse — I didn't have it on me in the van, so that shouldn't stick.
facts.court_record: 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) punishes possession of a firearm 'in furtherance of' a drug trafficking crime. Possession can be actual or constructive and need not be contemporaneous with a specific drug transaction. Where a firearm is kept in premises used as operational headquarters for a drug-distribution organization and is traceable to the defendant (e.g., found together with his identification in his backpack), the government may argue the weapon was available to protect the operation — which can satisfy 'in furtherance of.' Whether that inference can be drawn on these facts is a genuine factual dispute, but the client's framing ('not on me in the van, therefore not mine') understates the reach of constructive possession doctrine.

facts.client_belief: The government's big exhibit is a spreadsheet their detective made estimating how much weed each of us moved. The detective admitted he was guessing on some of the numbers. My lawyer can just object to it and it should be tossed out.
facts.court_record: A Federal Rule of Evidence 1006 summary chart can be excluded where the underlying data is not competent or the summary is inaccurate, but the effectiveness of that challenge on appeal depends heavily on whether specific ground — for example, mathematical inaccuracy or extrapolation beyond the record — is raised with enough particularity at trial to preserve the issue. A general Rule 1006 foundation objection does not necessarily preserve a distinct math-accuracy challenge, which can push the defense from abuse-of-discretion review down to plain-error review. The client's assumption that a simple objection at trial is enough oversimplifies federal evidence-preservation requirements.

facts.client_belief: I had a tough moment at the State A stop — I told the deputy I was hauling computer servers for a bank and I showed him a shipping document. I figure that was just me panicking. It can't really be used as serious evidence.
facts.court_record: Affirmative false statements to law enforcement during a drug-interdiction stop, combined with the production of fabricated shipping paperwork, are routinely admitted at trial as consciousness-of-guilt evidence and can also expose the defendant to separate federal false-statement exposure depending on jurisdiction and the officer's status. Beyond the evidentiary impact, the fake paperwork can be argued as an overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy. The client's view that this was a harmless reaction underestimates how prosecutors and juries typically treat such conduct.

facts.client_belief: I don't have any prior drug convictions worth mentioning and I never hurt anybody. I've heard about something called the safety valve — doesn't that mean I get to avoid the long mandatory minimum automatically?
facts.court_record: The statutory safety-valve provision (18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)) allows relief from certain drug mandatory minimums only if the defendant satisfies all of its criteria: limited criminal history (as amended by the First Step Act), no violence or firearm possession in connection with the offense, no death or serious bodily injury resulting, the defendant is not an organizer/leader, and the defendant truthfully provides all information and evidence he has concerning the offense to the government before sentencing. The § 924(c) firearm charge and the requirement of a full, truthful proffer both create meaningful risk that the client will not qualify. The belief that safety valve is automatic on a clean record is incorrect.

facts.client_belief: If it comes down to it and I take a plea, I'll just cooperate and name names. As long as I give them something, I should get a big reduction no matter what.
facts.court_record: Sentencing reductions for cooperation under U.S.S.G. § 5K1.1 and 18 U.S.C. § 3553(e) (motion of the government) and Fed. R. Crim. P. 35(b) (post-sentencing assistance) are within the government's discretion to move for; the defendant cannot unilaterally trigger them. The size of any reduction depends on the prosecutor's assessment of the value, truthfulness, completeness, and reliability of the cooperation, and on whether that cooperation leads to prosecutions or convictions of others. 'Naming names' without corroborating information of value may not yield a substantial motion at all. The client's view of cooperation as a guaranteed mechanical discount is a procedural misconception.

facts.client_belief: The scheme moved marijuana — and in a lot of states these days marijuana is legal or decriminalized. That has to cut in my favor somehow at the federal level, right?
facts.court_record: Marijuana remains a Schedule I controlled substance under the federal Controlled Substances Act, 21 U.S.C. § 812, regardless of state-level legalization or decriminalization. Federal prosecutions under § 841 and § 846 proceed on that basis, and state legalization is not a defense or a formal mitigating factor at federal sentencing. State-law status may be a talking point in a § 3553(a) variance argument, but it does not alter the federal charges, the guideline calculation, or the mandatory minimums. The client's assumption of federal leniency because of evolving state policy is a legal misunderstanding.

facts.client_belief: When they arrested me after the indictment, the agent started asking me questions before reading me my rights. I figure everything I said there can just be thrown out, and that's the end of that problem.
facts.court_record: Miranda v. Arizona requires warnings before custodial interrogation; violations generally result in suppression of the statements themselves, but not of independently obtained physical evidence (the 'fruits' doctrine is narrower after controlling precedent). In addition, voluntary pre-Miranda statements made in non-custodial settings, or spontaneous statements not in response to interrogation, are not covered by Miranda at all. Whether any particular statement is suppressible turns on a fact-specific inquiry (custody, interrogation, waiver). A blanket assumption that 'everything I said gets thrown out' is an evidentiary overgeneralization.

facts.client_belief: The case ended up being filed in State B, but a lot of what they're accusing me of took place in State C, State A, and other states. That sounds like the wrong court to me — shouldn't it be wherever each thing happened?
facts.court_record: Under 18 U.S.C. § 3237 and well-settled conspiracy venue doctrine, venue for a conspiracy offense lies in any district in which any act in furtherance of the conspiracy was committed by any co-conspirator. Because the organization's leadership, the headquarters premises, and the flow of drug proceeds were anchored in State B, venue there is permissible for all members of the conspiracy, including a courier whose driving took him through other states. The client's view that venue must match the location of his personal conduct is a procedural misconception.

expected_inquiries: Obtain a certified copy of the superseding indictment and every prior version of the charging documents, as well as the government's Rule 16 discovery, the PSR (if already prepared), and any Rule 404(b) notice, before committing to a defense theory.

Interview the client in detail about every trip he drove: dates, routes, pickup and delivery cities, what he was told about the cargo, who directed him, who else was present, what was paid and to whom, so that we can independently test the quantity the government will seek to attribute.

Ask the client to describe, step-by-step, the State A traffic stop: speed and following distance, duration from initial stop to K-9 deployment, exactly when the deputy told him he was free to go, the wording of any consent, and whether back-door access point was unlocked as the officers claimed.

Probe the client's exact statements to investigators — both at the State A roadside and at any post-indictment arrest — including whether Miranda warnings were given, whether counsel was requested, and whether statements were recorded, to evaluate suppression motions.

Press the client on the handgun found with his backpack at the organization's warehouse: whether gun was his, how often he went to that warehouse, who else had access, and whether he ever carried the backpack on drug-transport trips, as this is the linchpin of the § 924(c) exposure.

Confirm the client's complete criminal history (federal and state, including sealed or expunged matters) and his military or other sentencing-mitigating background, because the safety-valve criminal-history criterion and any § 3553(a) variance argument turn on it.

Obtain any bank records, tax returns, and cash-deposit history in the client's name over the relevant period, so that we can push back on any net-worth or unexplained-income theory and prepare for forfeiture exposure.

Request from the government (and review carefully) the full underlying data for the drug-quantity summary chart — every encrypted-app conversation, every message attributed to the client, every calculation step — to identify specific mathematical and attribution errors that must be objected to on the record with particularity.

Identify and interview defense-aligned witnesses who can speak to the client's limited role (e.g., no recruiting of other drivers, no access to leadership-level communications, no involvement in pricing or source selection) in preparation for a role-reduction and relevant-conduct argument.

Open an early, controlled dialogue with the AUSA about the realistic drug-quantity range and any cooperation pathway, without making any substantive proffer until a proffer-protection proffer letter is in place and the client has been fully advised of the risks.

Open an early, controlled dialogue with the AUSA about the realistic drug-quantity range and any cooperation pathway, without making any substantive proffer until a Kastigar-style proffer letter is in place and the client has been fully advised of the risks.
memo_expectations: Analyze relevant-conduct and reasonably-foreseeable-quantity attribution under U.S.S.G. § 1B1.3 for couriers in a multi-driver distribution conspiracy, and quantify the range of drug weight the government can realistically prove against the client as opposed to the aggregate attributed to the organization.

Evaluate whether government's theory on Count 3 rests on promotional money laundering under § 1956(a)(1)(A)(i) or concealment money laundering under § 1956(a)(1)(B)(i); flag the controlling circuit's tightening of concealment-prong proof for cash-courier fact patterns and identify the weaknesses in each theory on these facts.

Assess the § 924(c) firearm-in-furtherance count on a constructive-possession theory: the proximity of the client's identification and backpack to the seized handgun at the operational headquarters, competing inferences about ownership and purpose, and the risk profile at trial given mandatory consecutive sentencing.

Develop a Rule 1006 / Rule 403 roadmap for challenging the government's drug-quantity summary chart, including preserving a specific mathematical-accuracy and extrapolation-beyond-the-record objection separately from any generic foundation objection, to retain abuse-of-discretion (rather than plain-error) review of any appellate issue.

Map the client's safety-valve eligibility under 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f) as amended by the First Step Act, with particular attention to the § 924(c) charge, the 'organizer/leader' factor, and the full-truthful-proffer requirement, and advise whether pursuing safety valve is realistically available.

Analyze double-jeopardy and prosecutorial-declination doctrine to explain why the initial the federal department declination after the State A stop does not bar the current federal indictment, and rule out any suppression theory grounded in that declination.

Analyze suppression exposure for the State A traffic stop (length of detention, consent to extended questioning, K-9 deployment timing under the controlling traffic-stop precedent) and for any post-indictment custodial interrogation (custody, interrogation, waiver under Miranda).

Analyze venue under 18 U.S.C. § 3237 for the conspiracy counts and confirm whether a venue challenge in a federal district in State B has any viable basis, so the client understands this is not a strategic door that is open.

Develop the consciousness-of-guilt exposure from the false 'bank servers' statement and the fabricated shipping paperwork at the State A stop, including any separate § 1001 false-statement risk depending on the officer's federal status.

Outline the realistic plea-vs-trial posture: statutory exposure on each count if convicted, Guidelines calculation ranges under competing drug-quantity findings, the acceptance-of-responsibility reduction, and the discretionary § 5K1.1 cooperation framework and how it actually works.

opening: Hi, I'm X. I need some legal advice about a federal wire fraud matter involving my former company. I was hoping to understand where I actually stand and what my options look like going forward.

facts.client_belief: I founded Company A back in 2003 when I was in my early twenties, and I rthe company as CEO until 2018. My co-executive Y, who I was also in a personal relationship with for many years, joined in 2009 and eventually became President and COO. The two of us together were the face of the company on the fundraising side.
facts.court_record: The client founded Company A in 2003 and served continuously as CEO through 2018. Y joined in 2009 and served as President and COO. Both held senior executive roles and communicated with investors. These background facts about corporate role and tenure are documented and not disputed.

facts.client_belief: Between 2013 and 2014, Company A did two private funding rounds — call them two late-stage private rounds — and we brought in investments from around a dozen outside investors. None of the shares were publicly traded. I personally was on most of the investor calls and in most of the investor meetings, along with Y.
facts.court_record: In 2013 Company A raised a late-stage round and in 2014 it raised a further late-stage round, from approximately a dozen private investors. The shares were not publicly traded. The client and Y were both directly involved in investor outreach and communication. These transactional facts are documented through subscription documents, email records, and corroborated by investor testimony.

facts.client_belief: In late 2015 the federal laboratory regulator did an unannounced inspection of our clinical lab and wrote up a report. They flagged our practices as posing 'immediate jeopardy' to patient health. After that, Company A voided the patient tests that had been run on our proprietary device.
facts.court_record: In late 2015 the federal regulator conducted an unannounced inspection of Company A's clinical laboratory and issued a report citing deficiencies that it characterized as presenting 'immediate jeopardy' to patient health. Company A subsequently voided patient test results run on its proprietary analyzer. The existence of the regulator's report, its 'immediate jeopardy' finding, and the subsequent voiding of patient tests are historical facts that are not in dispute.

facts.client_belief: Honestly, I had a vision and I was selling the vision — the future state of the technology. Investors in the tech sector know that's what you do at this stage. You're not representing 'today,' you're representing where you're going. So statements about what the device will do, or what our partners will do, can't really be fraud when everybody in that room understands it's forward-looking.
facts.court_record: Federal wire fraud under 18 U.S.C. §§ 1343 and 1349 does not recognize a 'visionary founder' safe harbor. Statements become actionable when they are representations of present fact — e.g., that a device currently works at a specified accuracy, that pharmaceutical partners have already validated the technology, that specific revenue has already been generated — made with knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard, and with intent to induce reliance. Forward-looking projections can also become actionable when the speaker knew at the time that the stated basis for the projection did not exist. The 'selling the vision' framing collapses material present-tense misrepresentations into puffery and is a significant legal misconception.

facts.client_belief: A lot of the specifics that got repeated to investors — financial numbers, exact percentages, what the government counterparty was doing — came out of Y's mouth or Y's financial model. I may have been in the room, or I may have forwarded a deck he prepared, but he was the operations guy and the numbers guy. That should be on him, not on me.
facts.court_record: Under well-settled wire-fraud doctrine, co-schemer liability attaches to participants who knowingly use or cause to be used a misleading communication to further scheme, whethery personally drafted the content or not. Forwarding decks, appearing on investor calls where the misrepresentations are delivered, and signing off on communications that the executive knows or should know to be materially false are all independently culpable acts. The CEO's insistence that numerical specifics were 'his' numbers, not hers, does not extricate her where she understood the substance and used the communications to raise money. This is a material misunderstanding of co-schemer liability.

facts.client_belief: The lab director at Company A was, frankly, in over his head — there were problems in that lab that were his to fix, not mine. Any accuracy issues the government will try to pin on me are really issues that stayed inside his department. I can't be liable for things I wasn't told.
facts.court_record: A CEO who receives contemporaneous internal warnings from the lab director and other employees about quality-control failures, device inaccuracy, and reliability problems, and who nonetheless continues to make representations to investors that those very characteristics are met, has actual knowledge of falsity — which is the mens rethe government must prove. In this case, there is documentary and testimonial evidence that the lab director and others raised concerns directly to the client over an extended period. Willful blindness and conscious avoidance doctrines would also apply. Attempting to attribute everything to the lab director's incompetence does not defeat scienter and may in fact highlight it.

facts.client_belief: On the pharmaceutical side — yes, I took reports that our device had run against certain pharmaceutical company samples, and I put the logos of those pharma companies on the cover pages before sharing internally and with some investors. That's just branding. Nobody in the industry would mistake a logo on a cover for an official endorsement.
facts.court_record: Placing a third-party company's logo on a technical report — without that company's authorization — and then characterizing the document to investors as independent validation of the technology by that company is a paradigmatic misrepresentation of source and authority. At trial, representatives of the named pharmaceutical companies would testify that they neither validated the technology nor authorized use of their logos, and investors would testify that they treated the reports as independent third-party validation. This is strong circumstantial evidence of fraudulent intent, not neutral branding, and the client's framing badly underweights the prosecutorial potency of this category of evidence.

facts.client_belief: When we hosted VIP tours for investors and showed them our devices running samples, nothing was staged. If some samples later got processed on conventional machines for speed, that's an operational decision. It doesn't make the demo a lie.
facts.court_record: Multiple former Company A employees would testify that investor demonstrations involved the proprietary device running a 'null protocol' — i.e., not actually analyzing the sample — while the investor's blood was surreptitiously diverted to a third-party commercial analyzer. A demonstration designed to create the false impression that the proprietary device performed the analysis, when in fact a different device did, is a classic act of concealment in furtherance of fraud. The 'operational decision' framing is legally untenable and reflects either minimization or willful blindness.

facts.client_belief: I've been told the government's financial-fraud theory focuses on revenue projections. But projections are by definition forward-looking, and our auditors knew the company wasn't profitable. Anybody reading the deck could see the difference between current performance and what we projected for future years. No rational investor would rely on that.
facts.court_record: The projections at issue included, among other things, a statement that the company had already generated roughly $200 million in revenue from government-contract work — a statement about past performance, not a forecast — at a time when internal records show actual revenue of less than $2 million. Representations of already-earned revenue are statements of present fact and are textbook wire-fraud material misrepresentations. They are categorically different from forward-looking projections, and collapsing the two into a 'nobody relies on projections' argument fails. Investors testifying that they did rely on these numbers further defeats the 'no reliance' premise.

facts.client_belief: The case involves a biotech company, not some shell scheme. A jury of regular people will look at this and see a complicated scientific dispute about a hard engineering problem — not a crime. So I'd rather go to trial than plea. No jury will convict on something that technical.
facts.court_record: The controlling circuit and other circuits routinely affirm wire-fraud convictions in technically complex cases. The prosecution typically frames the case through lay-understandable categories — 'did the machine actually work?' 'did you tell investors it did?' 'did you know at the time it didn't?' — and supports those categories with employee testimony, contemporaneous emails, and regulator findings. Juries have repeatedly convicted in such cases. Further, a conviction on even one wire-fraud count in a case of this magnitude would carry a guideline-driven sentence in the 100+ month range under the U.S.S.G. § 2B1.1 loss table. 'A jury won't convict because this is too technical' is a dangerously optimistic assessment.

facts.client_belief: At some point during all this, Y was deposed by the SEC and he took the position under oath that he owned and controlled the financial model. If he said on the record that those were his numbers, that transcript should come into my trial to support my defense — it's basically an admission by him.
facts.court_record: Federal Rule of Evidence 804(b)(3) allows admission of a hearsay statement against the declarant's penal interest only if the statement 'so far tended' to subject the declarant to criminal liability that a reasonable person would not have made it unless it were true — i.e., the statement must 'solidly inculpate' the declarant. Taking ownership of a 'financial model' is not itself criminal; the government's interest was in the fraudulent projections, and in his deposition Y reportedly disclaimed responsibility for the projections themselves while claiming the model. Under the controlling circuit precedent, a statement that is merely exculpatory of the co-defendant, or that equivocates at the seam between lawful and unlawful conduct, is inadmissible under Rule 804(b)(3). The defense theory that the transcript 'should come in' is unlikely to survive a serious evidentiary motion.

facts.client_belief: The indictment talks about tests run on Company A's proprietary machine. But a lot of what the government might try to bring in at trial is about tests run on ordinary third-party machines we modified. That's outside the charges. If they go there, it's a constructive amendment of the indictment.
facts.court_record: Under the controlling circuit constructive-amendment doctrine, an indictment is read 'according to common sense with an appreciation of existing realities,' not in a narrow technical manner. An indictment that charges fraud on investors predicated on how the company performed its patient 'testing services,' combined with an express allegation that the defendants concealed the use of third-party analyzers, will generally be read to encompass evidence about the accuracy of tests on both proprietary and third-party machines. The client's proposed narrow reading — proprietary device only — is unlikely to be accepted as the fair construction of the indictment, and a constructive-amendment challenge on that theory carries real risk of failing.

facts.client_belief: Even if this goes badly, the loss figure will be modest. At the end of the day, the investors still hold Company A shares. Whatever the shares are worth today has to offset any restitution the court orders. So in the worst case, the restitution number should be small — maybe nothing at all.
facts.court_record: Restitution under the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act, 18 U.S.C. § 3663A, in a fraudulent-inducement investment case is generally calculated as the dollars each victim was induced to invest, not the subsequent mark-to-market value of the shares. Under the controlling circuit authority, any credit for 'residual value' requires evidence that the victim was actually able to liquidate those shares at that value — something the holders of closely-held non-public shares in a private company cratered by fraud typically cannot do. Separately, the Guidelines loss calculation under U.S.S.G. § 2B1.1(b)(1) drives the offense level dramatically upward at every $1.5M / $3.5M / $9.5M / $25M / $65M / $150M breakpoint, so the 'loss' number matters at sentencing even when restitution is ultimately collected from other sources. The client's intuition that residual share value will zero-out her exposure is a substantive misunderstanding on both the restitution and the Guidelines fronts.

facts.client_belief: There's also going to be evidence that Y was abusive toward me during the years the fraud is alleged to have happened. That's a defense, or at the very least it should get all of his side of the case severed from mine. I'd rather fight this alone than stand trial next to him.
facts.court_record: The district court severed X's and Y's trials on the basis of X's disclosure of Y's abuse in their personal relationship, and the trials proceeded separately. The court opinion does not analyze or validate a duress or coercion defense to the wire-fraud counts; it addresses the severance only as a procedural background fact. Whether abuse evidence supports a substantive affirmative defense — as opposed to a sentencing mitigator or a factor relevant to the jury's overall assessment — is a separate and legally demanding question that the controlling circuit has not answered in this case. Conflating the grant of severance with a recognition of duress as a defense substantially overstates what the ruling established.

facts.client_belief: Several of our former employees have stayed in close touch with the government and will obviously spin things against me. When we cross-examine them I'm confident we can show they're biased, and that should substantially weaken what they can say about the lab's problems.
facts.court_record: Experienced wire-fraud prosecutors anticipate and preempt credibility attacks by building a corroborated record — contemporaneous emails, Slack messages, meeting notes, regulator findings, and testimony from multiple independent employees whose accounts line up. Impeachment of one witness rarely unwinds the combined force of a corroborated documentary record. Further, recent the controlling circuit evidentiary rulings in comparable cases have limited defense cross-examination into collateral matters about former employees' later careers, on Rule 403 and relevance grounds. The 'we'll just discredit them' playbook materially overestimates what cross-examination can accomplish against a well-built prosecution record.

facts.client_belief: The retail-pharmacy partnership was one of our crown-jewel stories with investors — we told them it was expanding into more stores. That was true from our side: we wanted it to expand and we were working toward that. If the relationship hit some bumps, that's just normal business, not fraud.
facts.court_record: The court opinion records that while X and Y were representing to investors that Company A's partnership with a national retail pharmacy was expanding, the retail-pharmacy representative testified that the partnership was in fact contracting and the pilot program was not going as hoped. the retailer's decision to reduce the number of stores launching Company A's testing services was driven in part by the high percentage of blood draws being performed venously rather than by fingerstick — a direct indicator of the device's limitations. Telling investors the partnership is expanding when internal and counterparty evidence shows it is contracting is a material misrepresentation of present fact, not a forward-looking business aspiration, and the court treated it as part of the broader scheme to defraud investors.

facts.client_belief: Look, even if I'm convicted on something narrow, I've never been in trouble before, I have young children, I'm a first-time offender, and I'd cooperate with a probation officer on everything. I should reasonably expect something well under five years.
facts.court_record: Under the Sentencing Guidelines, the loss amount in a major investor fraud case is the dominant driver of the offense level. For loss in the mid-to-high nine figures, § 2B1.1(b)(1) produces enhancements of 20+ levels on top of the base offense level, and the 'number of victims' enhancement under § 2B1.1(b)(2) adds more. Even after full acceptance-of-responsibility credit and a downward variance, guideline ranges in comparable cases have driven sentences well above five years. First-offender status and family circumstances are relevant § 3553(a) variance arguments but have not historically produced dramatic reductions in cases of this scale. The 'well under five years' expectation is not realistic on present facts.

expected_inquiries: Demand from the client a complete timeline document: every investor call, investor meeting, fund-raising communication, board presentation, and press appearance from 2010 through 2018, with dates, participants, and the primary set of representations made — so that we can independently test every charged misrepresentation against what was contemporaneously known inside the company.

Interview the client under attorney-client privilege about her understanding at each critical juncture of (a) device accuracy and quality-control data, (b) revenue and cash-runway, (c) the status of the government-contract relationship, (d) the status of pharmaceutical validation, (e) the terms of the retail-pharmacy partnership. Document what she was told, when, and by whom, without yet committing to any external-facing narrative.

Collect and review every communication (email, text, encrypted messaging, internal chat, voice memo) between the client and her co-executive, the lab director, the corporate controller, and regulatory-affairs personnel from 2013 through 2016, to understand the universe of contemporaneous warnings the client received and the timing of her responses.

Identify and preserve every piece of evidence bearing on the voluntariness of the decision to void patient test results after the federal regulator's inspection, since that voluntariness determination is the fulcrum for any Rule 407 subsequent-remedial-measure exclusion argument.

Obtain a detailed accounting of the client's prior statements under oath — SEC depositions, civil-litigation depositions, board minutes — and any informal interviews with company counsel or outside counsel, so that we can assess the universe of potential prior-statement impeachment exposure and privilege-waiver risk.

Confirm the precise status of the government's investigation: target letter, subject letter, or witness; whether a grand jury has been empaneled and is active; and the scope of any non-prosecution or cooperation discussions that may already have begun with the co-executive or with former employees — because all of this reshapes the near-term defense posture.

Obtain the federal regulator's inspection record in full, including the underlying inspection notes, all of the client's responses, the patient-impact-assessment working papers, and the internal correspondence with the regulator, because this is a single-document cluster that the prosecution will build a large portion of its state-of-mind case around.

Retain a qualified expert in clinical laboratory operations and a separate expert in statistical analysis of proficiency-test data early, to evaluate the actual scientific merits and to be able to respond to the government's anticipated Rule 702 experts — and to avoid being blindsided by lay-percipient testimony that should properly be treated as expert testimony.

Develop a sentencing-exposure matrix now, at the consultation stage, that shows the client realistic outcomes across conviction on one count vs. multiple counts and across different loss-table findings under § 2B1.1(b)(1), so that any plea-vs-trial decision is made with clear expectations rather than against an optimistic anchor.

Investigate the client's history of intimate-partner abuse with a qualified expert (forensic psychologist or domestic-violence specialist) and preserve that record now, whether it is ultimately deployed as a severance argument, a narrow duress theory, a mitigation theme, or none of those — because retrospective reconstruction of that record becomes harder the longer it is deferred.

Investigate the client's history of intimate-partner abuse with a qualified expert (forensic psychologist or domestic-violence specialist) and preserve that record now, whether it is ultimately deployed as a severance argument, a narrow duress theory, a mitigation theme, or none of those — because retrospective reconstruction of that record becomes harder the longer it is deferred.
memo_expectations: Map each category of alleged misrepresentation (device capabilities; financial health; technology demonstrations; retail-pharmacy partnership; government-contract work; use of third-party devices; pharmaceutical validation) to (a) specific statements attributable to the client, (b) the time each statement was made, and (c) what the internal record showed at that time — the core § 1343 materiality and scienter analysis depends on each of these three-part alignments.

Analyze the mens-rea architecture: direct knowledge of falsity vs. reckless disregard vs. willful blindness, and identify which of the three the government is most likely to argue for each category. Flag the conscious-avoidance jury instruction and the risk profile it creates for the defense.

Assess the viability — and the cost — of a 'visionary founder / puffery / forward-looking statements' defense, including how to avoid letting this framing collapse material present-fact misrepresentations (already-earned revenue figures, already-completed validations, logos placed without consent) into non-actionable puffery.

Frame the realistic U.S.S.G. § 2B1.1 loss calculation across multiple candidate methodologies (aggregate amounts invested; diminution in value; actual loss net of residual value where recoverable), and plot sentencing exposure at each level; then frame realistic restitution exposure under the MVRA including the controlling circuit authority that residual value credit depends on actual realizability.

Analyze Rule 701 / Rule 702 exposure for former-employee lay-opinion testimony about device accuracy, quality-control failures, hemolysis, and proficiency testing — identify where the government is vulnerable to a 'specialized knowledge' objection and where the controlling expert-admissibility standard-style gatekeeping motions could narrow damaging lay testimony.

Evaluate the constructive-amendment theory (proprietary device vs. third-party device) realistically, recognizing that the controlling circuit practice reads indictments with 'common sense,' and decide whether to pursue it as a trial objection, a post-trial motion, or an appellate-preservation exercise rather than a live defense theory.

Assess Rule 804(b)(3) statement-against-interest admissibility of the co-executive's prior SEC deposition testimony, with close attention to the controlling circuit requirement that the statement 'solidly inculpate' the declarant and not merely exculpate the defendant, and identify whether any portion of the testimony actually meets that bar.

Map attorney-client privilege exposure from prior internal-investigation interviews and from communications with counsel retained by the company, distinguishing corporate privilege (held and waivable by the company) from any personal privilege the client may or may not have properly established under the controlling corporate-privilege precedent, and forecast what is recoverable by DOJ if the company decides to cooperate.

Evaluate severance under Rule 14 and the viability of a duress/coercion theory arising from the intimate-partner-abuse record, in light of the controlling circuit's narrow duress standard for long-running, corporate-office conduct, and sequence when (if ever) to raise this as a substantive defense versus a sentencing mitigator.

Build the controlling disclosure precedents checklist for tracking the government's obligations to disclose and correct witness testimony, cooperator agreements, SEC parallel proceedings, and any Jencks-Act materials — and confirm that any preservation objection at trial is made with enough specificity to avoid plain-error review on appeal.

opening: Hi counsel, I'm X. I've been indicted in federal court on some robbery-related charges and I'd like to talk through my options.

facts.client_belief: Between 2001 and 2003 I ran with a small crew — me, Y, and two other guys — and what we did was take money and drugs off people who were dealing. That's just what it was.
facts.court_record: During the 2001–2003 period the client was a member of a crew of approximately four individuals whose specialty was armed robbery of narcotics traffickers, with the objective of stealing drugs and drug proceeds. That role and that timeframe are documented through cooperating witnesses, physical evidence, and the client's own prior admissions, and are not disputed.

facts.client_belief: There were two jobs that ended bad. One was at a house out in the suburbs in late October 2002 — I helped plan it but I wasn't there when it went down. Y shot a woman during that one. The other was an urban apartment job in January 2003 where I was inside the apartment the whole time. Y shot a man during that one too.
facts.court_record: Two of the crew's armed-robbery attempts resulted in homicides. On approximately October 31, 2002, a robbery of a suburban residence resulted in the shooting death of victim S.L. by Y; the client was involved in planning but was not physically present. On approximately January 21, 2003, a robbery of an urban residence resulted in the shooting death of victim G.R. by Y; the client was physically present and an active participant. These dates, locations, and his respective roles are documented and not disputed.

facts.client_belief: The indictment against me right now has a bunch of counts: conspiracy to rob, attempted robbery on both jobs, two firearm counts tied to the urban job — one for firing the gun, one for the guy getting killed — and a marijuana distribution conspiracy count for around 1,000 kilograms or more.
facts.court_record: The operative superseding indictment charges the client with: (i) conspiracy to commit Hobbs Act robbery under 18 U.S.C. § 1951; (ii) two counts of attempted Hobbs Act robbery (one for each of the two residences); (iii) a § 924(c) count for use/carrying/brandishing/discharge of a firearm during the urban residence robbery; (iv) a § 924(j) count for causing death through use of a firearm during the same offense; and (v) a § 846 conspiracy to distribute 1,000 kg or more of marijuana. The charges, statutes, and counts are documented in the indictment and are not disputed.

facts.client_belief: We were robbing drug dealers, not stores or banks. Drug money is dirty money nobody's going to report to the cops anyway. The feds shouldn't have jurisdiction over a street robbery like this — that's a state-level thing.
facts.court_record: The Hobbs Act, 18 U.S.C. § 1951, reaches any robbery or attempted robbery that 'in any way or degree obstructs, delays, or affects' interstate commerce. The controlling circuit and other circuits have uniformly held that robbery of a narcotics trafficker satisfies the jurisdictional element, because narcotics trafficking is itself inherently interstate and any interruption of a drug dealer's operations has at least a de minimis effect on interstate commerce. The 'street robbery' framing therefore does not defeat federal jurisdiction; the client's belief reflects a misunderstanding of the Hobbs Act's reach.

facts.client_belief: The indictment charges me with both conspiracy to rob and attempted robbery for basically the same urban job. That's the exact same robbery twice. They can't stack those — the statute has a 20-year cap and that should be the end of it.
facts.court_record: The Supreme Court's decision in controlling Supreme Court precedent, addressing the federal bank-robbery statute, was expressly narrowed to that statute's 'unique' structure. By contrast, 18 U.S.C. § 3584(a) generally permits consecutive terms for multiple counts imposed at the same sentencing, and the controlling circuit has repeatedly held that 'Congress has not prohibited consecutive sentences for attempts and conspiracies that have the same object.' In practice this means a court may sentence the client to 20 years for the conspiracy count and a second, consecutive 20 years for the attempted-robbery count arising from the same underlying robbery — producing a 40-year exposure on the two Hobbs Act counts alone. The client's belief that a 20-year cap ends the analysis is a legal misconception.

facts.client_belief: For the urban job, Y is the one who pulled the trigger and killed the guy. I had a gun on me but I didn't shoot anybody. So that 'death by firearm' count belongs to Y, not to me.
facts.court_record: Under the controlling co-conspirator-liability precedent and the aiding-and-abetting statute, 18 U.S.C. § 2, a co-conspirator is criminally liable for reasonably foreseeable acts of his co-conspirators committed in furtherance of the conspiracy. Where the crew went armed into a drug dealer's residence intending to forcibly take drugs and money, and where the client himself was armed and physically present inside the residence, the foreseeability of a co-conspirator discharging a firearm and killing an occupant is strong. Both the § 924(c) discharge count and the § 924(j) firearm-murder count can attach to him on an aiding-and-abetting theory even without personally firing the fatal shot. The client's 'not my trigger' framing materially understates his real exposure.

facts.client_belief: The suburban residence robbery — that one I wasn't even there for. I helped with logistics earlier in the week but I was nowhere near the house. They shouldn't be able to hold me responsible for what happened in a room I wasn't in.
facts.court_record: Conspiracy liability does not require physical presence at the scene. Under the co-conspirator-liability doctrine, a co-conspirator is liable for any reasonably foreseeable substantive offense committed by a co-conspirator in furtherance of the conspiracy, whether or not the first co-conspirator was personally present. Participation in planning an armed home invasion of a drug dealer is more than sufficient to trigger the co-conspirator-liability doctrine liability for what the crew did during execution, including a death caused by a co-conspirator's use of a firearm. Physical absence on the night of the offense does not insulate him from criminal responsibility for the foreseeable consequences.

facts.client_belief: Even if I lose on the urban-district robbery itself, it was never 'completed' — we beat up the guy, tied them up, and tossed the apartment, but we didn't actually find drugs or real money there. If it was just an attempt and nothing was actually taken, the sentencing guideline should come down three levels because the crime wasn't finished.
facts.court_record: U.S.S.G. § 2X1.1(b)(1)–(2) provides a three-level reduction for a conspiracy or attempt — but only when the offense did not 'ripen into a substantially completed offense' or 'come close enough to fruition.' Where the crew forcibly entered the residence, physically assaulted and restrained the occupants, interrogated them about the location of drug proceeds, searched the premises, and dispatched another crew member to a follow-on location to continue the search, the conduct came 'close enough to fruition' to defeat the three-level reduction. The fact that no drugs or money were ultimately found at that particular location does not rehabilitate the argument. The client's belief that 'we didn't get anything so it doesn't count fully' misunderstands how § 2X1.1 actually applies.

facts.client_belief: On the drug count, they're charging me with over a thousand kilos of weed. I never personally moved that much — that's way more than I ever dealt with myself. The amount I'm on the hook for should be whatever I can be shown to have actually touched, not the whole crew's total. That's just piling everything on me.
facts.court_record: Conspiracy liability for drug quantity under 21 U.S.C. §§ 841(b)(1)(A) and 846 extends to all drug quantities that were reasonably foreseeable to the defendant as part of the conspiracy. The quantity to which the client is exposed at sentencing is the full aggregate marijuanthe conspiracy trafficked, subject to reasonable foreseeability — not only the quantity he personally handled. In a long-running multi-year crew operation targeting wholesale-level narcotics traffickers, even a relatively modest personal role can fall within a conspiracy whose aggregate falls far above the 1,000 kg threshold. The client's 'what I personally touched' framing is an under-read of the statute.

facts.client_belief: I have an older federal case from a few years back involving a conspiracy to rob drug dealers — same kind of activity as what they're charging me with now. So that prior case is really just part of the same course of conduct and can't be counted again in my criminal history score.
facts.court_record: Under U.S.S.G. § 4A1.2(a)(1) and § 1B1.3, a prior offense counts toward criminal-history score unless it is part of the 'same course of conduct' or 'common scheme or plan' as the instant offense. Courts analyzing this test look at temporal proximity, common leadership, common victims, common modus operandi, and common objectives. A prior drug-robbery conspiracy that ended before the current one began, had different leadership, different crew composition, and a materially different modus operandi (for example, prior crew impersonated police officers; current crew did not), will typically be treated as a distinct offense for criminal-history purposes — even where both involve robbery of narcotics traffickers. The client's intuition that 'same type of crime' equals 'same course of conduct' is not how the Guidelines actually work.

facts.client_belief: There's also a state-court conviction I picked up a while back for an attempted robbery in another urban district. That was a totally different situation, but one of the guys from my current crew was involved too. Since there's overlap with the same person, that state case should also get absorbed into this federal matter.
facts.court_record: Shared identity of a single co-conspirator does not convert two otherwise-separate offenses into a 'common scheme or plan' under § 4A1.2(a)(1). Courts look at whether two offenses occurred at the same time and place, targeted overlapping victims, involved common objectives, and shared a common modus operandi. A prior single-victim attempted-robbery conviction — even one involving a handgun later seized and offered as evidence in the instant case — will not be deemed the same course of conduct as an ongoing drug-trafficker robbery conspiracy if the underlying criminal episodes are separated in time, place, victims, and core purpose. The prior state conviction is likely to be counted in criminal history notwithstanding the co-conspirator overlap.

facts.client_belief: The firearm counts are where I'm most worried. But I've been reading that the Supreme Court has been cracking down on what the government can use as a 'crime of violence' to hang gun charges on, and a robbery conspiracy doesn't count as one anymore. So those gun charges should fall apart.
facts.court_record: The client is correct that Supreme Court decisions (United States v. Y; controlling Supreme Court precedent) have narrowed what qualifies as a 'crime of violence' predicate under § 924(c), and that Hobbs Act conspiracy and attempted Hobbs Act robbery are no longer categorical 'crimes of violence.' However, that observation addresses only the § 924(c) and § 924(j) counts, and only if the government is unable to anchor those counts to another valid predicate (for example, a completed Hobbs Act robbery or another qualifying offense). Further, the controlling predicate precedents line produces relief through post-conviction litigation under 28 U.S.C. § 2255 in many cases — a longer and more contingent path than trial-level dismissal. Importantly, stripping out the § 924(c) and § 924(j) counts does not reduce exposure on the remaining counts: the first-degree-murder cross-reference under U.S.S.G. § 2B3.1(c) and § 2A1.1 can still drive a life-imprisonment Guidelines calculation for the Hobbs Act convictions themselves, and the drug conspiracy mandatory minimums remain unchanged. The client's assumption that 'the firearm counts fall, and that changes the whole case' substantially overstates the systemic impact of those doctrines.

facts.client_belief: Best case, if I lose on everything, I'm looking at maybe twenty years — that's the Hobbs Act cap. Anything on top of that for the murder piece has to go away once I beat the firearm counts.
facts.court_record: Even without the § 924(c) and § 924(j) counts, the Guidelines include a cross-reference at U.S.S.G. § 2B3.1(c) that, where a victim was killed under circumstances that would constitute first-degree murder, bumps the offense level to the first-degree-murder Guideline at § 2A1.1 — offense level 43, which produces a life-imprisonment Guidelines range standing alone. A court can then impose consecutive statutory-maximum terms across the Hobbs Act conspiracy count (20 years), the attempt count (20 years), and the drug conspiracy count (up to 40 years), yielding an aggregate statutory cap well above any single-count maximum. The client's 'twenty years, that's the cap' projection reflects a fundamental misread of how the Guidelines, the cross-reference, and consecutive sentencing operate together.

facts.client_belief: If the government never actually proves I planned to hurt anybody — I was there for the money, not a murder — the first-degree-murder enhancement shouldn't apply. Intent to kill wasn't in the plan.
facts.court_record: The Guidelines § 2B3.1(c) cross-reference to first-degree-murder applies where 'a victim was killed under circumstances that would constitute first-degree murder,' and a sentencing court applying this in the conspiracy context asks whether killing was within the scope of the agreement or reasonably foreseeable in furtherance of it. Particularized findings that (i) the crew went armed with loaded guns, (ii) the client knew guns were loaded and available, (iii) the co-conspirators relayed a specific plan to kill the target in advance, and (iv) there was 'no riskier activity than going into a den of narcotics criminals and seeking to take away their drugs and their money' will support applying the cross-reference even where the client personally did not intend the killing. The belief that 'I didn't plan a murder' forecloses the enhancement is incorrect.

facts.client_belief: Two of the guys on my crew are going to cooperate with the government and point fingers at me and Y to save themselves. Juries don't trust rats. If my lawyer cross-examines them hard, the jury won't believe them and the case falls apart.
facts.court_record: The controlling circuit's standard jury instructions explicitly permit conviction on the uncorroborated testimony of a cooperator, provided the jury is instructed to scrutinize such testimony with care. In practice, experienced federal prosecutors build cooperator-based cases on a foundation of independent corroboration — phone records, physical evidence, surveillance, forensic evidence, other witnesses — precisely so that impeachment of any single cooperator does not collapse the case. A successful cross-examination can meaningfully affect sentencing or the willingness of a juror to credit a specific detail, but it rarely dismantles a corroborated multi-witness case. The client's intuition that the case 'falls apart' on cross is materially optimistic.

facts.client_belief: If it comes to it, I'd rather take my chances at trial on everything than plead to anything involving the murder. There's a difference between being in a robbery crew and being labeled a murderer for the rest of my life. If I go to trial on everything, at worst I'm in the same place I would be on a plea.
facts.court_record: This framing omits the trial-penalty reality of federal sentencing. A defendant who goes to trial and is convicted on all counts loses: (i) the two- or three-level acceptance-of-responsibility reduction under U.S.S.G. § 3E1.1; (ii) any prospect of a § 5K1.1 motion based on cooperation (which is the single largest downward driver in cases of this character); and (iii) the ability to negotiate dismissal of counts with the highest exposure, such as the § 924(j) firearm-murder count. The sentencing delta between 'convicted on everything at trial' and 'plead with full cooperation' in a case of this severity is routinely measured in decades, not years. 'Same place either way' is not an accurate representation of the plea vs. trial posture.

facts.client_belief: I heard that if the jury finds me not guilty on one of the robbery attempts, the judge can't hold that against me at sentencing. So even if I lose on other counts, if I beat the suburban-residence charge, that whole incident should be off the table when it comes to sentencing.
facts.court_record: Under longstanding Supreme Court precedent (controlling Supreme Court precedent), a sentencing court could historically consider acquitted conduct so long as it was proved by a preponderance of the evidence. A recent amendment to the Sentencing Guidelines (a recent Guidelines amendment to § 1B1.3(c)) excludes acquitted-federal-court conduct from the definition of relevant conduct prospectively, but — and this is the point most often missed — whether that amendment applies depends on whether it is in effect at the time of sentencing and whether it applies retroactively. In addition, even excluded acquitted conduct can resurface through co-conspirator testimony about the broader conspiracy. The client's belief that an acquittal fully erases related conduct from the sentencing picture is significantly more optimistic ththe doctrine warrants.

expected_inquiries: Obtain the full operative superseding indictment and the government's draft bill of particulars (or request one) to lock down the precise theory of liability on each count — particularly the predicate-offense theory for the § 924(c) and § 924(j) counts, because that shapes every subsequent motion.

Interview the client in detail about each of the two residence robberies: who planned each one, when and where planning occurred, who was armed and with what, who entered, who stayed outside, what was said to and about the victims, what was searched for, and what was actually taken — to map the co-conspirator-liability doctrine-foreseeability exposure and § 2X1.1 completion arguments.

Elicit from the client his full understanding of prior crew communications about the urban-robbery victim — specifically, whether any co-conspirator articulated a plan to kill the target in advance, and whether client heard or was told about such discussions — because that fact is central to the § 2B3.1(c) first-degree-murder cross-reference.

Obtain and review the client's full prior-conviction file: the prior federal robbery-conspiracy indictment, plea, presentence report, and judgment; and the state attempted-robbery conviction file, to evaluate the same-course-of-conduct analysis under § 4A1.2(a)(1) with concrete record support rather than generalities.

Identify and proffer-shield any known cooperating co-conspirators whose testimony the government will use, and obtain their cooperation agreements, § 5K1.1 letters, and prior proffer statements through Jencks Act, Giglio, and Rule 26.2 requests at the appropriate stage.

Request from the government a complete list of all firearms the crew used during each charged incident, the ballistics and recovery provenance for each, and the § 924(c)/§ 924(j) predicate theory of each firearm count — so that any the controlling predicate precedents-based motion to dismiss is properly founded on the government's actual theory.

Evaluate whether a pretrial suppression motion is viable for any seized firearm, any statement taken from the client, or any identification procedure used, because suppression of a specific piece of evidence can materially alter the leverage on certain counts.

Begin an early cooperation-posture assessment: assuming the client has information to offer about other, unindicted actors or about the broader narcotics distribution ecosystem, the value of a § 5K1.1 motion at sentencing is often the single largest variable in cases of this magnitude and must be evaluated clearly and soon, not at the eve of trial.

Retain a Guidelines-focused sentencing consultant early to model the offense-level calculation under each plausible conviction scenario, including the § 2B3.1(c) cross-reference, the § 2X1.1 reduction, the acceptance-of-responsibility reduction, and the client's criminal-history category on alternate treatments of the prior convictions.

Advise the client explicitly, in writing and with him initialing, on the realistic trial-penalty delta versus a pretrial resolution, so there is a clear contemporaneous record that every plea-vs-trial decision was made with full understanding of the Guidelines mathematics and cooperation mechanics.

Map the full set of exposure multipliers: consecutive vs. concurrent sentencing for conspiracy and attempt arising from the same underlying robbery under 18 U.S.C. § 3584(a); consecutive exposure on the drug conspiracy count; and the interaction with any § 924(c)/§ 924(j) consecutive-term statutory requirements.

Assess the co-conspirator-liability doctrine and aiding-and-abetting liability theories as applied to (i) the suburban residence robbery the client did not personally attend, and (ii) the urban residence shooting by a co-conspirator — with particular attention to foreseeability of firearm use and of death as the natural and probable consequence of an armed home invasion of a drug dealer.

Evaluate § 924(c) and § 924(j) predicate-validity under United States v. Y and controlling Supreme Court precedent, identify which predicate offenses in the indictment remain categorically 'crimes of violence,' and assess whether firearm counts could be dismissed pre-trial on predicate-invalidity grounds.

Evaluate the U.S.S.G. § 2B3.1(c) cross-reference to first-degree murder under § 2A1.1: identify the particularized findings the court would need to make to apply the cross-reference, and the factual record the government will develop to support those findings (armed approach, knowledge of loaded firearms, prior communication of lethal intent, inherent risk of armed invasion of drug dealers).

Assess eligibility for the U.S.S.G. § 2X1.1(b)(1)–(2) three-level conspiracy/attempt reduction on each of the two robberies, focusing on how close each robbery came to fruition — including physical entry, restraint of occupants, interrogation, search, and directed follow-on actions — and advise on the realistic prospects.

Analyze how the prior federal robbery-conspiracy conviction and the prior state attempted-robbery conviction will be scored in criminal history under U.S.S.G. § 4A1.2(a)(1) and § 1B1.3, applying the same-course-of-conduct / common-scheme test to temporal proximity, leadership, objectives, victims, and modus operandi.

Build a realistic plea-vs-trial sentencing matrix: (i) conviction on all counts at trial without § 3E1.1 credit; (ii) plea to a subset of counts with acceptance of responsibility; (iii) plea with cooperation and a § 5K1.1 motion — with the delta between these scenarios clearly identified so the client can make an informed choice.

Analyze drug-quantity attribution on Count Eight under 21 U.S.C. § 841(b)(1)(A): identify the reasonably-foreseeable aggregate to which the client is exposed, the 1,000 kg threshold, and the resulting statutory mandatory minimum and Guidelines calculation.

Assess the status and retroactivity of any U.S.S.G. amendments affecting treatment of acquitted conduct under § 1B1.3(c), and separately analyze whether acquitted-conduct evidence can still reach the sentencing picture through co-conspirator testimony about the broader conspiracy even if excluded from formal relevant-conduct calculation.
